title: Sky Safari horizon exporter (image-based PNG)
description: Add to_skysafari_png(rows) exporter. Sky Safari's custom horizon is a rendered image, not a point list: PNG spanning azimuth 0-360 across width and altitude -90..+90 across height, horizon drawn as a line with everything below opaque. We already have the mask as az->altitude and depend on PIL, so render the silhouette at Sky Safari's expected dimensions/convention. Wire into export_all and CLI export. Third target after N.I.N.A. (.hrz) and Stellarium (.txt).
design: PIL. Map az->x (0-360 across width), alt->y (-90 top .. +90 bottom or per SkySafari convention - verify). Interpolate the mask across full width. Opaque below the horizon line, transparent above.
acceptance_criteria: PNG produced at correct dimensions; horizon line matches mask; loads in Sky Safari as a horizon; unit test on output size + a below/above-line pixel.
notes: Cleaner-image option (Devon): instead of relying on the scope's blurry/narrow-FOV frames for the Sky Safari picture, let the user supply a phone PANORAMA of their horizon (like the ones Devon shot). The scope sweep provides the accurate az/alt horizon LINE; register/map the panorama to the measured points (horizon line + a few az/alt fiducials) to warp the pano into Sky Safari's 0-360 x -90..+90 image space. Result: a photo-real, in-focus, true-coordinate-aligned horizon image. So Sky Safari export has two modes: (a) synthetic silhouette rendered from the mask, (b) panorama-mapped photo. The scope stays the source of geometric truth; the pano is just prettier pixels.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
CONVENTION SETTLED FROM VENDOR DOCUMENTATION 2026-08-05 — this ticket is no longer blocked on your judgement for the format.

The ticket said 'or per SkySafari convention - verify'. Simulation Curriculum's own support documentation states it exactly:

  PNG, 32-bit RGBA (8 bits per channel), 2048 x 1024.
  HORIZONTAL: 360 deg of azimuth. North (0) at the LEFT edge, east (90) a
    quarter across, south (180) halfway, west (270) three quarters, wrapping
    to north again at the right edge.
  VERTICAL: 180 deg of altitude. Zenith +90 at the TOP, horizon 0 at the
    MIDDLE, nadir -90 at the BOTTOM.
  ALPHA IS REQUIRED and is the actual mechanism: opaque = ground, trees,
    buildings; transparent = sky. The alpha channel is what SkySafari reads
    as the horizon, not a drawn line.
  IMPORT: Settings -> Horizon & Sky -> 'Show Horizon & Sky as Panoramic
    Image', then pick the file from the Panorama Horizon list.

Sources: support.simulationcurriculum.com (SkySafari 6/7 Pro panorama articles), corroborated by nightskymiddleton.uk's walkthrough which independently gives 2048x1024 PNG and the same import path.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS TICKET: that is the SAME equirectangular layout as Stellarium's spherical maptex (terminus-26), modulo the altitude direction. So one renderer serves both exporters and our mosaic output is already in this projection — cmd_skymask reads it as alt = 90 - (y/h)*180, which is exactly this mapping. Mode (b), the panorama-mapped photo, is therefore nearly free: the mosaic PNG is already the texture and coverage.npy is already the alpha.

WHAT STILL NEEDS YOU, and it is now small: the acceptance criterion 'loads in Sky Safari'. I can assert dimensions, that the horizon line matches the mask, and that a pixel above the line is transparent while one below is opaque. I cannot open the app. That is a two-minute check on your phone once the file exists, not a design decision.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
SHIPPED as PR #17 (dac8ae8), after three review rounds.

to_skysafari_png writes a 2048x1024 RGBA PNG in the vendor's convention: north at the left edge increasing east, zenith +90 at the top through 0 at the middle to -90 at the bottom, and ALPHA as the horizon — opaque is ground, transparent is sky. That last point is the one the ticket's design note would have got wrong: 'horizon drawn as a line with everything below opaque' describes a line, and neither program reads one. Nothing is painted; the region below the horizon is filled. A silhouette on an opaque background imports as a completely blocked sky.

MODE (b) FROM YOUR NOTE CAME ALONG FOR FREE. Pass --texture with the mosaic PNG and --coverage with its .npy and the panorama becomes the picture, rotated into true azimuth first. Where coverage is zero the pixel is transparent, so the part of the canvas the phone never pointed at shows as sky rather than as black ground nobody photographed. The scope stays the source of geometric truth: the measured horizon bounds the opaque region even with a texture, and where picture and mask disagree the mask wins.

Same renderer serves terminus-26. That is why the two landed together.

WHAT IS TESTED: dimensions, RGBA mode, that a column's boundary sits at its measured altitude, that alpha is strictly 0 or 255 with no partial values to misread, that x and y run the right way (the assertions fail if either axis flips), that uncovered columns are transparent, and that the picture is drawn from the same buffered numbers as the .hrz beside it.

WHAT STILL NEEDS YOU, and it is only this: your acceptance criterion 'loads in Sky Safari'. I cannot open the app. Everything about the file is asserted; whether the app accepts it is a two-minute check on your phone. If it does, close this. If it does not, the bug report I would want is which of the four — dimensions, mode, orientation, alpha — looks wrong on screen.

title: Sweep: sky reference goes stale across a multi-hour run
description:
CAUGHT LIVE 2026-08-03 mid-sweep, before it did damage.

BUG. run_sweep seeds sky_ref ONCE from a near-zenith frame before the column loop, then passes that same value to every column. A full circle at 10 deg spacing takes 3-4 hours. Across twilight the sky itself changes by orders of magnitude while the reference stays pinned at its daylight value.

CONSEQUENCE. The blocked test is 'median < 0.5 * sky_ref'. With sky_ref = 254 that threshold is 127. Once genuinely open sky falls below 127 — which it does shortly after sunset — EVERY remaining column reports blocked_above. The sweep would run to completion and return a mask claiming an entire hemisphere is obstructed, with no error and no warning. Same class as the auto-exposure failure: a stale reference silently makes everything look dark.

EVIDENCE IT HAD NOT YET FIRED. At the moment of the catch, high-altitude samples read: az 0-30 lum 63-105 (the tall tree, correctly dark) and az 40-70 lum 248-253 (open sky, still matching the 254 reference). So columns 0-60 from part 1 are sound; the failure was pending, not past.

FIX APPLIED. SKY_REF_MAX_AGE = 420 s. Inside the column loop, if the reference is older than that, re-point to (Sun azimuth + 180, alt 75), re-measure, and log 'sky reference refreshed: OLD -> NEW'. Failure to refresh keeps the old value and resets the timer rather than aborting the run. Costs one extra pointing per ~7 minutes, roughly 15% more wall clock.

ALSO WORTH DOING: log the reference alongside every column so a saved run can be re-judged with the reference that was actually in force, and consider deriving a per-column reference from that column's own brightest sample when it clearly contains sky (free, adapts automatically); the external reference is only strictly needed for fully blocked columns.

RELATED: this is the third silent-failure-by-stale-or-unverified-state bug today (exposure lock not taking, goto not arriving, heater set_setting ignored). Worth a general rule in terminus: every state-changing scope call verifies its readback, and every cached measurement carries an age.
close_reason: PR #1: SKY_REF_MAX_AGE refreshes the open-sky reference every 420s inside the column loop.

title: Split responsibilities: scope measures altitude, photos identify obstructions
description:
ESTABLISHED 2026-08-03 from focus geometry plus Devon's site constraint.

THE SCOPE CAN NEVER RESOLVE A HORIZON FEATURE. Seestar S50 is 250mm f/4.9 focused at infinity, so the hyperfocal distance is H = f^2/(N*c) = 250^2/(4.9*0.003mm) ~ 4.3 km. Devon: 'from where the telescope is, there's literally no line of sight on anything farther than a house across the street except the sky' — every terrestrial target is within ~50 m, three orders of magnitude inside that limit. This is geometry, not a focus error, and no setting fixes it.

MEASURED CONFIRMATION across 130+ scan frames: gradient p99 runs 0.73-1.34 (best single frame 2.55); a focused frame would be in the tens. The spread tracks CONTENT not range — the 'blurriest' frames are saturated open sky (lum 253.4, nothing to resolve) and the 'sharpest' are terrain with real brightness structure. There is no azimuth where the view sharpens.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DESIGN. The two instruments are complementary, not redundant, and neither is a fallback for the other:
  * SCOPE measures ALTITUDE — accurate, in true az/alt, at night, no registration needed. It cannot identify anything.
  * PHOTOS identify TYPE — SegFormer already returns tree/building/fence/railing per pixel because phone frames are in focus. Their absolute orientation must be borrowed from the scope.

ACTION: the mask should carry BOTH — altitude from the scope, obstruction type from the photo segmentation, each labelled with its source. The existing obstruction_type() veg-vs-structure tag infers from colour blobs in a blurred frame and is unreliable by construction (it already degrades to 'structure' for everything after sunset); it should be demoted to a hint or dropped once photo-derived types are available.

WHY IT MATTERS PRACTICALLY: a deciduous tree's horizon changes between summer and winter; a roofline does not. Knowing which columns are 'tree' tells the user which to re-measure seasonally and which are permanent — and that is a planning feature, not a cosmetic label.
close_reason: Shipped across PRs #1, #4, #6 and #9. The split is the architecture now: photographs are the mask (mosaic registration, SegFormer segmentation, skymask.segment_classes carrying obstruction TYPE into the export) and the telescope is the calibration (orient.fit solving yaw/pitch/tilt from a handful of measured columns, plan choosing them by information gain). All five modules are exported from the package API and two are on the CLI. NOTE the premise has since been narrowed: terminus-32 found the scope CAN autofocus in scenery mode and resolve terrestrial detail, so 'the scope cannot identify obstructions' is true of infinity focus rather than of the instrument, and the two sources become cross-checkable. That is tracked there, not here.

title: Scenery RTSP stream freezes on long runs, returning identical frames
description:
OBSERVED 2026-08-03 ~22:00 after ~3.1 hours of continuous scenery view (lapse_ms 11.2M).

SYMPTOM. capture_rgb returns a BYTE-IDENTICAL frame regardless of pointing:
  az 120 alt 70 -> p99 2.67 mean 0.76
  az 300 alt 45 -> p99 2.67 mean 0.76
  az 300 alt  5 -> p99 2.67 mean 0.76
Zenith and ground give the same numbers. get_view_state reports state 'working', mode 'scenery' — the scope believes it is fine. stop_view + start_view did NOT clear it.

DAMAGE DONE. The western arc (az 260-350) was recorded as blocked_above 60 for 8 of 10 columns because every frame read 0.8. That fabricated ~100 degrees of obstruction out of open sky, and when those columns were added to the orientation fit it moved yaw from a stable 130 to 70, pitch to -17.7, tilt to 21.2, RMS 10.3. Devon spotted it immediately as implausible ('going up to 140 degrees from 40? only with new nighttime measurements? color me skeptical') — the fit blowing up was the confirmation.

VERIFIED NOT the same as the earlier state: at ~20:45 the same pointings gave az 300 alt 50 = 11.25, alt 10 = 0.09, az 120 alt 50 = 5.52 — real, position-dependent values with >100:1 sky/terrain contrast. So night measurement WORKS; the stream degraded later.

LIKELY CONTRIBUTORS: (a) a scenery view left running for hours, (b) concurrent control connections — the Seestar tolerates only ONE, and this session repeatedly attached diagnostic scripts while a sweep held the socket, which also produced 'cannot read current pointing' and a BrokenPipeError.

FIXES NEEDED:
  1. DETECT IT. Hash or compare consecutive frames: if a capture is identical to the previous one after the mount has moved, the stream is stale. Refuse to record a measurement rather than emitting blocked_above. Partial work exists — capture_rgb now retries when a frame is essentially black — but that does not catch a frozen NON-black frame, which is the general case.
  2. RECOVER. Periodically restart the view on long runs, and on detection try stop_view/start_view then a full reconnect; if the frame is still identical, abort the run with a clear error instead of continuing.
  3. SERIALISE ACCESS. One connection only. A sweep should hold a lock; diagnostics should read the log, not the scope.
  4. INVESTIGATE exp_ms: get_view_state reports exp_ms 240.0 while get_setting reports isp_exp_ms 20.0. The setting we verify is not the exposure the camera uses, which also explains why lock_exposure appears to clamp every requested value. See seestar_alp for how the view's own exposure is set.

DATA STATUS: part1 (az 0-70) and part2 (az 70-250 incl. refinement) are GOOD — 26 columns taken in daylight and twilight with position-dependent values. part3/part3b (az 260-350) are void and must be re-measured.
close_reason: PR #1: capture_rgb rejects a frame identical to the previous one. Note it deliberately does NOT reject dark frames — unlit terrain reads 0.09 counts while the frozen frames read 0.8, so darkness cannot separate them.

title: Mask carries obstruction type from the instrument that cannot determine it
description:
SPOTTED BY DEVON 2026-08-03: 'note, 6 of the 9 are trees, so I think 2 models would be good here' — while the residual table showed all four large disagreements as 'structure'. The counts differ because two different labels are in play, and the one being displayed is the untrustworthy one.

THE BUG. sweep.obstruction_type() infers vegetation from green/yellow dominance in a scope frame. That frame is (a) a blur — 250mm f/4.9 focused at infinity, every terrestrial target three orders of magnitude inside the ~4.3 km hyperfocal distance — and (b) after sunset, a neutral silhouette. So at night it labels essentially everything 'structure', which is what the report showed. The mask stores that as the column's type and downstream code uses it.

Meanwhile SegFormer on the in-focus phone frames returns real semantic classes (tree / building / fence / railing) and is the label Devon was reading off the imagery. His 6-of-9-are-trees is from the reliable source; the table was from the unreliable one.

FIX: type comes from photo segmentation, altitude comes from the scope, and each field records its source. obstruction_type() should be demoted to a daylight-only hint or removed once segmentation types are available. This is the instrument split already filed separately — the scope measures where the boundary is and cannot say what it is.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TWO-MODEL WORK. BOUNDARY_MODELS (tree vs structure: different repeats, run length, SNR gate, expected transition width, export buffer) currently keys off the scope's type, so at night every column silently gets the 'structure' model — including the tree columns that most need the vegetation one. Wiring the photo's class in is what makes the two-model split actually operate.

ALSO, AND NOT YET DONE: if 6 of 9 visible errors sit at tree boundaries, the same split is needed in the PHOTO pipeline. skymask.horizon_rows applies one rule (first sustained run of non-sky) to canopy and roofline alike. horizon_band already measures the canopy's porosity and extent; the extraction should use the vegetation-aware path where segmentation says tree, and the sharp-edge path elsewhere.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
PART 1 IN PR #15 (unreviewed, opened at a deliberate stopping point).

Done: obstruction_type returns '' below the horizon instead of 'structure', Sun altitude is re-read per column so a sweep crossing sunset does not let its late columns inherit a daylight claim, and the mask records type_source per column (photo | scope). Also fixed a latent bug found on the way — load_columns coerced every optional field with float(), so the first string-valued field was unreadable.

STILL OPEN, and both larger than part 1:

1. BOUNDARY_MODELS is defined but never called. The ticket says wiring the photo's class in is what makes the two-model split operate, but nothing calls boundary_model() in the scan at all yet, so this is a feature rather than a rewiring.

2. The photo pipeline's own split. skymask.horizon_rows applies one rule (first sustained run of non-sky) to canopy and roofline alike. horizon_band already measures gap fraction and extent, so the pieces exist.

NEEDS YOUR JUDGEMENT — one thing I could not settle:

The daylight gate is Sun altitude > 0, which is where direct illumination stops and is not a tuned number. But it is not the whole problem: for some minutes either side of sunset the light is strongly reddened, which pushes r and g above b across the WHOLE frame and biases the vegetation test the other way — the opposite error from the night one, and this fix does not catch it. Nobody has measured how wide that window is.

Two ways to settle it, your call:
(a) Measure it. A colour target or a known wall photographed through the scope from Sun alt +10 down to -2 would give the real boundary, and then the gate is evidence rather than a principle.
(b) Sidestep it. Gate on the frame's own colour saturation instead of the Sun: if the obstruction pixels are near-neutral, colour is not evidence regardless of where the Sun is. Self-calibrating, catches night AND reddened sunset AND backlit daytime branches. Costs a fifth return value from classify(), which has five call sites.

(b) is better engineering and I would default to it, but it changes classify()'s contract and I did not want to do that unreviewed while stopping.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
PART 1 MERGED as PR #15 (2a5bd33), after three review rounds.

WHAT LANDED. obstruction_type returns '' below the horizon instead of 'structure'; Sun altitude is re-read per column, guarded, falling back to the last known value rather than to None; the mask records type_source per column; load_columns types each optional field individually; boundary_model refuses an unnamed column rather than defaulting it to the wall rule; and a merge now combines a column field by field rather than replacing it wholesale.

THAT LAST ONE WAS THE INTERESTING BUG, and it only existed because terminus-5 and this ticket landed in the same week. A targeted re-measure at 2 a.m. of a column the photo had segmented as 'tree' overwrote it with type: '' — the scope cannot name anything after sunset — so a real in-focus segmentation was discarded by a measurement that had nothing to say about type, and the column then exported without its seasonal buffer. A re-measure that exists to improve a column made it worse. The rule now: altitude is the scope's answer and the fresh one always wins; type is whichever instrument could actually name it, so a fresh naming replaces an old one and a fresh silence does not. Same logic sorted the photo fields: gap_fraction and uncertainty describe the OBSTRUCTION and survive; clipped describes the ALTITUDE and is dropped once the scope supplies a real crossing.

STILL OPEN ON THIS TICKET, unchanged:
1. BOUNDARY_MODELS is defined but never called. Wiring it into the scan is a feature, not a rewiring.
2. The photo pipeline's own split — skymask.horizon_rows applies one rule to canopy and roofline alike.

SPUN OUT: terminus-48 (orient.from_mask matches type strings no writer produces — returns zero fiducials for every real mask, and __init__.py documents it as the worked example) and terminus-49 (an unnamed column loses the vegetation buffer it probably deserves — a decision for you, three options written up).

STILL NEEDS YOUR JUDGEMENT, unchanged from before: the daylight gate is Sun alt > 0, which does not catch the reddening window either side of sunset. Measure it, or sidestep it by gating on the frame's own colour saturation.

title: find_edge noise estimate counts the sky gradient as noise
description:
FOUND 2026-08-03 23:50 while measuring bright western columns after polar realignment.

BUG. find_edge estimates noise as the mean absolute difference between CONSECUTIVE samples. Under light pollution the open sky is not flat with altitude — skyglow brightens toward the horizon, measured at az 300 rising 36.9 at alt 60 to 73.7 at alt 11. That smooth gradient enters the noise estimate, inflating the denominator, so a real step is divided by the trend it sits on and fails the SNR gate.

MEASURED ON FIVE SAVED PROFILES (step / noise_1stdiff / noise_2nddiff / snr_now / snr_fixed):
  az 300  19.9   9.44  0.75   2.11  26.6
  az 310  35.1   6.53  0.54   5.37  64.5
  az 320  15.8  10.78  2.65   1.47   6.0
  az 340   9.8   6.78  0.88   1.44  11.0
  az 350   3.7   2.42  0.82   1.53   4.5
True scatter is 0.5-2.7 counts; the current estimator reports 2.4-10.8. Four of five columns were rejected as 'no edge' purely because of this.

FIX DIRECTION: estimate scatter from SECOND differences (median |x[i+2]-2x[i+1]+x[i]| / sqrt(6)), which is blind to any linear trend, or from residuals after removing the fitted two-level model.

DO NOT SHIP THAT ALONE — IT IS THEN TOO PERMISSIVE. With a noise floor under 1 count, trivial steps clear the gate: az 350 'passes' at SNR 4.5 on a step of 3.7 counts against a sky reference of 19.7, i.e. a 19 percent wobble in the skyglow gradient rather than a horizon. A SECOND gate is needed on ABSOLUTE step size relative to the current sky reference (a step of >= ~25 percent of sky_ref would admit 300/310/320/340 and reject 350). The existing EDGE_SNR is scale-free and therefore cannot express 'were there enough photons'.

ALSO UNRESOLVED, DO NOT ADOPT THE NEW NUMBERS YET: with the fixed estimator az 340 and az 350 come out at 10.0 deg, while tonight's western sweep recorded both as blocked_above 60 and the photo mosaic puts them near 56. Three sources disagree. The saved frames for all of these exist under captures/2026-08-03-night-targeted/scan/, so this can be settled offline by inspection before any refit.
notes:
CORRECTION TO THIS TICKET (00:05, same night). The severity above is overstated and the diagnosis was partly wrong.

The trend-insensitivity argument is sound, but my demonstration used the MEDIAN of second differences, which is robust to large excursions — and in a scatter-only profile those excursions ARE the noise. That is the wrong kind of robustness: it discounted real scatter and made the gradient look responsible. It also broke the existing regression test (a 2026-08-02 auto-exposure column of pure scatter started passing as an edge), which is exactly what that test exists to catch.

REDONE PROPERLY with RMS of second differences (trend-insensitive, but not outlier-insensitive), plus the absolute step floor:
  az 200 -> 35.0  snr 3.25  step 22.4
  az 310 -> 15.0  snr 4.10  step 35.1
  az 300 -> no edge, snr 2.42 (marginal)
  az 320/340/350 -> no edge, snr 1.2-1.4
  az 10/30 -> no edge, NEGATIVE step: uniformly dark, correctly the tree
For az 300 the RMS second-difference noise is 8.2 against the first-difference estimate of 9.44 — near-identical. THE PROFILES ARE GENUINELY NOISY, NOT MERELY TRENDING. The fix recovers nothing.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE: at a sky reference near 20 counts the measurements are too noisy for reliable edge detection except where the step is very large. Only the two strongest columns survive. This is the same limit that produced 'no edge' at az 180 and az 50 earlier — insufficient absolute signal, seen now in the bright northwest as well as the dark south.

KEEP THE CODE CHANGE ANYWAY: trend-insensitive noise plus a minimum absolute step is more defensible than a first-difference estimate with no floor, and all 47 tests pass including the scatter regression. Just do not expect it to rescue faint columns.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
SAME ERROR CLASS FOUND IN night.find_horizon, filed as terminus-47 (P0) and worth fixing and
testing alongside this one.

This bead: find_edge's noise estimate is computed over a region that includes the sky gradient it
is trying to detect against, so the gradient inflates the noise floor.

terminus-47: fit_skyglow is handed the whole column including terrain, so the terrain sets the
model slope, and the model that is supposed to describe SKY ends up describing the column. It then
cannot see a 103-count cliff.

Both are the same mistake in different clothes — estimating a reference statistic over a region
that contains the signal, which drags the reference toward the signal and hides it. The general
fix is the same in both places: estimate the reference from the region KNOWN to be background (the
top of the column), not from everything. Fixing one without the other leaves the pipeline with the
identical failure one function away.

title: stop_view does not reliably stop the scenery view
description:
OBSERVED 2026-08-04 00:30. Three consecutive stop_view calls, three seconds apart, each followed by get_view_state reporting state='working' mode='scenery'. The view had been up about 1.4 hours at that point.

WHY IT MATTERS: a scenery view left running for hours is the condition that preceded the frozen RTSP stream earlier the same night, which served one stale frame regardless of pointing and fabricated ten blocked columns before it was caught. If the view cannot be stopped on demand, that failure cannot be cleared in software either — the recovery earlier required Devon physically restarting the scope.

WHAT WAS DONE: left the mount idle (move_type none, not slewing, tracking on, arm open) and closed the connection. Not unsafe — nothing is pointed anywhere hazardous and sunrise is ~8 hours out — but the view is stuck and the scope will likely need a restart before the next session.

TO INVESTIGATE: whether stop_view needs a different argument or a companion call; whether the view can only be stopped from the state it was started in; what seestar_alp does to tear down a view (it manages long sessions and must handle this). Also worth checking whether tracking left on for many hours risks a mount limit — 8 hours of tracking is 120 degrees of RA travel.

RELATED: the session should stop and restart the view periodically rather than holding one open for the whole run, which is already noted on the frozen-stream ticket.

title: At night the two-level sky/terrain model breaks: artificial lights sit inside terrain
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 01:00, and it explains every night-time 'no edge' result plus a three-way disagreement.

THE MODEL. find_edge assumes a column is two levels: bright sky above, dark terrain below, one step between. That holds in daylight and twilight. After dark it does not, because terrain contains streetlights and windows that are far BRIGHTER than the night sky.

EVIDENCE (6-frame averaged profiles, sky reference ~20 counts):
  az 340 — dark 5.8-10.7 from alt 60 down to 17.5, then 53.9 at alt 15 and 56.4 at 12.5, then dark again below. A STREETLIGHT at 12-15 deg inside otherwise fully blocked terrain.
  az 320 — 20.9, 24.8, 7.2, 31.7, 10.0, 20.0, 44.9, 7.4 ... alternating bright and dark: a gappy tree with skyglow showing through.
  az 300 — smooth rise 22 -> 71 counts from alt 60 down to 12.5 (the light dome brightens toward the horizon), then a drop to 7.8. A REAL horizon near 10-12.

CONSEQUENCES:
1. My earlier targeted run reported az 340 = 10.0 deg. That was the LAMP, not the horizon. The evening sweep's 'blocked_above 60' was correct, and so is the photo's ~56. The three-way disagreement recorded earlier resolves in favour of the two sources I doubted — the newest measurement was the wrong one.
2. Az 300's night value (~10-12) agrees with the evening sweep's 11.2. Night measurement is fine where terrain is genuinely unlit.
3. The 'noise' find_edge divides by is not measurement noise. Per-frame scatter measured with 6 repeats is 0.00-0.16 counts — captures at one pointing are essentially identical. The variation between ALTITUDES is real scene structure. Averaging repeats therefore cannot help, and my attempt to beat down noise that way was based on a wrong premise.
4. The light dome itself is a large smooth gradient — az 300 rises threefold from zenith to horizon — which a two-level fit also has to contend with.

DIRECTION: a night-capable detector cannot be a two-level step fit on raw brightness. Options worth testing against the saved profiles (captures/2026-08-04-averaged/scan/ and the 2026-08-03 sets): detrend the skyglow gradient before fitting; treat isolated bright excursions inside otherwise dark runs as lights and mask them; or classify per-frame with the segmentation model, which does not care about absolute brightness at all and already distinguishes sky from building from tree.

SCHEDULING IMPLICATION UNCHANGED: twilight remains the better time, because the sky is bright enough to silhouette everything and the lamps are not yet dominant.
close_reason: PR #1: night.find_horizon fits the skyglow gradient, masks lamps brighter than the local model, and tests the top of the column against an absolute open-sky reference.

title: Observing ran 14 minutes past the stated safety cutoff
description:
PROCESS FAILURE, 2026-08-04. The /goal skill sets a hard rule: no slews within 45 minutes of astronomical twilight. With twilight at about 04:06 that put the cutoff at 03:37. The last measuring run finished at 03:51 — fourteen minutes over.

NO HARM RESULTED. The Sun was at -21.2 deg when the run ended, three degrees below astronomical twilight and nine below the -12 hard stop, so there was never a hazard. But the 45-minute buffer exists precisely to absorb the kind of drift that occurred, and it was consumed without anyone noticing.

CAUSE: a long background run was launched and the clock was not re-checked while it executed. Each column took longer than estimated because the sky brightened toward dawn, which raised the sky reference from 25 to 82 counts and let more columns resolve — so the run got slower exactly as the deadline approached.

FIX: the deadline must be enforced INSIDE the measuring loop, not by the caller before launch. Before each column, compute the Sun's altitude and the time to the cutoff, and stop cleanly if the next column would cross it. A caller that starts an N-column run cannot know how long N columns will take, and the estimate degrades in the direction that matters.

SECOND, SEPARATE ISSUE FROM THE SAME RUN: the sky reference climbed from 25 to 82 during it, meaning the later columns were measured in early dawn twilight rather than at night. The night detector (terminus/night.py) assumes a dark sky with a skyglow gradient; the daytime detector assumes bright sky against silhouetted terrain. Columns straddling that transition are judged by whichever model happens to be applied, and the two disagree materially — az 190 gives 35.0 by find_edge and 12.5 by the night detector, az 150 gives 35.0 versus 'open to the floor'. Any run spanning a lighting transition should record the sky reference PER COLUMN (it already does) and select the detector from it, rather than applying one model to the whole run.

title: Photo pipeline is unreachable: export skymask/mosaic/orient/plan/night from the package API
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 reading the PR branch. The five modules that implement the photo-first
architecture — skymask, mosaic, orient, plan, night — are not imported in

photo-first workflow needs:
  skymask  sky_mask, horizon_rows, horizon_band, upper_envelope, obstruction_classes,
           type_uncertainty, available

title: CLI: offline photo-to-mask workflow (register, segment, extract horizon)
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. The photo-derived mask that produced the published result was built by
driving the modules by hand. There is no command for it. A user who clones the repo can
run 'terminus sweep' — the 36-column blind circle the PR supersedes — and nothing else.

This half needs no telescope and no network: it is the offline desktop step. Proposed
surface, subject to naming:

  terminus mosaic <image_dir> [--work <dir>] [--lens hfov] [--min-points 12]
      pto_gen -> cpfind --multirow --celeste -> cpclean -> drop under-constrained frames
      -> autooptimiser -> pano_modify equirectangular -> nona, then composite with solved
      per-layer gains. Report every dropped frame and its control-point count; a silently
      discarded frame is silently missing sky. Write the manifest.
  terminus skymask <equirect.tif> [--backend segment|heuristic|auto]
      sky mask -> horizon_band -> upper envelope -> per-column type and uncertainty ->
      mask YAML in native panorama azimuth (i.e. UNORIENTED — yaw is not known yet).

Two things must survive to the mask and currently have nowhere to live in the schema:
CLIPPED columns (obstruction reaches the top of the data — a record of where the frame was
cropped, never a measurement) and POROSITY/type uncertainty. Blocking terminus-13 depends
on the type actually reaching the mask from segmentation rather than from the scope.

Both hugin and torch are optional; the command must fail with the clear install message
that mosaic.require_hugin already produces, not an ImportError traceback.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #6 (78d2670) after four review rounds. terminus mosaic + terminus skymask, offline. Schema gained clipped/porosity/uncertainty; load_mask keeps its 3-tuple contract. Unoriented masks refused by every exporter, with MaskError/UnorientedMask so the CLI reports rather than tracebacks. Added skymask.segment_classes, without which obstruction_classes had no reachable input.

title: Night and dusk classifiers (auto-select by Sun altitude)
description: The current classifier is daytime-only (blue sky vs green/yellow tree vs structure). Add: NIGHT classifier (Bortle-8 skyglow is bright orange-gray, obstructions are black silhouettes -> discriminate by brightness/luminance, not blue-dominance; tree-vs-structure color tagging is LOST at night, so that comes only from a daytime pass; night gives clean geometry, covers Sun-blocked southern azimuths, and enables plate-solve refinement off real stars). DUSK classifier (gradient sky, low contrast, changing fast -> brightness-based with looser threshold, or skip the narrow twilight window). Architecture: terminus already computes Sun altitude, so classifier auto-selects via mode='auto' (Sun up=day/color, Sun<=-18=night/brightness, between=dusk). One config knob, no manual switching.
design: Refactor classify() into mode-aware dispatch: classify_day (current), classify_night (luminance threshold sky vs silhouette), classify_dusk. Pick by Sky.sun() altitude when mode=auto. Thresholds tuned live against the real sky at dusk/night, not guessed.
acceptance_criteria: mode=auto picks the right classifier by Sun altitude; night sweep produces geometry with type=silhouette; documented that seasonal tree tagging requires a daytime pass; thresholds validated on-sky.
notes:
EMPIRICAL FINDINGS 2026-08-02 (attempted live sweep at sunset, Sun alt 9->5 deg):

1. COLOUR IS THE WRONG PRIMARY DISCRIMINATOR (fixed). The original blue-dominance test scored dark tree branches as SKY: a silhouette against bright sky keeps a blue cast from scattered skylight + optical blur. Verified at az90/alt8 - visibly ~20% branches, classifier said sky=0.96. Replaced with a luminance split (sky is the light source; terrain silhouettes darker), which correctly found obstruction at az90/alt5 (23%). Clouds classify as SKY under luminance, which is CORRECT for a horizon mask - it records terrain, not weather.

2. exp_ms is FIXED at 240 in scenery mode (not auto), so absolute luminance is comparable between frames.

3. TWILIGHT BREAKS ANY SINGLE-THRESHOLD APPROACH (unsolved - this is the core of this ticket). At dusk the sky has a huge VERTICAL brightness gradient: bright sunset glow near the horizon, dim sky overhead. A per-column reference sampled at the top of the column (alt 40) is therefore far dimmer than the sky at alt 0, so everything low reads as 'sky' -> false 'open_to_min'. In other directions the dim upper sky itself fell below the threshold -> false 'blocked_above'. Observed exactly this: columns saturated to alt 0 'open' or alt 40 'blocked', never a real transition (az0 open, az15 blocked, az30 open, az45/60 blocked). Sweep aborted after 6 columns; results discarded.

PROPOSED FIX (threshold-free, works day/dusk/night): instead of a fixed sky threshold + bisection, scan the column in coarse altitude steps (~2 deg) recording mean luminance, then take the horizon as the location of the largest DROP in the altitude-vs-brightness profile (a step edge). Optionally refine around that step. This needs no absolute reference and is immune to the vertical gradient. Costs more captures per column (~20) but each is ~3s. Alternative/companion: compare top-half vs bottom-half luminance within each frame (the boundary is a horizontal step inside the 0.7x1.3 deg FOV).
ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-02 (second live attempt, sunset->nautical twilight):

**AUTO-EXPOSURE IS THE BLOCKER.** get_setting reports manual_exp=False by default (auto sentinels isp_exp_ms=-999000, isp_gain=-9990). The camera renormalises every frame toward mid-grey, which cancels the sky-vs-terrain brightness difference the sweep is trying to measure. Measured proof: 15 columns swept, every profile hovered at 80-115 mean luminance regardless of pointing. Change-point analysis (mean above split minus mean below) gave step sizes of 4-23 against sample-to-sample noise of 5-18 — SNR ~1, i.e. indistinguishable from scatter. Only az200 (43 vs 10) and az260 (37 vs 11) were real. The whole mask was discarded.

FIX AVAILABLE AND VERIFIED: Seestar.lock_exposure() added — set_setting {manual_exp: True, isp_exp_ms, isp_gain}. Confirmed manual_exp flips to True and isp_exp_ms pins (auto sentinel replaced by the set value). CAVEAT: changing the value again mid-session did not take (stayed at the first locked value) — probably needs iscope_stop_view/start_view between changes; needs testing. Settings keys of interest: manual_exp, isp_exp_ms, isp_gain, isp_range_gain, isp_range_exp_us_scenery.

DETECTOR HARDENED: find_edge rewritten from 'largest single drop' to a change-point fit (maximise mean-above minus mean-below) gated on SNR >= 2.5 against the column's own noise. The old detector reported a horizon at az20/alt30 from the sequence 76->116->88, which is a one-frame spike, not terrain. A regression test now pins that real profile as 'no edge'. This means noisy columns come back unmeasured instead of wrong — the right failure mode for a horizon file other software trusts.

NEXT SESSION ORDER: (1) lock exposure BEFORE start_view, verify a dark pointing and a sky pointing give clearly different luminance, (2) then sweep. Best done in daylight where we already proved the luminance split works; only after that is a night sweep worth attempting.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
NEEDS DEVON'S JUDGEMENT — hardware time, not code time.

Everything offline about this ticket is already done and shipped. The luminance split replaced blue-dominance, exposure locking exists and cmd_sweep locks BEFORE start_view, find_edge is a change-point fit with two gates, and night.py fits the skyglow gradient rather than thresholding brightness. What is left is the part the ticket itself says cannot be guessed: 'thresholds tuned live against the real sky at dusk/night, not guessed', and acceptance requires a night sweep producing geometry.

THE SPECIFIC ASKS:

1. Do you want a DUSK classifier at all, or should terminus refuse the twilight window outright? Your own note says twilight breaks any single-threshold approach and that you aborted a sweep in it. Refusing is defensible and is much less code than a third classifier that is wrong in a way nobody notices. Your call because it costs you observing time either way. If you do want one, the auto boundary as specified is Sun up -> day, Sun <= -18 -> night, between -> dusk.

2. A dusk/night sweep to tune against. night.py needs real profiles at Sun altitudes between -6 and -18 to know whether the skyglow fit holds through twilight or only after astronomical dark. Saved frames are enough; I do not need to be there.

3. The mid-session exposure-change caveat is still untested — changing isp_exp_ms a second time stayed at the first locked value, probably needing stop_view/start_view between. That matters if a dusk sweep wants to re-expose as the sky darkens.

Nothing here is blocked on me.

title: CLI: guided orientation loop (plan a column, measure it, refit, stop on stability)
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. plan.py and orient.py implement the result the PR is built on — seven
information-chosen columns converging to a spread of 0.06 deg, ~20 minutes of scope time
replacing a 36-column blind circle — and there is no way to run it. It exists as a library
that only the author's ad-hoc session ever called.

This half needs the telescope, so it is the one that must be safe. Proposed surface:

  terminus orient <mask.yaml> [--fiducials <prior.yaml>] [--dry-run]
      loop: plan.next_column ranks candidates by D-optimality against the photo-derived
      horizon gradient -> Pointer.point_to (Sun-guarded, every waypoint re-checked) ->
      scan_horizon -> plan.as_fiducial (a column that hits the ceiling becomes a BOUND,
      never a dropped measurement) -> orient.fit -> plan.is_stable. Stop on stability of
      the solved yaw, NOT on RMS: RMS is blind to uniform bias because the fit absorbs it
      into pitch, and is meaningless while n is near the parameter count. One fit reported
      RMS 0.28 deg from four edges interpolating four parameters and was nearly published.
      Print the running yaw and its spread after every column so the operator can see it
      settle.
  terminus orient --apply <mask.yaml>
      rotate the photo mask by the solved orientation and write the oriented mask + exports.

REQUIREMENTS THAT ARE NOT NEGOTIABLE:
  * every slew through Pointer.point_to, no exceptions, no new goto path;
  * honour the observing deadline INSIDE the loop, not only between columns (terminus-17:
    one run went 14 minutes past it);
  * pick the night or twilight detector by Sun altitude (terminus-2/16) — dark directions
    want twilight, bright directions work at night;
  * resumable. The loop is 20 minutes of hardware time and a dropped socket should not
    cost the columns already measured. Persist fiducials as they are taken.

Also expose --plan-only, which ranks the next columns from an existing mask and prints them
without touching the mount. That is the useful half on a cloudy night and needs no hardware.

title: README documents the superseded method as the method
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. The README describes terminus as working "by pointing the scope around
the sky and, at each azimuth, finding the altitude where clear sky meets an obstruction —
classifying that obstruction as tree or structure by color." That is exactly the approach
the photo-first PR replaces, and the reason it replaces it is that the scope physically
cannot classify anything (terminus-11: every terrestrial target is ~1000x inside the
hyperfocal distance).

Also stale in the README:
  * "36 columns at 10 degree spacing ... runs several hours" is now the fallback, not the
    recommendation. Seven chosen columns and ~20 minutes is the method.
  * "How it decides" describes the colour classifier only. Segmentation is unmentioned.
  * requirements list ffmpeg but not the optional hugin-tools or torch/transformers, and
    does not say which parts work without them.
  * "accurate to your polar alignment (~1 deg on a repeatable setup)" understates the risk
    the PR actually hit: an undetected 3.7 deg polar drift moved the published orientation
    by 4.75 deg. The README should tell the user to plate solve before trusting the result.

THIS BLOCKS OPEN-SOURCE VALIDATION. The plan is to have other people run this at their own
sites and send results back. A stranger will do what the README says, which is the method
that produces the worse answer — and their data will then be evidence about the wrong
pipeline. Fix the docs before asking anyone to run it.

title: Contributor result bundle: make an outside run reproducible and diagnosable
description:
PLANNED 2026-08-04 (Devon). The validation strategy is to open-source this and have other
people run it at their own sites, returning results for debugging and validation. Every
result the project currently trusts comes from one site, one instrument, one season.

For that to work, an outside run has to come back with enough context to be re-judged. A
mask alone is not enough — it is a conclusion with the evidence discarded. mosaic.write_manifest
exists for exactly this reason and is currently the only piece of it.

A result bundle should carry:
  * the mask, oriented and unoriented, plus the exports;
  * the fiducials actually measured — azimuth, altitude, whether it was a bound, its ceiling,
    its SNR — and the fit output including per-column residuals, and the yaw history that
    the stability rule stopped on;
  * the raw column profiles (already saved as *_profiles.json), so a future detector can
    re-judge them without the contributor re-observing;
  * which detector ran per column, and the Sun altitude at the time;
  * the mosaic manifest: frame count, frames dropped and their control-point counts, solver
    residual, the lens the solve converged to versus the EXIF starting guess;
  * versions, backend used (segment vs heuristic), and whether the mount was plate solved.

NO IMAGES BY DEFAULT and no location precision beyond what the physics needs. Photographs of
someone's house and yard are the input to this tool; a bundle that uploads them by default is
a privacy problem, and lat/lon to four decimals is their front door. Make image inclusion an
explicit opt-in flag, and say plainly in the docs what the bundle contains.

Reciprocal, and the actual point: an outside run is only useful as validation if it can be
checked against something independent. Public airborne lidar (USGS 3DEP in the US) covers most
sites; a DSM ray-traced from the contributor's coordinates gives a synthetic skyline in true
azimuth from a source with its own known accuracy. If that is a tool in the repo, every
contributor's run becomes a real validation rather than another self-consistency check.
See also terminus-4.

title: Answer the Scenery-mode focus objection with a measurement
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 in a prior-art sweep. The project's central rationale — the scope can
measure an altitude but can never identify what it is looking at, because at 250mm focused
at infinity every terrestrial target is ~1000x inside the 4.3 km hyperfocal distance
(terminus-11) — has an obvious counter that a reviewer or a forum commenter will reach for
immediately: ZWO documents a Scenery mode with MANUAL FOCUS for terrestrial subjects.
https://www.seestar.com/blogs/tutorial/seestar-shooting-modes

The rebuttal is most of the way there but not stated where anyone will find it:
  * terminus already runs start_view("scenery") everywhere (cli.py:92,115, __init__.py:77) —
    the blur was measured IN scenery mode, not in the astro imaging path;
  * terminus-11 has the numbers: 130+ scan frames, gradient p99 0.73-1.34 (best single frame
    2.55, a focused frame would be in the tens), and the spread tracks CONTENT not range.

WHAT IS MISSING: there is no focus command anywhere in client.py. So the claim the code can
currently support is "we never adjusted focus and it was blurred", which is much weaker than
"we focused as far as the protocol allows and it was still blurred".

ACTION:
  1. Determine whether the control protocol exposes a focuser in scenery mode at all
     (seestar_alp is the reference for method coverage). If it does not, that IS the answer
     and it should be recorded as such — the manual focus may be app-side or absent over the
     wire.
  2. If it does, sweep it at a terrestrial column and record the gradient statistic at each
     focus position, the same measure terminus-11 used. Either it sharpens or it does not,
     and either result is publishable.
  3. Write the conclusion into the README and into terminus-11, with the numbers.

This is P1 because it is not a feature — it is whether the project's stated reason for
existing survives first contact with someone who owns the same telescope.

title: Independent ground truth: synthetic skyline from public DEM/lidar
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. Every number the project trusts is internal consistency: the photo agrees
with the scope, and the scope agrees with the photo. The out-of-sample checks (az 0/20/340
predicted at 61.0/61.4/56.2 having only ever been recorded as ">=35") are the strongest
evidence so far and they are still the same two instruments checking each other.

There is an independent source that costs nothing and needs no second site. Public airborne
lidar — USGS 3DEP in the US — covers most of the country at sub-metre vertical accuracy. Ray
tracing a DSM outward from the observer's exact coordinates yields a synthetic skyline in
TRUE AZIMUTH from a survey that has never seen this telescope, this camera or this mount.
That converts "the two agree" into "the photograph agrees with an airborne survey", and it
independently tests the polar-drift correction, because the DSM does not care what the mount
was doing.

PRIOR ART CONFIRMS THE APPROACH: Georg Zotti's Stellarium landscape workflow uses exactly
this as its azimuth truth — a DTM-rendered panorama, matched against the photo panorama in
Hugin, is how he fixes north. Andrew Smith's HORIZON (https://agksmith.net/horizon/, note the
TLS cert is broken) is the archaeoastronomy tool that renders horizon profiles from a DEM and
exports Stellarium polygonal horizons. See Zotti's SEAC2025 course notes:
https://www.archeoastronomy.org/assets/downloads/slides/ast/ast-12_seac2025-stellarium-landscape-course-notes.pdf

WHERE IT WILL AND WILL NOT AGREE, which is the interesting part:
  * Rooftops and walls should agree closely — hard surfaces, well sampled by lidar.
  * The tall tree is the test. A DSM records a canopy return, terminus records a porosity
    band. Comparing them is a real experiment about what "the horizon" even means for
    foliage, not just a validation check.
  * Lidar has a survey DATE. A deciduous canopy measured by an overflight three years ago is
    not this August's. Disagreement there is a finding about seasonality, not an error.

Also scales: any contributor whose site has lidar coverage gets validation for free, which is
what makes terminus-22 worth building.
notes: NEEDS DEVON'S JUDGEMENT ON SOURCE (flagged 2026-08-05). The code is buildable offline and worth doing — an independent synthetic skyline from public elevation data is the only ground truth here that does not come from the same instruments as the thing it checks. What needs your call first is WHICH source, because it is a licensing and coverage decision as much as a technical one: USGS 3DEP lidar is public domain and 1 m where it exists but coverage is patchy; SRTM/Copernicus is global at 30 m, which is too coarse for a 5 m fence and fine for a ridge; commercial lidar may cover your site with terms that do not suit an Apache-2.0 repo. Note the near/far split matters here — terminus-44 measured that a 2 m fence at 5 m moves 11.9 deg for 2 m of observer displacement while a 100 m ridge at 2 km moves 0.003, so a DEM can only ever validate the far field. Tell me the source and I will build it.

title: README: credit the prior art this builds on, and say plainly what is new
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 in a prior-art sweep. The README currently reads as though photographing a
skyline to get an obstruction profile were a new idea. It is not, and the project is better
served by saying so and then being precise about what actually is new.

MUST CREDIT — the pipeline is well-trodden:
  * Georg Zotti, Stellarium Panorama (Landscape) Tutorial, SEAC2025 — documents the exact
    Hugin sequence terminus automates (add images, cpfind, optimise positions/lens,
    equirectangular export), then a manual GIMP sky mask, then landscape.ini. Also the
    authoritative spec for polygonal_horizon_list / angle_rotatez / maptex_top+bottom.
    https://www.archeoastronomy.org/assets/downloads/slides/ast/ast-12_seac2025-stellarium-landscape-course-notes.pdf
  * Existing .hrz generators: HRZ-Creator (https://neuronburner.com/hrz-creator/) and
    danngalann/panorama-horizon-maker (https://github.com/danngalann/panorama-horizon-maker).
    Both manual-trace, both set north by hand.
  * N.I.N.A. Horizon Creator plugin workflow — phone frames at horizon inflections, angles
    from a phone alt/az app, skyline read by eye. The same ~19-frame instinct.
  * THE SOLAR INDUSTRY GOT THERE FIRST, twenty years ago and commercially. Solmetric SunEye
    210 (https://www.solmetric.com/product/suneye-210-shade-tool/) is a calibrated fisheye
    plus compass, tilt sensor and GPS producing horizon altitude for every 1 degree of
    azimuth, exported as .HOR for PVsyst. Also HORIcatcher/Meteonorm, Solar Pathfinder.
    Photo-to-horizon-profile is a solved, shipped product — in a different field.
  * Nearest ecosystem neighbours: njefferson/clear-horizons
    (https://github.com/njefferson/clear-horizons), which already solves north from the SUN;
    and OrangeAgente/seestar-mcp (https://github.com/OrangeAgente/seestar-mcp), which infers
    obstruction arcs from where plate solving fails.
  * Closest published work: Mephisto unobservable-region segmentation
    (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.19335) and LenghuSky-8 (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.16429) —
    all-sky cameras with star-based alt/az calibration, where the static obstructions (dome,
    tower) are a HAND-DRAWN mask rather than a segmentation output.

WHAT THE SWEEP FOUND NOWHERE, and what the README should therefore claim narrowly:
  * semantic segmentation as the sky/terrain decision for an astronomy horizon export;
  * obstruction TYPE carried from segmentation classes into the horizon product;
  * a telescope used purely as an angular fiducial source for a 3-parameter orientation solve
    of an independently built photogrammetric sphere;
  * information-gain (D-optimal) choice of which column to measure next, with a stopping rule
    on parameter stability rather than residual RMS;
  * ceiling-limited columns as one-sided censored bounds;
  * a night detector built ON the skyglow altitude gradient rather than subtracting it.

DILIGENCE GAP TO CLOSE FIRST: Cloudy Nights and Stargazers Lounge both refuse automated
fetches, so the amateur-forum record was searched only through snippets. Two threads went
unread and should be read by hand before any novelty claim is published: CN 1005210
(horizon-mapping app feasibility) and CN 872380 (Horizon Creator plugin). Also unsearched:
the N.I.N.A. Discord, ZWO bbs, indilib forum, and the Seestar Facebook groups.

README has a Prior art section crediting Zotti's Stellarium landscape tutorial, HRZ-Creator and panorama-horizon-maker, the N.I.N.A. Horizon Creator plugin, the Solmetric SunEye and the solar-industry precedent, clear-horizons and seestar-mcp, and Mephisto/LenghuSky-8. Novelty is claimed narrowly as a combination and the text states the search was not exhaustive and invites correction. Gap-fraction terminology carries Jonckheere 2004 and Rich 1990, verified against Crossref. What remains — how strongly to assert novelty — is terminus-30.7 and needs Devon's judgement.

title: Ship a full Stellarium landscape, not just a polygon list
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. to_stellarium_txt emits a bare polygonal horizon, which was all the old
architecture could produce: a 36-column sweep has no imagery worth showing. The photo
pipeline changes that — a registered equirectangular panorama IS the texture Stellarium
wants, and it already exists as a by-product of the mosaic.

So the natural product is now a complete landscape package rather than a list of numbers:
  landscape.ini with type=spherical (or polygonal with a texture), maptex, maptex_top and
  maptex_bottom for the vertical extent, angle_rotatez for the solved yaw, plus
  polygonal_horizon_list with polygonal_horizon_list_mode = azDeg_altDeg so the numeric
  horizon and the picture agree. Spec and worked example in Zotti's SEAC2025 course notes:
  https://www.archeoastronomy.org/assets/downloads/slides/ast/ast-12_seac2025-stellarium-landscape-course-notes.pdf

This is the one place the orientation solve becomes visible to a person: angle_rotatez is
literally the fitted yaw, and a wrong yaw shows up as the observer's own house in the wrong
place. That makes it a better validation surface than any residual.

WHILE IN THE EXPORTERS, two smaller items from the same sweep:
  * Match the conventions of the existing .hrz generators (HRZ-Creator,
    danngalann/panorama-horizon-maker) so terminus output is drop-in for people already using
    those files.
  * Consider a .HOR export (Solmetric/PVsyst horizon format). It is a short exporter, it
    makes the mask useful for solar siting, and it is an honest nod to the field that had
    photo-derived horizon profiles first. See terminus-25.

Mode B's limitation must be honoured here: a phone panorama cannot see above its own frame,
so maptex_top has to reflect the real vertical extent rather than being assumed. A landscape
that claims coverage it does not have is worse than one that admits the gap.
notes:
PRIOR ART 2026-08-04, from reading clear-horizons: THIS IS ALREADY DONE, in the weaker form. src/model/panorama.js paints video strips onto a 2048x1024 equirectangular canvas during the sensor sweep (x=0 = TRUE NORTH, matching its Stellarium export convention so image and horizon list share one origin) and exports landscape.ini + horizon.txt as a Stellarium SPHERICAL landscape — its own comment: 'the measured DATA drives Stellarium horizon math while the PHOTO draws it'. That is this bead's deliverable, shipped.

Its own listed v1 simplifications are exactly the list Hugin already solves for terminus, which is the differentiator and should be stated as such: roll (gamma) ignored so strips paint as vertical world columns assuming an upright phone; later strips overwrite earlier ones leaving hard seams; per-device FOV error skews the vertical scale. Their words: 'a rough stitched strip, not a photographic panorama'. terminus has control points, a bundle-adjusted solve, and per-frame exposure gains.

So this bead is no longer 'add a capability' but 'do properly what exists roughly'. Also note Zotti et al. 2021 (J. Skyscape Archaeology 6(2), doi:10.1558/jsa.17822) is the academic version of the same product — Hugin panorama imported into Stellarium as a calibrated landscape, with the horizon polygon surveyed by TOTAL STATION. Both must be cited here and in terminus-25.
CONSTRAINT 2026-08-04, found in a literature review — affects whether this bead's deliverable is even expressible. STELLARIUM'S LANDSCAPE MODEL HAS NO TILT OR ROLL PARAMETER. It has angle_rotatez, a single rotation about the vertical, and nothing else. The established community practice for setting it is: take known real azimuths of landmarks and their pixel coordinates, compute angle_rotatez per landmark, and use THE ARITHMETIC MEAN.

Two consequences:

1. terminus solves four quantities (yaw, pitch, two tilt components) and Stellarium can receive exactly one of them. The pitch and tilt must therefore be BAKED INTO THE RENDERED IMAGE — the panorama has to be re-projected through the solved rotation before export, with only the residual yaw left in angle_rotatez. Exporting the raw mosaic plus angle_rotatez=yaw silently discards the tilt and puts the picture back where the orientation solve found it was not. That is a real bug waiting in this bead as originally written.

2. It sharpens the paper's framing (terminus-25). The most-used tool in this field fits one parameter by averaging; terminus fits a 3-DOF rigid rotation with censored bounds and a robust loss. That is a direct, honest generalisation of established practice rather than a claim of novelty, and it is a better sentence than any of the alternatives.

The estimator also has a NAME that should be used: this is Wahba's problem (Wahba 1965, SIAM Review 7(3), 409, doi:10.1137/1007077) — least-squares rotation between sets of direction observations. Closed forms exist (TRIAD, QUEST, Davenport q-method, SVD/Kabsch) but assume uncensored, unweighted residuals, which is precisely why terminus needs an iterative solve. title: Interop with the two ecosystem neighbours, and use one as a check
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. Two projects occupy adjacent ground and neither overlaps terminus enough to
compete; both are more useful as inputs than as rivals.

seestar-mcp (https://github.com/OrangeAgente/seestar-mcp) bins PLATE-SOLVE OUTCOMES by az/alt
across nights and proposes obstruction arcs from where solving fails, with weather-gating,
cross-night and GPS-drift checks. Same telescope, inverted logic: it learns the horizon from
failure rather than measuring it.

THAT IS A GENUINELY INDEPENDENT SIGNAL AND WORTH USING AS A CHECK. A plate solve fails
because photons did not arrive; segmentation says a pixel is a tree. Neither derives from the
other, and they disagree in informative ways: a column terminus calls open but that never
solves is either a bad mask or something the photo missed (a wire, a pole, thin branches
against bright sky); a column terminus calls blocked that solves fine is a canopy gap — which
is exactly what horizon_band's porosity is trying to quantify. Cross-tabulating the two is a
cheap validation experiment for anyone already running both, and it needs no new hardware.
Compare against porosity specifically, not just the horizon altitude.

clear-horizons (https://github.com/njefferson/clear-horizons) is an offline planner built on
"your real, measured horizon — not a flat 0 degrees", with a phone-sensor sweep that is
SUN-CALIBRATED FOR TRUE NORTH, a 36-point manual editor, and Stellarium import. It is the
closest thing in the amateur world to solving the north problem astronomically, and it is a
natural consumer of a terminus mask.

ACTION: make the mask importable by both — confirm the exported formats already satisfy them
rather than assuming, and file the delta if not. Then, separately, write up the seestar-mcp
cross-tabulation as a validation procedure a contributor can run (see terminus-22).
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-08-04, after reading the source. clear-horizons is NOT Sun-calibrated for true north. Its README says so (line 36) but the code explicitly rejects that method: src/model/geomag.js replaces 'the old sight-the-Sun-through-a-filter compass calibration' with the World Magnetic Model, computing declination from the site coordinates — 'no Sun, no filters'. src/model/capture.js:13-17 confirms every device heading is MAGNETIC and corrected by applyOffset() from WMM declination, with a manual offset left available for local iron.

That makes it a WEAKER north than terminus, not a comparable one: a magnetic compass plus a global field model, against a mount tied to the celestial frame. WMM declination is good to a fraction of a degree, but the phone magnetometer under it is not, and local iron (a car, a shed, rebar in a patio) is exactly the error the manual offset exists to paper over. The honest framing for terminus is 'the same problem, solved with the sky instead of a field model' — and both are worth citing, because they bracket the accessible and the accurate.

LICENSE CONSTRAINT, important: clear-horizons is PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, not an OSI open-source licence and NOT compatible with terminus's Apache-2.0. No code, no test fixtures, no lifted algorithm. Interop through file formats only — which is fine, since its horizon model is plain {points:[{az,alt}]} serialized as [[az,alt]] pairs with Stellarium import/export, and it accepts altitudes down to -60 deg (ALT_MIN), so terminus's negative southern columns import cleanly.

title: Plate solve with the scope's own solver: measure pointing error instead of assuming it
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 reading OrangeAgente/seestar-mcp. THE SEESTAR HAS AN ONBOARD PLATE SOLVER.
seestar-mcp calls it as two native methods and reads the answer back:

    await self.alpaca.method_sync("start_solve")
    result = await self.alpaca.method_sync("get_solve_result")
    # src/seestar_mcp/server.py:340

They reach it through Alpaca/seestar_alp, but those are native method names, so terminus can
call them straight through its existing generic entry point: sc.call("start_solve") then
sc.call("get_solve_result"). No ASTAP, no astrometry.net, no local index files — which keeps
the Raspberry-Pi/ARM-wheel constraint intact. seestar-mcp also notes a second route: the
solved position appears at Stack.Annotate.result.annotations[] in the view state
(docs/CONTRACT.md:52).

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The published orientation was invalidated once already
by exactly the error a plate solve measures. Plate solving late in the night showed the
mount's polar axis had drifted 3.7 deg in azimuth; refitting against columns re-measured on a
corrected mount moved yaw by 4.75 deg (130.25 -> 135.00/135.81) and took the residual from
3.10 to 0.55. That error was invisible from inside the run — every column was self-consistent
and wrong together, which is why the single-column control test wrongly concluded the fit was
insensitive to it.

TWO USES, IN ORDER OF VALUE:

1. PREFLIGHT: measure the polar error before a run and report it. A run that starts with an
   unmeasured mount produces fiducials whose shared systematic cannot be detected afterwards
   from residuals. Solve, compare the solved RA/Dec against the commanded RA/Dec, and print
   the discrepancy. Refusing outright is probably too strong — but the number has to reach the
   operator and the manifest (terminus-22), because a mask is only as good as the alignment
   it was measured under. The README's "~1 deg on a repeatable setup" is optimistic by nearly
   4x against real data.

2. FIDUCIAL AZIMUTH BECOMES MEASURED RATHER THAN COMMANDED. Today a fiducial's azimuth is
   where the mount was ASKED to go. A plate solve gives where the tube ACTUALLY is, so the
   azimuth entering the orientation fit is observed rather than assumed. This attacks the
   systematic directly: a shared pointing bias currently propagates straight into yaw, since
   the fit has no way to distinguish "the photo is rotated" from "the mount is rotated".

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS, from facts already paid for:

 * A PLATE SOLVE NEEDS STARS. A fiducial column ends in terrain by definition. Solve at the
   TOP of the column, in open sky, then trust the mount's relative motion down the column —
   relative motion over a few degrees is far better than the absolute polar alignment. Do not
   try to solve inside terrain and do not treat a failed solve there as an error.
 * SOLVING PROBABLY NEEDS THE IMAGING PATH, NOT SCENERY VIEW, and terminus holds scenery view
   over RTSP for the whole sweep. Mode switching mid-run lands squarely on terminus-15
   (stop_view does not reliably stop the view) and terminus-12 (the RTSP stream freezes and
   serves stale frames). So the cheap, safe design is ONE solve at the start of a run, before
   scenery view starts — not a solve per column. Per-column solving is a second phase and
   should be treated as such.
 * THE METHOD NAMES ARE UNVERIFIED. seestar-mcp marks them "FIRMWARE-DEPENDENT: solve method
   names" and, unlike their filter-wheel code, does NOT mark plate_solve hardware-verified.
   Probe them on the actual scope before trusting either one, and verify the readback rather
   than the return code — four commands on this hardware have already reported success while
   changing nothing.

Note terminus-27 covers the INVERSE use that seestar-mcp actually built: inferring obstruction
arcs from where solving fails. That is a different feature and a genuinely independent signal;
this bead is about using a successful solve as pointing truth.

title: Rename porosity to gap fraction before the API is public
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 in a literature review. 'Porosity' is the wrong word and using it will mark
the project as out-of-field to exactly the readers best placed to help.

POROSITY IS WINDBREAK/SHELTERBELT VOCABULARY ('optical porosity'), not overhead-canopy
vocabulary, and it is absent from the canopy-photography canon. The established term for the
quantity horizon_band computes — the fraction of a direction that is still open sky through
foliage — is GAP FRACTION, and specifically DIRECTIONAL GAP FRACTION. Anchor reference:
Jonckheere et al. 2004, Agric. For. Meteorol. 121(1-2), 19-35,
doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2003.08.027. Also Rich 1990, Remote Sensing Reviews 5(1), 13-29.

Two more terminology corrections from the same field, worth fixing at the same time:
  * 'fuzzy boundary' -> MIXED PIXELS (Macfarlane 2011,
    doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2011.01.019). That is the field's name for the ambiguous canopy
    edge horizon_band is trying to characterise.
  * SKY VIEW FACTOR IS NOT CANOPY OPENNESS and the two must not be used interchangeably. SVF
    is cosine-weighted (sin.cos) for radiative exchange (Steyn et al. 1986); openness is the
    unweighted open-sky fraction. Conflating them is the classic out-of-field tell.

NOTE the quantity terminus actually computes — gap fraction retained BELOW a per-azimuth
skyline altitude — appears to have no exact established name, because the forestry field
computes gap fraction on zenith-ring x azimuth-sector grids and never produces h(az), while
the solar horizon-profile field produces h(az) and treats obstructions as opaque. So there is
room to name it, but it must be named IN the field's language: 'gap fraction above the
horizon line' is the phrasing both fields parse without objection.

WHY P1 AND WHY NOW: this is a public API name (skymask.horizon_band returns 'porosity';
type_uncertainty consumes it) and the project is about to be open-sourced and possibly
written up. Renaming after strangers depend on it costs a deprecation cycle; renaming now
costs one sed and a docstring. Same reasoning applies to the mask schema field if porosity
reaches it via terminus-19.

Terminology consolidated in skymask's module docstring, including the SVF distinction (SVF is cosine-weighted, gap fraction is not) and the finding that gap fraction retained below a per-azimuth skyline has no established name. Masks written with the old key still load; it is never written back.

title: EPIC: publish the method
description:
Decide whether terminus's method is worth writing up, and if so, do it. Opened 2026-08-04
after three independent prior-art sweeps (amateur tooling, academic literature, publishability
assessment).

WHERE IT STANDS. The pipeline is well-trodden and must be credited as such (terminus-25):
Hugin panoramas for astronomy landscapes are documented move-for-move by Zotti; photo-derived
horizon profiles have been a commercial product in the solar industry for twenty years; sky
segmentation, Huber loss, censored regression, Rodrigues rotations and D-optimal design are
all textbook somewhere. What appears genuinely unoccupied is narrower and should be claimed
narrowly:

  * no published work uses a precision-pointed ASTRONOMICAL instrument as the goniometer that
    fixes a terrestrial panorama's absolute orientation. Patat 2011 names the idea in one
    sentence — 'calibration of a few points using direct theodolite readings coupled to
    digital, rectified photography' — and does not develop it. Everyone else uses a theodolite,
    a total station, a magnetometer, a placed marker, or a 3D city model.
  * no published work keeps a per-azimuth horizon altitude h(az) that RETAINS gap fraction
    below the skyline. Forestry computes gap fraction on rings and sectors and never produces
    h(az); solar produces h(az) and treats obstructions as opaque. Narrower than first
    reported: Fujiwara et al. 2024 already model transmissive canopy, but collapse it to a
    scalar sky view factor.
  * D-optimal selection of the next pointing is standard in ROBOT kinematic calibration
    (Sun & Hollerbach 2008 is the citation) and appears nowhere in telescope pointing,
    attitude determination, or any skyline work. Claim the application, never the method.

FRAMING THAT SURVIVED REVIEW. Lead with the telescope as a SELF-VERIFYING absolute angular
reference — trustworthy in angle because it plate solves against the star field — not with the
hyperfocal blur argument, which is the weaker half and has an obvious counter (terminus-23).
The 3.7 deg polar drift is the proof: the encoders were wrong and only plate solving found it.

Also: terminus fits 4 quantities where Stellarium's landscape model accepts ONE
(angle_rotatez), set in practice by taking the arithmetic mean of per-landmark values. 'A
direct generalisation of what the field's most-used tool does by averaging' is a better
sentence than any novelty claim.

VENUE. arXiv astro-ph.IM preprint regardless — the listing is empty on this topic. Then PASP
or Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation once the validation children below are done. JAAVSO
is a serious option, not a consolation. Not a CV/robotics venue: every component there is
off-the-shelf and the design criterion has been standard since 1991.

horizon that DEMs already solve; Zotti for the manual workflow this automates) / method
overview / panorama and sky mask / horizon extraction with gap fraction / orientation model and
fit / which columns to measure / night detection / results and validation / negative results
and failure modes / downstream impact / limitations. Roughly eight pages.

Children carry the work that does not exist yet. The writing is the easy part; the validation
