title: Night panorama, plate solved: answer the objection and gain a second independent mask
description:
THE OBJECTION a referee will raise first, and the paper has no answer without this: if a
long-exposure phone panorama can register stars, plate solving gives absolute orientation with
no telescope at all — and Components 4 and 5 of the method become unnecessary.

DEVON'S ANSWER 2026-08-04, and it is stronger than treating night as a fallback. The two
panoramas are not competitors, they are complementary products that FAIL DIFFERENTLY:

  * A DAYTIME photo has utility a night photo does not: a person looking at the interface can
    see their own yard. Recognising your neighbour's roofline is how a human validates a
    horizon mask, and it is what makes the segmentation classes (tree vs structure) meaningful
    to look at. A night panorama is a field of black shapes.
  * A NIGHT photo is also of use, and carries the stars that make it self-orienting.
  * HUMAN EYES CAN DISCRIMINATE DIFFERENT SOURCES OF ERROR BETWEEN THE TWO. Day and night
    images of the same skyline have independent failure modes — segmentation confusion under
    cloud, silhouette bleed and bloom around lamps at night, different registration errors from
    different feature content. Two masks that disagree tell a person WHERE to look and often
    WHICH one is wrong, in a way one mask plus a residual never can. That is the same argument
    the Mode A vs Mode B cross-check already made quantitatively (self-residuals 2.38 vs 2.51
    while the two modes disagreed by 5.55 RMS / 12.1 worst) — here it is available to the eye.

So the honest framing is not 'night plate solving does not work' but 'night plate solving is a
SECOND independent orientation, and having two beats having one'. If it works, terminus gains
a free cross-check on yaw that needs no telescope and no scope time. If it fails — light
pollution, no tripod, insufficient limiting magnitude near the horizon where it matters most —
that failure is itself the result that justifies the telescope, and it must be reported with
numbers either way.

PLANNED: shoot the night panorama 2026-08-04 evening.

WHAT TO CAPTURE AND MEASURE:
  * the same frame set geometry as Mode A, so the comparison is like for like;
  * plate solve the frames (astrometry.net locally, or the scope's own solver per terminus-28
    if it will accept an external image) and record which frames solved, which failed, and the
    limiting magnitude actually reached AS A FUNCTION OF ALTITUDE. The prediction is that
    solving degrades exactly where the horizon is, which is the crux;
  * derive orientation from the night solve alone, and compare yaw against the 135.81 the
    telescope fiducials gave. That number is the headline either way.
  * segment the night panorama and compare its skyline against the daytime one, per azimuth.
    Where they disagree by more than the mask quantisation, look at both images and record what
    the eye says the cause was. That catalogue of discrepancies is the actual deliverable and
    the thing no residual can produce.

title: Test the orientation fit against a closed form
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04. The orientation fit is an instance of WAHBA'S PROBLEM (Wahba 1965, SIAM
Review 7(3), 409, doi:10.1137/1007077): the least-squares rotation between two sets of
direction observations. It has well-known CLOSED-FORM solutions — TRIAD, Davenport's q-method,
QUEST, and the SVD/Kabsch construction.

Those closed forms assume uncensored, unweighted, equally-trusted residuals. terminus has
one-sided censored bounds, per-column weights and a Huber loss, which is exactly why it needs
an iterative solve — a good thing to be able to say plainly rather than looking like an
omission.

BUT IT ALSO HANDS US A FREE TEST ORACLE, and there is currently no independent check on the
most important function in the package. Strip the special cases — synthetic fiducials, no
bounds, unit weights, robust=False — and QUEST or the SVD solution must reproduce fit()'s
rotation to numerical precision. Any disagreement is a bug in the grid search, the local
refinement, the native-column iteration, or the parametrisation, and right now nothing would
catch it: every existing test scores the fit against fiducials generated by terminus's own
forward model, which is the same shape of mistake as the round-trip test that was already
found flattering its own result.

Implementation is small: the SVD form is B = sum w_i b_i r_i^T, then R = U diag(1,1,det(U)det(V)) V^T.
Twelve lines of numpy, no new dependency, no reference implementation to vendor.

Also worth recording in the module docstring: naming the problem correctly (Wahba's problem;
the residual treatment is Type-I censoring, which astronomy calls UPPER LIMITS and handles with
survival analysis — Feigelson & Nelson 1985, ApJ 293, 192) costs nothing and makes the code
legible to anyone who arrives from either field.

ONE CAVEAT WORTH KNOWING, not fixing: combining censoring with a Huber loss LOSES the convexity
that makes Huber attractive on its own (Bradic & Guo 2019, Electron. J. Stat. 13, 582). The
coarse-grid-then-refine search is a reasonable response to a non-convex landscape, but it is
currently an accident rather than a decision. Say so in the docstring.

title: Prove or retract the overcast texture claim against SkyFinder
description:
skymask.py's docstring makes a strong empirical claim and stakes a design decision on it: local
variance, the textbook 'sky is smoother than buildings' cue, INVERTS under overcast — measured
here, sky reached a 90th-percentile local deviation of 55.8 against structure's median of 23.5,
because heavy cloud is more textured than siding. The docstring says 'do not reinstate it
without re-measuring'.

WITH ONE PANORAMA THAT IS AN ANECDOTE, NOT A RESULT. If it goes in a paper, it must be defended,
and it is the single cheapest claim to upgrade.

THE EXPERIMENT: SkyFinder (Mihail, Workman, Bessinger & Jacobs, WACV 2016) is ~90,000 labelled
sky/non-sky images from 53 outdoor webcams, and critically it carries WEATHER METADATA per
image. Compute the same local-deviation separability statistic across it, grouped by weather
label. Either the inversion reproduces under overcast across 53 independent cameras — in which
case it is a citable negative result against a public benchmark, and a genuinely useful warning
to a field that keeps reaching for texture cues — or it does not, and the claim gets narrowed
to this site or retracted.

Cost is a weekend of laptop time and no new hardware. Of every additional experiment on the
table this has the best ratio of evidential value to effort.

CLOSEST PUBLISHED WORK, which does NOT already own this: Nice et al. 2020 (Urban Climate 31,
100572) evaluated 14 techniques and parameter sets including Sobel filters across SkyFinder and
Google Street View and concluded no single technique performs with high accuracy across varied
datasets. That is weather-GENERAL degradation. It does not isolate overcast and it does not
report the inversion. La Place et al. 2017 (arXiv:1712.09161) is similarly generic. So the
claim is unclaimed — which also means if it is made, it is owned.

Also worth doing while the benchmark is loaded: report terminus's heuristic backend's
sky-segmentation accuracy on SkyFinder. It is the CI-relevant path (no torch), it currently has
no external number at all, and a benchmark figure costs one more script.

title: Bibliography in the repo, not just in the paper
description:
Three prior-art sweeps produced a large, verified citation set. It should live in the repository
as a durable file (docs/references.bib plus a short prose guide), not only inside a manuscript,
because the README needs most of it anyway (terminus-25) and because a citation the code can
point at is how a reader checks a design decision.

THE LOAD-BEARING ONES, each attached to the decision it justifies:
  * Wahba 1965, SIAM Review 7(3), 409, doi:10.1137/1007077 — names the estimator. See
    terminus-30.2.
  * Wallace 2002, Proc. SPIE 4848, 125, doi:10.1117/12.460914 — TPOINT's own author arguing
    for exact rotation composition over first-order sinusoidal pointing terms, for the same
    reason terminus does. This is the citation that makes the exact-rotation choice unarguable,
    and it is in our own domain.
  * Sun & Hollerbach 2008, ICRA, doi:10.1109/ROBOT.2008.4543308 — maps robot-calibration
    observability indices onto the alphabet optimalities and concludes D-optimality is correct
    when minimising parameter variance. Justifies plan.py's criterion by name.
  * Wynn 1970, Ann. Math. Statist. 41(5), 1655, doi:10.1214/aoms/1177696809 — sequential
    generation of D-optimum designs, with the convergence proof. This is literally the
    algorithm in next_column.
  * Tobin 1958 (doi:10.2307/1907382) and Powell 1984 (doi:10.1016/0304-4076(84)90004-6) for
    censored regression; Feigelson & Nelson 1985 (ApJ 293, 192) for what ASTRONOMY calls the
    same thing (upper limits / survival analysis). Use the astronomy citation in an
    astronomy-facing README.
  * Huber 1964, doi:10.1214/aoms/1177703732; Bradic & Guo 2019, doi:10.1214/18-EJS1463 for the
    censoring-breaks-convexity caveat.
  * Jonckheere et al. 2004, doi:10.1016/j.agrformet.2003.08.027 — gap fraction, the correct
    term. See terminus-29.
  * Xie et al. 2021 (SegFormer, arXiv:2105.15203) and Zhou et al. 2017/2019 (ADE20K) — cite so
    a reader sees the segmentation is a commodity call and not a claim.
  * Brown & Lowe 2007, doi:10.1007/s11263-006-0002-3; Triggs et al. 2000,
    doi:10.1007/3-540-44480-7_21 — behind the Hugin pipeline, and behind why an unconstrained
    frame must be rejected rather than placed.
  * Lang et al. 2010 (Astrometry.net, doi:10.1088/0004-6256/139/5/1782) — the mechanism that
    makes the telescope self-verifying. Load-bearing for the physical argument (terminus-28).

CLOSEST COMPETITORS, which must be cited AND differentiated, never omitted: Patat 2011
(arXiv:1107.1957); Zotti et al. 2021 (doi:10.1558/jsa.17822); Lee, Lee, Ng & Hsu 2020
(doi:10.3390/s20174728); Yue et al. 2025 (doi:10.3390/rs17152725); Fujiwara et al. 2024
(doi:10.1016/j.buildenv.2024.112071); Kapali et al. 2025 (arXiv:2508.17146); Groves 2011
(doi:10.1017/S0373463311000087); Nagy 2020 (doi:10.1007/s41064-020-00093-1).

DO NOT COPY ANY ENTRY IN WITHOUT CHECKING IT. The sweeps flagged several as unverified or
metadata-only, and at least one agent explicitly warned against citing a dataset it could not
confirm exists. A fabricated citation is worse than a missing one. Resolve every DOI before it
lands in the file.

title: Show what the horizon error costs in targets
description:
Every number the project reports is an angle: 0.55 deg RMS, 0.06 deg spread, 4.75 deg of
movement after the polar correction. None of them says what a reader actually wants to know,
which is WHAT DIFFERENCE IT MAKES.

terminus already owns the machinery to answer that — Horizon.is_visible(ra, dec, sky) is the
whole point of the library. So compute, over a real catalogue and a real night:

  * which targets change observability status between the 36-column blind sweep's mask and the
    photo-derived mask, and by how much observing time;
  * the same between the pre-correction orientation (yaw 130.25) and the converged one
    (135.81). A 4.75 deg rotation of the whole horizon is not a small thing near a tall tree,
    and this is the honest way to show it;
  * how much usable dark time the 3 deg vegetation buffer costs, since that is a deliberate
    safety margin nobody has priced.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE PAPER: an instrumentation referee will ask why 0.55 deg is good
enough, and there is no answer without this. But it also serves the user directly — 'this mask
gains you 40 minutes on M31 and costs you nothing on M27' is the sentence that tells someone
whether the whole exercise was worth an evening. It belongs in the README as much as in a
manuscript.

Cheap, needs no hardware and no new data, and it is the only figure in the publishing epic that
is purely a matter of running code that already exists.

title: Obstruction type as fit weight, and class sequence as an independent yaw signal
description:
DESIGN 2026-08-04 (Devon), following the finding that scope frames cannot be pixel-matched into
the panorama (27-33x scale ratio, terminus-33). Devon: 'we can still classify, and that
classification gives us information about what kind of classifications can match. e.g. if we hit
plant, we can factor out the part of the horizon that is plant on the match.'

CLOSES AN EXISTING HOLE. skymask.type_uncertainty(classes, porosity) is defined and tested and
CONSUMED BY NOTHING. Fiducial.weight is set only from SNR (plan.py:160, min(1.0, snr/8.0)).

WHY TYPE IS NOT A REFINEMENT OF SNR BUT A DIFFERENT FAILURE MODE. Vegetation MOVES between the
photograph and the telescope measurement — the panorama is 2026-08-03, the scope measured
2026-08-04, and wind alone means a branch that was up is down. A crisp, high-contrast canopy edge
scores EXCELLENT under SNR weighting and is still a bad fiducial, because what it measured is no
longer where it was. SNR cannot see this; type can. A roofline photographed yesterday is the same
line today to sub-pixel accuracy. With the seasonal case and the band-not-a-line case, vegetation
is systematically worse for three independent reasons, none of which SNR measures.

ACTION 1 — weight the orientation fit by type. type_uncertainty already returns the right
quantity (3 deg vegetation against 1 deg solid, scaled by 1+gap fraction); route it into
Fiducial.weight as 1/sigma^2. The scope can now classify its own frames, so type can come from
the same instrument at the same instant as the altitude rather than from a photograph taken a day
earlier at 1/27th the resolution.

ACTION 2 — the class sequence around the circle is an INDEPENDENT YAW SIGNAL. If yaw is wrong,
scope-says-tree aligns against panorama-says-roof. Aligning two class strings is a 1D
correlation: independent of altitude, indifferent to pitch and tilt, and COMPLETELY INDIFFERENT
TO RESOLUTION. It sidesteps the scale wall that killed pixel matching. A coarse independent prior
that can disambiguate a yaw the altitudes fit ambiguously — not a replacement for the fit.

The two actions pull opposite ways and that is not a contradiction: DOWNWEIGHT vegetation for the
altitude fit, but the tree<->structure TRANSITIONS are where the yaw information concentrates.

BE SKEPTICAL OF THREE THINGS: one bit per column is coarse and informative only on a varied
horizon; both classifiers must share a taxonomy, and a SYSTEMATIC disagreement between the
scope's macro view and ADE20K's scene-level training would bias the alignment rather than merely
noise it; and the transitions are simultaneously the most informative azimuths and the ones where
both classifiers are least certain.
notes: SPLIT 2026-08-04: the code half of Action 1 moved to terminus-36 (route type_uncertainty into Fiducial.weight), so this bead stays a design and claim. Action 2 — the class sequence as a resolution-independent yaw signal — remains here and is listed as claim 14 in the register at terminus-30.7. Kept parented under the publishing epic deliberately: with JOSS as a target the engineering contribution IS a claim, not merely support for one.

title: Novelty claims register: what we assert, how strongly, and against what
description:
Opened 2026-08-04. The claims terminus can defend, tiered by how well they survive
decomposition, consolidated from four independent prior-art sweeps (amateur tooling, academic
literature, publishability review, patents). Targets are BOTH a JOSS software paper and an
astro-ph.IM preprint, so engineering contributions belong here as first-class claims — JOSS
reviews the software and explicitly does not require methodological novelty.

Rule that governs the whole register: claim narrowly. Every broad framing tested so far gets
decomposed and handed back a citation per part.

=== TIER 1 — METHOD CLAIMS (for the preprint; survive decomposition) ===

1. A TELESCOPE AS THE GONIOMETER THAT ORIENTS A TERRESTRIAL PANORAMA. The strongest one.
   Everyone else fixes panorama orientation with a theodolite, total station, magnetometer, a
   physically placed marker, or a 3D city model; everyone who uses the sky uses celestial
   objects seen by the SAME camera that holds the mask. Here a SEPARATE instrument, tied to the
   celestial frame, supplies ALTITUDE-ONLY SCALARS into a 3-DOF rotation of an independently
   built photogrammetric sphere. Patat 2011 names the idea in one sentence and does not develop
   it. Verified empty from astronomy, GNSS, geolocalization, Crossref, AND patents
   (SPEC/'telescope' AND SPEC/'horizon profile' returns zero).
   DO NOT state this as 'role inversion' — that framing gets you handed Auto-Cal (Kapali 2025).

2. A HORIZON PROFILE h(az) THAT RETAINS GAP FRACTION BELOW THE SKYLINE. Forestry computes gap
   fraction on zenith-ring x azimuth-sector grids and never produces h(az); solar produces h(az)
   and treats obstructions as opaque; GNSS skymasks are binary. NARROWER THAN FIRST REPORTED:
   Fujiwara 2024 already models transmissive canopy in an equirectangular segmentation pipeline
   but collapses it to a scalar sky view factor. The claim is RETAINING IT AS A PER-AZIMUTH
   PROFILE, not having thought of porous obstructions.

3. D-OPTIMAL SELECTION OF THE NEXT POINTING — AS AN APPLICATION IN ASTRONOMY. The method is
   Wynn 1970; Sun & Hollerbach 2008 already mapped robotics observability indices onto the
   alphabet optimalities. Absent from telescope pointing (TPOINT prescribes 'stars all over the
   sky'), star trackers (selection by brightness), radio-telescope calibration (even coverage),
   and every skyline paper (all consume one fixed image). Claim the transplant, never the method.
   Sub-result with no published statement anywhere: d(alt)/d(yaw) = -dH/daz, so heading
   information lives ONLY in the steep parts of the skyline.

=== TIER 2 — EMPIRICAL RESULTS (measurements; cannot be pre-empted by prior ideas) ===

4. SELF-RESIDUAL IS MISLEADING. Two masks with self-residuals of 2.38 and 2.51 disagreed with
   each other by 5.55 deg RMS and 12.1 deg worst case.
5. A RELATIVE SKY TEST IS SELF-DEFEATING. A column blocked all the way up fits a skyglow model
   to its own terrain and passes; 5.8-10.7 counts against a 20.7 open-sky reference.
6. A SINGLE-COLUMN CONTROL TEST CANNOT DETECT A SYSTEMATIC SHARED BY THE WHOLE SET. The polar
   drift lesson; correcting one column inside such a set only proves the fit is insensitive to
   that column.
7. SHARPNESS BEATS BRIGHTNESS AT FINDING THE EDGE IN DAYLIGHT (measured 2026-08-04). Across the
   roofline at az 281.7: gradient p99 26.79 -> 1.28, while mean luminance moved 99.0 -> 101.5.
   Under auto-exposure the two-level brightness model fails in daylight exactly as night.py
   documents it failing after dark. Code work extracted to terminus-37.
8. LOCAL VARIANCE INVERTS UNDER OVERCAST. Sky p90 deviation 55.8 against structure median 23.5.
   An anecdote from one panorama until terminus-30.3 tests it against SkyFinder.
9. FOCUS DOES NOT IMPROVE REGISTRATION (measured 2026-08-04, negative result). 27-33x scale
   ratio; the whole scope frame is 40x71 px at panorama scale. The limit is the phone, not the
   telescope, so better scope data cannot fix it. See terminus-33.
10. FOCUS POSITION IS REPEATABLE TO 1 STEP IN 2600 (1838 manual, 1839 autofocus), which is what
   makes a distance measurement credible rather than suggestive.

=== TIER 3 — ENGINEERING CONTRIBUTIONS (JOSS-legitimate, and the part Devon is proud of) ===

11. THE INTEGRATION ITSELF: which instrument does which job, decided by what each can physically
    know. Not derivable from any component. This is the README's story and JOSS's subject.
12. AUTOFOCUS AS A SKY DETECTOR. Image gradient alone cannot separate sky from out-of-focus
    terrain; if autofocus converges, something is there. A physical measurement standing in for
    a classification.
13. FOCUSER STEP COUNT AS A PER-COLUMN DISTANCE IN A HORIZON MASK. No horizon mask found in any
    of the four sweeps carries distance. Bears on which trees are the neighbour's (seasonality)
    and which obstructions are near-field, where a lidar DSM comparison is least trustworthy.
14. CLASS SEQUENCE AS A RESOLUTION-INDEPENDENT YAW SIGNAL — semantic matching survives exactly
    the scale wall that kills pixel matching. See terminus-30.6.
15. A WORKING, TESTED, EXPORTING IMPLEMENTATION across N.I.N.A., Stellarium and a planner
    library, with the hardware failure modes documented rather than papered over.

=== NOT CLAIMS — cite and move on ===
Exact rotation over the first-order sinusoid (Wallace 2002 made this argument, in this domain,
as TPOINT's author). The estimator itself (Wahba 1965). Censored bounds (Tobin 1958; Feigelson &
Nelson 1985 in astronomy). Huber. SegFormer/ADE20K. Hugin panoramas for astronomy landscapes
(Zotti). Photo-derived horizon profiles (Solmetric, commercial for twenty years). Dropping
unconstrained frames (bundle-adjustment practice).

CODE WORK EXTRACTED so this stays a claims register: terminus-36 (type -> fit weight),
terminus-37 (daylight sharpness edge detection). Claims 2 and 3 additionally depend on
terminus-19 and terminus-20 shipping the CLI that produces them.
notes: NEEDS DEVON'S JUDGEMENT (flagged 2026-08-05). The register is buildable, the CALIBRATION is not: how strongly to assert each claim is a call about your own reputation and appetite. The README already states the narrow version — segmentation as the sky/terrain decision with type carried into the export, the scope as a fiducial source for a 3-parameter solve, D-optimal column choice with a stability stopping rule, censored bounds, and a night detector built on the skyglow gradient — and explicitly says the search was not exhaustive. Two Cloudy Nights threads (1005210, 872380) remain unread by hand, and the N.I.N.A. Discord, ZWO bbs, indilib forum and Seestar Facebook groups were never searched. Tell me how strong a claim you want to make and I will write the register to match; interacts with terminus-31.

title: Re-measuring a high-residual column: the method, and what it cost to learn
description:
2026-08-04 evening. Re-measured az 190, the column with the second-largest residual (+16.1
between the telescope's 12.5 and Mode A's 28.6). Devon: 'this, much more careful analysis is what
I want for when we are trying to fix error.'

=== RESULT ===
    az 190   old telescope  12.5 deg
             Mode A photo   28.6 deg
             RE-MEASURED    ~21.8 deg   (sky 170 at alt 22.4 and 140 at 22.0, terrain 94 at 21.6)
The new value sits BETWEEN the two. The old 12.5 was taken with a 35 deg search ceiling and looks
like a false edge — 'a too-low search ceiling manufactures confident false edges' is already a
documented failure here (terminus-8), and this is an instance of it.

=== THE METHOD THAT WORKS ===
  1. LOCK EXPOSURE AND VERIFY THE READBACK. Without it the profile is auto-exposure chasing the
     scene, not the horizon. Unlocked, the same column gave 118, 98, 86, 79, 75, then back up to
     104 — noise. Locked at 5.5 ms the sky/terrain contrast was 165 counts (alt 30 lum 253, alt 1
     lum 88). This is the single highest-value step and I skipped it on the first attempt.
  2. WALK DOWN FROM THE TOP, not up from the bottom.
  3. FINE STEPS NEAR THE EXPECTED EDGE. 1 deg down to ~22, then 0.4 deg through the transition.
  4. FIND THE SUSTAINED MONOTONIC DECLINE, not the largest single drop. The largest single drop
     fired at alt 27 on a 185->149 wobble in the SKY, and sent the autofocus to point at empty
     sky. The real edge is where luminance begins falling and keeps falling: 94, 85, 80, 66, 59,
     46, 43, 41. A single-step rule cannot tell a cloud edge from a roofline; a run of four
     consecutive decreases totalling >20 counts can.

=== THE FOCUS HALF IS UNRESOLVED, AND THREE OF MY EXPLANATIONS WERE WRONG ===
Autofocus never achieved focus on this column. gradp99 stayed 1.1-1.6 and gradmax never exceeded
7.5, against 27.5 and 55.9 on this morning's sunlit roof.
  * 'It is too dark' — WRONG. Devon: 'it's still very bright out, it's not even sunset, I can
    *see* the sun.' Do not reach for this.
  * 'The house is a similar colour to the sky, so luminance hides it' — plausible but NO. All
    three channels plus R-B, G-B and saturation give gradmax 3.6-4.6. There is no edge in any
    channel, not merely in luminance.
  * 'It is closer than the minimum focus distance' — NO. A fine sweep at the top of travel
    (2440-2600 in 20-step increments) is flat at 1.12-1.44 with sd constant at 28.2. If the
    subject were beyond range, sharpness would climb toward the stop. It does not.
A coarse sweep across the WHOLE range (200-2500) also found no peak — but note that at f/4.9 the
depth of focus is about 28 microns, roughly 7 focuser steps, so a 100-step sweep can miss the
peak entirely. This morning's autofocus converged 1838 -> 1839, a one-step result, which is what
a peak that narrow looks like. So the coarse sweeps are not evidence of absence.
STILL UNEXPLAINED. Next things to try: a genuinely fine sweep (5-step increments) over a bounded
range; check whether tracking is smearing the frame at longer exposures; and repeat on a sunlit
target of known distance to confirm the instrument still focuses at all.

title: Patent clearance before the release announcement
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 in a patent landscape search. NOT LEGAL ADVICE and not an FTO opinion — these
are facts read off patent documents, recorded so a qualified attorney knows where to look.
JOSS submission is a public release, so this belongs before that, not after.

THE ONE THAT MATTERS, and it was not the one we went looking for:

US 7,873,490 B2, 'Solar access measurement device', Solmetric/Fluke, filed 2005-12-28, granted
2011-01-18, ACTIVE TO 2029-01-03. Most of its independent claims require MAGNETIC orientation
and compute SOLAR RADIATION — both cleanly absent here, since terminus's orientation is
celestial and it computes no irradiance. But CLAIM 28 carries neither limitation:

  'An apparatus comprising: a calibrated electronic camera in communication with a first
  processor operable for capturing an image from the electronic camera; an ORIENTATION
  DETERMINATION UNIT in communication with the calibrated electronic camera and enabled to
  determine the orientation of the calibrated electronic camera; a second processor ...
  operable for DETERMINING ELEVATION AND AZIMUTH ANGLES OF OBJECTS IN THE CAPTURED IMAGE; and
  an output device for conveying the elevation and azimuth angles of one or more objects in
  the captured image.'

Three of four elements look present in terminus (calibrated camera via the Hugin lens solve;
elevation/azimuth of objects, which IS the horizon profile; output device, which is the
exporters). The open question is claim construction of 'orientation determination unit ... in
communication with the calibrated electronic camera' — terminus determines camera orientation,
but by fitting to a separate instrument's measurements rather than by a sensor coupled to the
camera. That is a lawyer's question, not an engineer's. PUT THIS CLAIM IN FRONT OF COUNSEL.

Claim 27 of the same patent (skyline analysed against a database of satellite locations to
determine obstruction) is also in force to 2029-01-03.

ALSO LIVE:
  * US 2024/0087227 A1 — a Solmetric/Fluke CONTINUATION still being prosecuted. Claims can
    still be drafted. Docket watch, not a one-time clearance.
  * US 11,842,510 (Pano AI, 'true north orientation', active to 2043) with live continuations.
    Its independents require a mechanical rotation axis, an angle encoder, a calibration object
    detected IN the image, and a bearing from ephemeris — all apparently absent — but the family
    is actively being written.
  * US 8,477,419 (Celestron, active to 2032-02-08) fits a mount model by minimising pointing
    error, but its claimed free parameters are time, date and location, not a rigid rotation.

THE TWO WE WENT LOOKING FOR ARE LARGELY NON-ISSUES:
  * US 8,311,285 (skyline localization) EXPIRED 2024-11-13 for non-payment. Constrains nothing.
    Its claims also require a 3D environment model, synthesized virtual images, and an UNKNOWN
    location — none of which apply.
  * US 7,861,422 is active to 2027-08-22, but its claims require a heading reference, an
    inclination reference providing pivotal mounting within a housing, and images that are
    orientation-referenced AT CAPTURE. Three of four elements appear absent: no compass, no
    gimbal, no housing, and terminus's frames are deliberately NOT oriented when taken.

DEFENSIVE ASSETS — expired, free to practise, and citable as invalidating prior art:
  * US 8,386,179 claim 18, EXPIRED 2026-03-18, priority 2005-12-28: capturing A PLURALITY OF
    IMAGES of a horizon including a skyline, recording orientation of two or more of them, and
    determining access from the skyline across those images. That is the multi-frame panorama
    capture step, now public domain. Best single defensive document.
  * US 7,382,448 (Celestron SkyAlign) EXPIRED 2026-02-12 and US 7,518,792 (Bushnell) expired —
    together the public-domain ancestry of 'recover orientation by fitting instrument-frame
    measurements to celestial-frame directions', i.e. prior art protecting terminus's step 4
    from anyone claiming it later. Plus the whole expired Meade Autostar family.

CLEAR SPACE, from claims-level searches:
  * SPEC/'telescope' AND SPEC/'horizon profile' returns ZERO. No patent connects horizon
    profiling to telescopes or astronomical siting.
  * No patent found claims semantic segmentation of a panorama into sky/building/vegetation
    as such.
  * No D-optimal or Fisher-information selection of calibration measurements anywhere in this
    domain.
  * No patent claims gap fraction in a horizon or obstruction context.
  * ACLM/'solar access' AND ACLM/'skyline' returns 18 documents and every one is Solmetric.

BIGGEST UNKNOWN, close this first: Thales EP 3472557 B1, 'Method of estimating a direction of
absolute orientation of an optronic system' (priority 2016-06-21, granted 2022-12-14). The
title is a near-exact description of terminus's step 4 and ITS CLAIMS WERE NEVER RETRIEVED.

CAVEAT ON EVERYTHING ABOVE: no maintenance-fee record was independently verified for any
patent. 'Active' is largely term-derived. Google does flag fee lapse when it holds the event,
so absence is evidence but not proof.

Note Apache-2.0 carries an express patent grant from contributors plus defensive termination,
which is part of why it is the right licence here.
notes: NEEDS DEVON'S JUDGEMENT (flagged 2026-08-05, offline sweep). Not actionable by an agent: patent clearance is a legal decision about acceptable risk before a public announcement, and the questions are yours to answer — whether to pay for a professional search, whether the novelty claims in terminus-30.7 are ones you want to assert publicly at all, and what you are willing to publish before that is settled. I can gather prior art and draft claim language; I cannot decide the exposure you accept. Blocks the release announcement, so it is worth answering before terminus-30 progresses.

title: Scan defocused for the edge, then autofocus on it: the scope regains obstruction type and gains distance
description:
DESIGN 2026-08-04 (Devon), after discovering the scope can autofocus in scenery mode
(terminus-11, terminus-23). Supersedes the assumption in terminus-13 that obstruction type can
only come from photographs — it can now come from the telescope too, and the two become
cross-checkable.

THE SHAPE, and its virtue is that almost nothing new gets built:

  plate solve at infinity focus       pointing truth (terminus-28)
  scan the column, DEFOCUSED          edge altitude — find_edge UNCHANGED
  point BELOW the edge by ~1/2 frame
  start_auto_focuse + verify readback
  capture, segment, record type + focuser step
  restore infinity focus by number    deterministic; the EAF is absolute-position

find_edge needs no changes because a brightness step does not care whether it is sharp. Blur
arguably helps, by smoothing the sample-to-sample noise the SNR gate is measured against. So
autofocus fires once per column at the one altitude that matters — about seven runs under the
information-gain plan, not thousands.

POINT BELOW THE EDGE, NOT AT IT. Autofocus maximises contrast across the frame; landing exactly
on the boundary leaves half the frame as featureless sky, which is the case most likely to make
AF hunt or fail. Offsetting down by roughly half a frame height fills the frame with terrain
for AF to work on while keeping the boundary near the top — which is also the better
composition for SegFormer, since ADE20K expects scene context rather than a texture crop. One
offset serves both.

RETRY ONLY WHEN THE EDGE WAS MISSED, and let the frame say so (Devon). A single capture answers
both questions with numbers the project already computes:
  * SKY FRACTION from the segmentation says whether the boundary is in frame and which way the
    miss went — ~100% terrain is too low, ~100% sky is too high — and the shortfall is
    measurable in units of frame height, which is a known angle. The retry step size comes from
    the frame rather than a guess.
  * GRADIENT P99 says whether focus is still valid: 27.52 measured on a focused terrestrial
    frame against 0.73-1.34 across 130+ defocused ones. Two orders of magnitude apart, so the
    test is trivially reliable. Still in the tens means re-point WITHOUT refocusing.
Most retries should therefore be free: small angular moves along one surface barely change the
target distance. Refocus only when p99 collapses, which is the signature of having landed on a
genuinely different object — a treeline behind the roof rather than further up the same roof.

BOUND THE LOOP. A column that will not converge in two or three tries is reporting something
real: thin branches against bright sky, or a boundary that is not a line. Record it as
ambiguous rather than retrying into the observing deadline — 'flag ambiguity, never average it
away' per .claude/skills/goal/SKILL.md, and see terminus-17.

FREE BONUS, AND POSSIBLY NOVEL: the focuser step count IS A DISTANCE MEASUREMENT. It is an
absolute-position ZWO EAF with 2600 steps of range; 1838 read as 'roof at about 40 m'. Recording
it per column gives a horizon mask carrying altitude, type AND DISTANCE. No horizon mask found
in any of the four prior-art sweeps carries distance. It bears directly on two open problems:
which trees are the neighbour's and therefore which columns are seasonal (terminus-13), and
which obstructions are near-field, which is exactly where a lidar DSM comparison is least
trustworthy (terminus-24).

OPERATIONAL COST, TO BE CLEAR-EYED ABOUT: THIS WANTS DAYLIGHT. Segmentation needs colour and
context to separate vegetation from structure, and matching the phone panorama's appearance
argues for the same illumination. That inverts the README's 'run it on a clouded-out night'
advice and puts the Sun guard in the loop for every slew — the apparatus terminus-3 exists to
validate and which has never been exercised with the Sun above the horizon.

DEPENDENCIES: needs a focus command in client.py (terminus has none). Native methods confirmed
from seestar_alp: start_auto_focuse / stop_auto_focuse (ZWO's spelling), get_focuser_position,
get_focuser_state. Completion is signalled by an AutoFocus EVENT (seestar_device.py:1177-1212,
via wait_end_op) which terminus's request/response client cannot hear — so poll get_focuser_state
until it leaves working AND confirm get_focuser_position actually changed. Never trust the
return code alone.

comments.text:
NEAR-FIELD LIMIT, measured 2026-08-04 evening. This bounds the design above, and it explains an
entire evening of frames that would not sharpen at any focuser position.

WHAT HAPPENED: every frame taken on az 170 and az 190 was soft — gradient p99 1.1-1.5 against
the 27.52 measured that morning — at every focuser step from 200 to 2600, in R, G, B, R-B, G-B
and saturation alike. Six explanations were proposed and each was killed by measurement:
darkness (Sun was at +7.02 deg), colour blindness (all channels flat), coarse sampling (a
10-step sweep across 41 positions, against a ~7-step depth of focus, is equally flat), dew
(ambient was 71 F), a degraded stream (frames are 1080x1920 both times), and a decoupled
focuser (the optics do move — correlation falls to 0.5887 between travel extremes).

WHAT IT ACTUALLY WAS: a full-range sweep on az 170 alt 19 gives contrast rising MONOTONICALLY
to the mechanical stop and never turning over —

    step   200    400    600    800   1000   1200   1400
    sd    2.63   3.19   3.51   3.89   4.18   4.45   4.96
    step  1600   1800   2000   2200   2400   2600 (= max_step_range)
    sd    5.51   5.86   6.29   6.93   7.56   8.08

Best focus lies BEYOND the travel. The target is nearer than the scope's minimum focus
distance. Those columns point at Devon's own house, a few metres away; the morning's roof
across the alley at ~40 m focused normally at step 1839. Nothing is wrong with the instrument.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS TICKET, in two parts:

1. AUTOFOCUS-ASSISTED EDGE REFINEMENT HAS A NEAR LIMIT, and the columns inside it are not
   exotic — they are the observer's own roof and fence, which is exactly where the horizon is
   highest and therefore where the altitude matters most. The design must detect the case
   rather than retry into it. The signature is unambiguous and costs three captures: contrast
   still rising at max_step_range means give up on focus for this column, do not hunt. Note
   this is NOT the 'p99 collapsed, re-point' case already described above — refocusing cannot
   fix it, so it needs its own branch.

2. IT QUALIFIES THE DISTANCE CLAIM. 'Focuser step count IS a distance measurement' holds only
   between the near limit and the point where the curve flattens toward infinity. Outside that
   band the step count saturates and reports a bound, not a distance — which is the same
   censored-observation shape the mask already uses for blocked_above (terminus-7), and should
   be recorded the same way rather than as a number that looks precise.

NEAR LIMIT IS ESTIMATED, NOT MEASURED. Geometry gives o - f = f^2 / extension with f = 250 mm;
assuming star focus near step 1500 and ~4.6 um/step puts the limit near 12 m. The assumed
infinity-focus position is untested and the whole number hangs on it. Measuring it is cheap and
is filed separately.

Brightness-profile edge finding is unaffected and kept working all evening — a brightness step
does not care whether it is sharp, exactly as this ticket argues. Only the focus-dependent
parts break. Cross-refs terminus-37, whose sharpness-based daylight edge detection inherits
this same limit.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-08-05 to the NEAR-FIELD LIMIT comment above. The evidence cited for it does not
support the conclusion, and an independent measurement in terminus-30.8 contradicts it.

WHAT I CLAIMED: a full-range sweep on az 170 gives contrast rising monotonically to the
mechanical stop (sd 2.63 -> 8.08 at step 2600 = max_step_range), therefore best focus lies beyond
the travel, therefore the target is nearer than the minimum focus distance.

WHY THAT IS WRONG: sd is whole-frame standard deviation — overall contrast, driven by scene
content and exposure. It is not a focus metric. The focus metric in the same sweep is gradient
p99, and it does not rise at all:

    step        200   600  1000  1400  1800  2200  2600
    sd         2.63  3.51  4.18  4.96  5.86  6.93  8.08
    grad p99   1.50  1.16  1.12  1.18  1.12  1.24  1.17

Flat, and slightly FALLING. Had focus been improving toward the stop, the sharpness metric would
have risen with it. The sd trend is something else — scene or exposure drift across the ~5 minutes
the sweep took, in fading twilight.

CONTRADICTED INDEPENDENTLY: terminus-30.8 records a fine sweep at 2440-2600 on az 190, 20-step
increments, flat at 1.12-1.44 with sd constant at 28.2, and explicitly reasons 'if the subject
were beyond range, sharpness would climb toward the stop. It does not.' That is the correct test
and I contradicted it without noticing.

WHAT STILL STANDS, and it is the operationally important part:
  * NO FOCUSER POSITION SHARPENS THESE TARGETS. gradient p99 flat at 1.12-1.50 across the entire
    travel, in R, G, B, R-B, G-B and saturation alike, against 27.52 on a sunlit roof at 40 m the
    same morning. Six alternative explanations were killed by measurement and remain killed.
  * THE FALLBACK IS UNCHANGED AND STILL CHEAP. Flat gradient p99 across the range means stop
    hunting and use the brightness profile, which is unaffected and kept working on these columns
    all evening.
  * The NEAR-FIELD LIMIT IS STILL THE LEADING HYPOTHESIS — these columns point at Devon's own
    house at a steep angle, the 40 m roof focuses normally, and Devon confirmed the pointing. It
    is plausible and unproven.

max_step_range means give up on focus for this column' — must NOT be implemented as written. It
keys on the wrong metric. The correct signal is flat sharpness across the range. And the ~12 m
figure should not be quoted as a measurement; it hangs on an assumed infinity-focus position and
is now doubly unsupported. terminus-46 settles it properly by measuring infinity focus and the
step-to-distance curve.

Recorded in LESSONS.md as I-02, and as an instance of F-07: a number moved in the direction the
hypothesis wanted, and it was not measuring the thing the hypothesis was about.

title: Scope frames cannot be pixel-matched into phone imagery: 27-33x scale wall
description:
MEASURED AND CLOSED 2026-08-04. Recorded as a negative result so it is not re-attempted.

THE IDEA (Claude's, in conversation): now that scope frames are sharp, register them into the
photo mosaic by feature matching — treat them as frames in the Hugin solve with orientation
frozen from plate solving, let autooptimiser place everything else relative to them, and let the
orientation problem dissolve into the registration problem. It would have deleted find_edge,
night.py and the censored-bounds machinery along with every failure mode they exist to survive.

IT DOES NOT WORK, AND THE LIMIT IS NOT THE SCOPE.
    scope frame          1080 x 1920 px = 0.718 x 1.276 deg  ->  1505 px/deg
    Mode B panorama      19968 px / 360 deg                  ->    55 px/deg
    Mode A single frame  ~3000 px / ~65 deg                  ->    ~46 px/deg
Rendering the scope frame at panorama scale gives 40 x 71 PIXELS; at Mode A single-frame scale,
33 x 59. Everything focus buys — shingle granules, leaf veins, the louvres on the ridge vent — is
destroyed by the downsample. What survives is a diagonal edge and one dark blob, which is what a
DEFOCUSED frame would have given. cpfind has nothing to work with.

The two phone modes are comparable, so obtaining the 19 Mode A frames would NOT rescue it. This
is a property of the instruments, not of the data on disk.

THE APPARENT RESCUE IS NOT ONE. Matching at the silhouette level instead of the texture level —
a roofline is a long linear feature with a well-defined angle — is exactly what the orientation
fit already does with horizon altitude against azimuth. The registration information available
between scope and panorama IS the horizon curve, and terminus already extracts it optimally. The
extra resolution has nowhere to go in the registration.

WHERE THE RESOLUTION DOES GO — the measurement, all demonstrated the same session:
  * the fiducial is a knife edge rather than a boundary smeared across the blur width;
  * SHARPNESS BEATS BRIGHTNESS AT FINDING THE EDGE in daylight — across the roofline at az 281.7,
    gradient p99 went 26.79 -> 1.28 while mean luminance went 99.0 -> 101.5. Under auto-exposure
    the two-level brightness model fails in daylight exactly as night.py documents it failing
    after dark;
  * autofocus is a SKY DETECTOR — gradient alone cannot separate sky from out-of-focus terrain,
    but if AF converges there is something there;
  * focus position repeatable to 1 step in 2600 (1838 manual, 1839 auto);
  * obstruction type per column — terminus-30.6.

SEMANTIC matching, unlike pixel matching, is indifferent to resolution and survives — terminus-30.6.

Caveat on the metric used above: gradient p99 is DILUTED BY SKY FRACTION. The same focused
pointing read 26.79 with the frame full of roof and 17.94 with about 35% sky. As a focus check it
must be computed over the terrain side of the boundary only.
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-08-04. THIS BEAD OVERREACHED. It tested whether the frame's CONTENTS could be feature-matched — they cannot — and then generalised that failure to matching in general. That was Claude's error, not the idea's. Devon: 'the point wasn't that we remove the edge detector, it's that the high resolution gives us much greater ability to match ALONG THE HORIZON EDGE to get a quick lock on orientation.'

MEASURED, same frame, full resolution against the 40x71 rendering:
    edge angle          -48.197 deg  vs  -48.171 deg   ->  differ by 0.026 deg
    boundary position     0.9821 deg vs    0.9751 deg  ->  differ by 0.0070 deg

The TEXTURE is destroyed by the downsample; the GEOMETRY survives to a hundredth of a degree. A
line's parameters are estimated from every pixel along it, so downsampling averages the edge
rather than moving it — forty samples of a straight boundary still fix its angle precisely.

SO THIS NEGATIVE RESULT IS NARROWER THAN WRITTEN ABOVE: texture and feature matching between
scope frames and phone imagery is dead. EDGE-GEOMETRY matching is not, and is the subject of
terminus-39. The px/deg measurements above stand; the conclusion drawn from them does not.

Retained rather than rewritten because the reasoning error is instructive: a scale ratio destroys
high-frequency content and leaves low-frequency geometry alone, so 'the image is unrecognisable'
does not imply 'nothing can be measured from it'.

title: available('segment') returns True when the backend cannot run
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 installing the segmentation backend. skymask.available('segment') checks only
that torch and transformers import (skymask.py:38-42). SegformerImageProcessor also requires
TORCHVISION, which is not checked. With torch and transformers present and torchvision absent,
available() returns True and sky_mask() then dies:

    ImportError: SegformerImageProcessor requires the Torchvision library but it was not found

This is the project's recurring failure mode in a new place — a check that reports success while
the thing it vouches for does not work. sky_mask(backend='auto') consults available() to choose
between segment and heuristic, so a host with torch but no torchvision gets a hard crash where
the entire point of the auto path is to degrade gracefully to the numpy heuristic. That is the
Raspberry Pi case, and it is where a crash is least welcome.

FIX, one line: add torchvision to the import probe. Better still, probe what is actually used —
attempt the processor construction once and cache the result — but the import check catches this.

TEST: available() must be false when any of the three is missing. Monkeypatching the import to
raise is enough, and it is worth having because the failure is silent until a real host hits it.

For terminus-19/20: whichever CLI chooses a backend must surface WHICH backend ran, in the output
and the manifest. A run that silently fell back to the heuristic produces a measurably different
mask, and terminus-22 needs that recorded for an outside run to be re-judged.
close_reason: PR #12. available('segment') now checks torchvision, which SegformerImageProcessor needs and which fails at construction. More importantly sky_mask(auto) now degrades on a failure to RUN, not only to import, since from_pretrained fails on a fresh/offline host with all libs present; explicit backend='segment' still raises. sky_mask(report=True) returns the backend that actually ran, and cmd_skymask records THAT in the mask meta rather than the one requested — it previously wrote 'segment' for masks the heuristic produced. Exception-type carve-outs were tried and reverted: version skew surfaces as TypeError, so type cannot separate environment from bug.

title: MERGE INTO terminus-32 WHEN readme-photo-first LANDS: segmentation validated on telescope frames
description:
BOOKKEEPING BEAD. terminus-32 ('Scan defocused for the edge, then autofocus on it') exists only
on branch readme-photo-first (commit 7d49440) and not on main, so these notes could not be
appended to it. When that branch lands, fold this into terminus-32's notes and close this.

VALIDATED 2026-08-04 on real scope frames, az 281.7, after installing torch/torchvision/
transformers (CPU wheels).

SEGFORMER HANDLES THE TELESCOPE'S MACRO VIEW. The concern that ADE20K would fail on a texture
crop lacking scene context was WRONG:
    pure roof   alt 3.0  ->  sky  2.0%   building 98%
    boundary    alt 3.5  ->  sky 45.2%   building 55% / sky 45%
    open sky    alt 5.0  ->  sky 92.7%   sky 93%
A macro of asphalt shingles with a sliver of sky in one corner still reads building at 98%.

THE RETRY RULE IN terminus-32 IS CONFIRMED WORKING, untuned: sky fraction is monotonic and
cleanly separated — 2% too low, 45% boundary in frame, 93% overshot. One threshold correction:
pure sky reads 92.7% not 100%, because the model must guess on a featureless frame (7% went to a
spurious class), so 'overshot' should trigger near 85-90%, not unity.

TARGET BAND: terminus-32 specifies pointing below the edge by about half a frame height so the
boundary sits near the top. 45% sky at alt 3.5 with the edge near 4.0 means the boundary landed
mid-frame; aim for roughly 20-25% sky for the intended composition.

STILL UNTESTED — VEGETATION. All three frames were roof and sky. Tree/plant classification and
gap fraction at 2.4 arcsec/px are next, and they are the ones that matter: vegetation classes
drive type_uncertainty (terminus-30.6), and gap fraction is the novelty claim with no external
validation (terminus-30).

INSTALL NOTE: CPU wheels chosen deliberately over CUDA — SegFormer-B0 on a handful of frames is
seconds on CPU, ~200 MB against ~2.5 GB, and it keeps development honest against the Raspberry Pi
target. torch 2.13.0+cpu, torchvision 0.28.0+cpu, transformers 5.14.1. NOT added to pyproject
dependencies: skymask treats this backend as optional by design and the Pi constraint argues
against making it mandatory. If it should be declared, the right shape is an optional extra.

title: Route type_uncertainty into Fiducial.weight
description:
CODE WORK extracted from terminus-30.6 so that bead stays a design/claim and this stays
buildable. The rationale lives there; this is the change.

NOW: plan.py:158-161 sets Fiducial.weight from SNR alone —
    weight = 1.0 if bound else min(1.0, (edge.get('snr') or 1.0) / 8.0)
and skymask.type_uncertainty(classes, porosity) is defined, tested, and consumed by NOTHING.

WANTED: weight = 1/sigma^2 where sigma comes from type_uncertainty — base 1 deg for solid
structure, 3 deg for vegetation, scaled by (1 + gap fraction). Combine with the SNR term rather
than replacing it: they measure different things. SNR says how well this edge was DETECTED;
type says how well the thing it detected STAYS PUT between the photograph and the measurement.
A crisp canopy edge can score excellently on the first and badly on the second.

REQUIRES a type to reach the fiducial. Two sources, and they should be recorded separately
rather than merged: the panorama segmentation at the fiducial's azimuth, and — once terminus-32
lands — the scope's own classification of the frame it measured. Where both exist, disagreement
is itself informative (terminus-30.6) and must not be silently averaged.

TEST: two synthetic fiducials with identical SNR and identical residual, one vegetation and one
structure, must move the fitted yaw by measurably different amounts. That is the whole point and
nothing currently asserts it.

Do not tune the 1 deg / 3 deg constants to improve a fit. They are a stated prior about how far
foliage moves, not a knob; if they are wrong, measure how far the foliage actually moved between
two captures and set them from that.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #9. Fiducial gains sigma (how far the boundary may MOVE, from type) alongside weight (how well the edge was DETECTED); orient.objective standardises the residual by sigma BEFORE the robust loss rather than scaling the finished loss, which review showed is inverse-variance weighting only inside Huber's quadratic core (3.556 vs 5.556 at r=10 sigma=3). photo_type and scope_type recorded separately, never merged. Sigma floored at the mosaic's 0.1 deg resolution, not an epsilon, so no column can capture the fit. Untyped columns unchanged.

title: Daylight edge detection: sharpness where brightness fails
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-04 at az 281.7, real roofline, Sun at alt 43. Across the sky/terrain boundary:

    mean luminance   99.0 -> 101.5     (a 2% step — undetectable)
    gradient p99     26.79 -> 1.28     (20:1 — unmissable)

find_edge is built on the brightness step. In daylight it had nothing to work on, while image
SHARPNESS separated the boundary cleanly. This is the daytime twin of the failure night.py
documents after dark: the two-level bright-sky/dark-terrain model breaks at both ends of the day,
for different reasons.

HONEST CAVEAT, DO NOT SKIP: that run used AUTO EXPOSURE (view state reported manual_exp False).
terminus normally LOCKS exposure for sweeps, and a locked exposure might restore the brightness
step in daylight. The experiment did not separate 'daylight' from 'auto-exposure', so the first
task here is to repeat it with exposure locked and find out which. If locking fixes brightness,
this becomes a much smaller change — a documentation note and an exposure guard rather than a new
detector.

IF A SHARPNESS DETECTOR IS STILL WANTED, two constraints from the same session:
  * GRADIENT CONFLATES SKY WITH OUT-OF-FOCUS TERRAIN. A treeline at 200 m while focused at 40 m
    reads as low as open sky. Sharpness alone is not a sky/terrain classifier — it is a
    'sharp thing at the focused distance' detector. Autofocus resolves it (terminus-32): if AF
    converges, something is there.
  * P99 IS DILUTED BY SKY FRACTION. The same focused pointing read 26.79 with the frame full of
    roof and 17.94 with about 35% sky. Compute the statistic over the terrain side of the
    boundary only, or the metric drifts with composition rather than with focus.

This becomes a THIRD regime alongside daytime-brightness and night-skyglow, so it belongs in the
detector selection of terminus-2 (auto-select by Sun altitude) rather than as a standalone path.
Note the regimes do not partition by Sun altitude alone: this failure was caused by exposure
policy, not darkness.

That is not an edge case for this ticket. The observer's own roof and fence are near-field by
