title: Investigate the Seestar S30 Pro: two boresighted cameras, one integration target
description:
IDEA 2026-08-04 (Devon): 'on the Seestar S30 Pro it has two cameras, so we can collapse on that
platform to one integration target, though because it's two discrete cameras, it still maintains
the multi device spirit.'

WHY THIS IS BIGGER THAN A PORT. terminus's architecture needs two instruments with different
capabilities: something wide and in focus that identifies obstructions, and something
narrow and celestially referenced that supplies absolute angles. Today those are a phone and a
telescope, which is why an ORIENTATION FIT exists at all — the two instruments have no fixed
relationship, so yaw/pitch/tilt must be solved every time from scratch.

TWO CAMERAS ON ONE MOUNT ARE BORESIGHTED. Their relative transform is MECHANICAL and fixed. If
it is stable, it is calibrated ONCE and inherited forever: plate solve with the narrow camera,
and the wide camera's frames acquire absolute orientation directly, with no per-session fit. The
three-parameter solve stops being a measurement problem and becomes a factory-style calibration.

Note what this does NOT do — it does not retire the idea, it instantiates it more cleanly. The
telescope is still the goniometer; the linkage is just rigid instead of fitted. And terminus-33's
27-33x scale wall stops mattering entirely, because nothing needs feature matching when the
transform is mechanical.

A SECOND ADVANTAGE, possibly larger: a mount-driven wide camera can TILE THE WHOLE SPHERE,
including the zenith. The published report notes a dark patch at the centre of the polar view —
sky nobody photographed, because no phone frame pointed straight up. A wide camera on a mount has
no such blind spot and no hand-sweep coverage gaps to chase.

CONCRETE LEAD ALREADY IN HAND: the view state read from the S50 today contains "cam_id": 0. A
camera index in the protocol is exactly what a dual-camera device would need. That is the first
thing to check.

QUESTIONS TO ANSWER, roughly in order of how much they would change the design:
  1. IS THE BORESIGHT STABLE? Across slews, across meridian flips, across a temperature swing,
     across power cycles. A fixed transform is only worth having if it is actually fixed. Measure
     it rather than assuming it; this is the whole premise.
  2. Does the protocol expose both cameras — cam_id, a second RTSP stream, simultaneous
     capture, or does selecting one stop the other?
  3. Specs of each: focal length, sensor, field of view, and px/deg. Compare the wide against a
     phone panorama's ~55 px/deg. If the wide is substantially coarser, the phone still makes the
     better mask and this becomes a convenience rather than an upgrade.
  4. Does the wide camera focus at terrestrial distances, and is its focus independent of the
     narrow camera's? (On the S50 the two roles conflict: focused on terrain means unable to
     plate solve — terminus-11. Two cameras may dissolve that conflict entirely, which would be
     the single most useful consequence.)
  5. Does the narrow camera on the S30 Pro autofocus the same way (start_auto_focuse), and is
     its focuser also absolute-position?

KEEP THE ABSTRACTION HONEST. Whatever this becomes, terminus should not hard-code an S30 Pro
path. The interface is 'a wide identifying instrument' and 'a narrow referencing instrument',
with the transform between them either FITTED (phone + scope) or FIXED (dual-camera). Devon's
framing is the right one: one integration target, multi-device spirit preserved. If the code
reflects that, a phone plus an S50 and an S30 Pro are two configurations of one design rather
than two codebases.

Do not buy hardware on the strength of this ticket. Question 1 decides whether any of it holds.
notes: NEEDS DEVON'S JUDGEMENT (flagged 2026-08-05). This is a purchasing decision before it is a technical one — whether to acquire an S30 Pro to investigate its two boresighted cameras. I can research published specs and the seestar_alp protocol surface, but cannot evaluate hardware nobody here owns, and the interesting claim (one integration target across two cameras) is only testable with the device. Say whether you want the desk research now or the whole thing parked until a unit exists.

title: Lock orientation from the edge: one frame constrains yaw, pitch and roll
description:
IDEA 2026-08-04 (Devon): use the texture and shape AT THE HORIZON EDGE, resolved by the focused
scope, to get a quick lock on yaw/roll/pitch — rather than measuring one altitude per column and
fitting seven of them.

MEASURED PREMISE (terminus-33): edge geometry survives the 27x scale gap to phone imagery.
Angle agrees to 0.026 deg and position to 0.0070 deg between the full-resolution frame and its
40x71 rendering. So a precisely-measured local edge can be compared against a coarse dense curve
without the resolution mismatch destroying it.

WHAT ONE FOCUSED FRAME YIELDS, where today a column yields a single scalar:
  * INTERCEPT — the boundary altitude. Already used. Constrains pitch and tilt.
  * LOCAL SLOPE dH/daz — matched against the panorama's slope profile, this constrains YAW and
    is INDEPENDENT of altitude. Note it is the same quantity plan.py already names as the yaw
    sensitivity, d(alt)/d(yaw) = -dH/daz: the fit would be measuring its own Jacobian entry
    directly rather than estimating it from a coarse profile.
  * EDGE ANGLE IN THE FRAME — the field rotation, hence roll. Currently a fitted parameter.

That is a quick lock: three constraints per pointing instead of one, so convergence should need
far fewer than the seven columns the stability rule currently takes.

TWO COUPLINGS AND LIMITS TO RESPECT:
  1. SLOPE AND ROLL ARE DEGENERATE IN A SINGLE FRAME. The observed edge angle is the world slope
     rotated by the field rotation; one frame gives their combination, not each. Break it with
     the mount's parallactic angle (computable) or with two frames at different azimuths. Do not
     pretend one frame gives both.
  2. THE MATCH IS LIMITED BY THE PANORAMA, NOT THE SCOPE. At 55 px/deg the panorama's own slope
     estimate over a 0.7 deg window is poor. Match against a LONGER, smoothed window of the
     panorama's curve rather than a same-width segment, and let the scope supply the precision.

DISTINCTIVENESS, IN A BETTER FORM THAN BEFORE. A straight roofline slides along itself, so an
edge segment localises only where the boundary has SHAPE — a corner, a peak, a vent breaking the
silhouette. That is much closer to what D-optimality already asks for (steep, structured horizon)
than 'distinctive texture' ever was, so the existing planner and this are more aligned than in
opposition. Worth checking whether the D-optimal criterion should gain a curvature term, since
curvature is what makes a segment localisable.

FIRST EXPERIMENT, cheap and decisive: take the az 281.7 frame already captured, extract its edge
curve, and search the Mode B panorama's horizon curve for the best match by slope. Report where
it lands and how sharply peaked the match is. A broad, flat correlation means a straight edge and
no lock; a sharp peak means this works. That single number decides whether to build it.
notes:
SHARPENED 2026-08-04 (Devon): 'if we take our three 120 degree columns, and focus at the edges, we can probably increase the likelihood that we have an RMS match compared to other possible ones, and can probably express that vector in a way that lets us reduce the number of columns needed.'

THE ARGUMENT, stated properly. Three columns at 120 deg is not an arbitrary minimal set: for
fitting c0 + A cos(az) + B sin(az) — the pitch-and-tilt part of the model — EQUALLY SPACED POINTS
ARE THE D-OPTIMAL CONFIGURATION. It is also the geometry Celestron's SkyAlign used (US 7,382,448,
expired 2026-02-12, so free prior art supporting the choice).

What has blocked three columns is arity, not precision: three altitude scalars against four
parameters is underdetermined, which is why the stability rule currently takes seven. Focusing at
the edges changes the arity.

THE COUPLING RESOLVES BETTER THAN FIRST WRITTEN ABOVE. In EQ mode the field rotation at a given
pointing is COMPUTABLE from mount geometry — it is not a free parameter. So measured frame angle
plus computed field rotation yields the WORLD SLOPE directly. Per column that is TWO independent
constraints, altitude and slope. Three columns give 6 against 4 parameters: overdetermined, which
is exactly the redundancy needed to reject a near-tie rather than accept it.

AND THAT IS THE DISAMBIGUATION. With three altitudes the cost surface in yaw can carry near-ties
that RMS cannot separate — the same blindness that made stability rather than residual the
stopping rule. Slope constraints break them because they are sensitive to a different thing: a
false yaw that happens to fit three altitudes will generally not also fit three slopes. Worth
measuring directly — plot cost against yaw for altitudes-only versus altitudes-plus-slopes on the
same three columns and compare how sharply each minimum is peaked. That plot is the whole
argument in one figure, and it belongs in the writeup (terminus-30.7).

WHAT MAKES A COLUMN WORTH MEASURING CHANGES, and plan.py must follow. D-optimality on altitude
alone says point where the horizon is STEEP. Slope matching says point where the slope profile is
locally DISTINCTIVE — a corner, a peak, a break in the silhouette. Steep-but-uniform becomes a
poor choice, because a straight edge slides along itself and localises nothing. Consider a
curvature term in the criterion: curvature is what makes a segment localisable.

CONCRETE SHAPE, and it slots into the existing machinery rather than replacing it:
  * each column contributes z = [altitude, world slope] with a covariance;
  * jacobian_row gains a second row per column (d(slope)/d(params), which for yaw is the
    horizon's second derivative);
  * information() accumulates 2 rows per pointing instead of 1, so det(J^T J) grows far faster
    per column and next_column naturally converges in fewer;
  * orient.py's weighted robust fit takes the extra residuals unchanged.

If this holds, the headline moves from 'seven columns, twenty minutes' to three — and three
columns at 120 deg is a configuration a user can be told to shoot without any planner at all,
which matters for the one-device story in terminus-38.

title: Panorama registration report: plan a sweep from a phone photo
description:
Let a user drop in a handheld panorama of unknown tilt, bearing and angular span, register it to az/alt, and produce a report showing the detected skyline plus WHERE MEASUREMENTS ARE STILL NEEDED. Inverts the current workflow: instead of sweeping a uniform grid and discovering structure by accident, the photo shows where the horizon is interesting before the scope moves, so scope time is spent where it pays. A panorama has ~17000 columns against a sweep's 16 — it resolves features the sweep is blind to.

VALIDATED METHOD (prototyped 2026-08-03 on Devon's 17408x3104 pano, works):
1. Mask no-data (phone panos are not rectangular; lum<12 is border, not ground).
2. Detect skyline per column: first non-sky row below the top of valid data. Sky test = bright AND not red-dominant; the same luminance-first logic the sweep classifier uses.
3. Smooth the skyline (~81px boxcar) to kill foliage speckle.
4. Fit 6 parameters against known-good scope columns as fiducials: azimuth of left edge, angular span, vertical px/deg, horizon row, and TWO TILT TERMS (A*cos(az)+B*sin(az)). Grid-search the two nonlinear params (edge, span); solve the rest by least squares at each grid point.
5. **The tilt term is essential, not optional.** Without it RMS was 5.5 deg with residuals +10.3 at az80 and -9.3 at az280 — 180 deg apart, the signature of a non-level camera. With it, RMS 2.6 deg and the fit independently recovered a 358 deg span, confirming a full wrap.
6. Gradient of the fitted skyline -> bands needing finer sampling. On Devon's site: az 55-58 moves 5.2 deg altitude per deg azimuth, which a 10 deg sweep steps straight over; and bands at az 156-177 coincide with columns the sweep returned 'unresolved', evidence of real structure rather than noise.

HONEST LIMITS: RMS ~2.6 deg is comparable to the scope's own uncertainty, so the panorama must NOT supply mask numbers — it decides where to point. Absolute bearing is unreliable (fit placed the left edge at az 43 when the user believed the pano started at north); relative structure is what is trustworthy. Parallax matters for near objects since photo and scope are at different heights/positions.

BOOTSTRAP WITHOUT PRIOR MEASUREMENTS (needs design): the fit currently needs scope fiducials. Options: (a) coarse sweep of ~8 columns for fiducials, then register, then targeted refinement — likely the main workflow; (b) if the Sun or Moon is in frame, EXIF timestamp + GPS gives its exact az/alt as a free fiducial, allowing calibration with zero scope time; (c) EXIF heading/level data where present.
design: New module terminus/panorama.py (detect_skyline, fit_panorama, sampling_plan) plus 'terminus panorama PHOTO --mask mask.yaml' emitting a self-contained HTML report. Reuse the existing sweep classifier logic for the sky test. Report shows the photo with skyline trace, fiducials, steep bands, and a recommended azimuth list that can be fed straight back to the sweep.
acceptance_criteria: Given a panorama and an existing mask, produces a fit with reported RMS, an HTML report showing skyline/fiducials/steep bands, and a concrete list of azimuths to sample; refuses to write mask altitudes from photo data; documents the RMS and absolute-bearing caveats in the report itself.
notes:
TILT IS A FEATURE, NOT ERROR (Devon, 2026-08-03): the 12 deg tilt the fit recovered was INTENTIONAL — he tilted the camera up to fit a very tall tree in frame. Consequences for design:

- Do NOT instruct users to hold the camera level. The correct instruction is the opposite: 'frame however you need to get the obstructions in — tilt up for tall trees; the fit solves for it.' Tall obstructions are exactly the ones worth capturing, and they are the reason a user tilts.
- This raises confidence in the model rather than lowering it. A deliberate, consistent tilt is a single rigid rotation, which is precisely what one A*cos(az)+B*sin(az) term represents. Random handheld wobble would NOT collapse into one sinusoid — it would appear as per-column scatter. Cutting RMS 5.5 -> 2.6 with one sinusoid therefore indicates the fit recovered a real physical parameter.
- Report the recovered tilt back to the user as a stated result ('camera tilted 12 deg toward az 152'), not as a warning. It is a sanity check they can confirm from memory, exactly as Devon did here.
- Residual 2.6 deg is therefore NOT unmodelled tilt. Remaining candidates: parallax (photo taken at ~5ft5 eye level, scope at ~6ft, and possibly a different spot — matters most for the near fence), panorama stitching distortion, skyline detection error against foliage, and the scope's own ~1 deg alignment uncertainty plus alt_tol. Worth separating these before chasing more fit parameters.
DECIDED WORKFLOW (Devon, 2026-08-03) — this resolves the bootstrap question above:

  1. BASELINE SWEEP (~16 columns). Coarse, even spacing around the full circle. Purpose is two-fold: a usable first mask, and fiducials for the fit.
  2. USER ADDS A PANORAMA. Any framing, any tilt, unknown bearing.
  3. SYSTEM REGISTERS IT against the baseline columns and produces the report.
  4. SYSTEM PLANS NEW MEASUREMENTS from the panorama gradient — a concrete azimuth list, not a uniform grid.
  5. TARGETED SWEEP of that list, merged into the mask.
  6. OPTIONALLY LOOP: more measured columns means a better-constrained fit, which means a better plan. Converges quickly.

Design notes this implies:
- Baseline should target a number of USABLE fiducials, not columns. Devon's 16-column run yielded only 10 measured columns (4 hit the altitude ceiling, 2 unresolved), and the fit has 6 free parameters — 10 fiducials is thin at 4 degrees of freedom. Either raise the baseline count, or report fiducial count and warn when the fit is under-constrained.
- Fiducials must be spread around the full circle to pin the azimuth offset and span. A daytime baseline loses a wedge to the Sun cone and weakens exactly those two parameters; a night baseline does not. Prefer night for the baseline.
- Needs a 'sweep --azimuths 55,57,82,...' option to scan an explicit list, so step 5 can consume the plan directly. Today sweep only walks a uniform range.
- Report the fit quality (RMS, fiducial count, recovered tilt and span) in the report so the user can judge whether to trust the plan or shoot a better panorama.
- Re-registering after step 5 should improve RMS; if it does not, that is a signal of parallax or stitching distortion rather than insufficient fiducials.
ITERATE ON PANORAMAS TOO (Devon, 2026-08-03): the loop should also request NEW panoramas, with a specific diagnosis rather than a vague 'try again'. The tool knows what is wrong because it knows both the photo's coverage and the mask's gaps. Cases it can detect and the request each should generate:

- ALTITUDE COVERAGE SHORTFALL. Devon's pano spans 1-40 deg altitude, but four columns (az 0/20/60/340) are recorded blocked above 35 — the obstruction continues past where the photo ends. Request: 'four directions are blocked higher than your photo reaches; shoot one tilted further up, roughly 20 deg more.' Detect by comparing per-azimuth photo coverage against mask floors.
- AZIMUTH GAP. Photo does not wrap, or a wedge is missing. Detect from the fitted span and coverage; request a pano covering the missing bearings.
- LOCAL FIT FAILURE. RMS acceptable overall but residuals cluster in one region — suggests parallax against a near object (the fence) or a stitching seam. Request a re-shoot from nearer the mount position, or a second pano started at a different bearing so the seam lands elsewhere.
- SEASONAL CHANGE. Columns tagged 'tree' are seasonal. A winter panorama gives the bare-branch horizon, which is a genuinely different and useful mask. Request one per season and keep them as separate dated registrations rather than overwriting.
- POSITION CHANGE. If the tripod moves, both mask and panorama are invalidated together; detect via a re-measured spot check disagreeing with the mask.

Design: keep panoramas as dated, versioned inputs alongside the mask, each with its own fit record (RMS, fiducial count, tilt, span, coverage range). The report then shows which photo is authoritative for which part of the sky, and what to shoot next.
ARCHITECTURE CORRECTION (Devon, 2026-08-03): fit the PHOTOS TO EACH OTHER first, then register the composite to the scope once. Do not fit each photo independently against scope fiducials.

Why this is the right order:
- Photo-to-photo is strongly constrained: overlapping frames share thousands of features (fence, rooflines, tree crowns). Photo-to-scope is weakly constrained: ~10 sparse fiducials, and a narrow frame may contain one or none.
- It solves the coverage problem. Devon shot four inputs 2026-08-03: a level ~360 pano (19968x2912), a second wide sweep (18560x3008), a tilted pano centred on the tall tree (8320x3232), and a PORTRAIT frame (3000x4000) that brackets the treetop with clear sky above it. The portrait is the only input containing the answer for the columns recorded 'blocked above 35' — but it spans maybe 40 deg of azimuth and cannot be fit alone. Registered against the wide pano it inherits calibration.
- One absolute fit for the whole set (6 params) instead of 6 params per photo. Fewer unknowns against the same fiducials.

Implementation note: cv2 is NOT installed and feature-matching would add a dependency. A lighter route that reuses what already exists — cross-correlate the DETECTED SKYLINE CURVES between photos. The skyline is a strong 1D signal and is already computed by detect_skyline; correlating two skylines recovers relative azimuth offset and scale, and the vertical offset between them gives relative tilt. Falls back to feature matching only if that proves insufficient. (Phase correlation solved an analogous registration for the M27 hero, so the technique is known to work on this data.)

Result: a spherical mosaic in a common angular frame, absolutely calibrated once, with per-region provenance (which photo is authoritative for which azimuth/altitude).
INPUT PHOTOS STAGED (2026-08-03): copied out of Dropbox into captures/panoramas/2026-08-03/ (gitignored, local only). Five inputs, not four — 14.12.15 was missed in the earlier survey:

  14.12.15.jpg  19968x3040  wide sweep
  14.14.37.jpg  19968x2912  wide sweep (the one already fit: left edge az 43, span 358, 79.5 px/deg, tilt 12.2 deg toward az 152, RMS 2.6)
  14.15.23.jpg  18560x3008  wide sweep
  14.16.10.jpg   8320x3232  tilted, centred on the tall tree
  14.16.32.jpg   3000x4000  PORTRAIT, brackets the treetop with clear sky above it

Three wide sweeps rather than two is good news for the photo-to-photo stage: they mutually overlap almost everywhere, so relative az offset/scale/tilt is heavily over-determined before the scope is involved at all. The two narrow frames (14.16.10, 14.16.32) chain onto that composite, and 14.16.32 is the only input that answers the four columns recorded 'blocked above 35'.

Originals remain at '/mnt/d/Dropbox (Personal)/Camera Uploads/2026-08-03 HH.MM.SS.jpg'.
CORRECTION: there are FOUR photos, not five. 14.12.15.jpg is an indoor workshop shot, not a panorama — the earlier 'five inputs' note was wrong and is retracted. Confirmed by Devon and by inspection. Staged copies in captures/panoramas/2026-08-03/ still include it; ignore that file.

PROTOTYPE RESULT 2026-08-03 (photo-to-photo registration WORKS; absolute calibration does NOT yet). Scratchpad: skyline.py, register.py, mosaic.py, plot.py.

WHAT FAILED — SKYLINE-CURVE MATCHING. The planned approach (cross-correlate detect_skyline curves, no cv2) does not work on this data. A suburban skyline is a repetitive 1D signal: matching rooflines, evenly spaced fence posts, near-identical neighbouring houses. The SAME photo landed at 44, 214 and 335 deg under small defensible changes to the objective, with no way to tell which was right. Two specific scoring traps, both of which fired:
  * RMS rewards a small flat overlap — the search slid photos apart until only featureless fence agreed, reporting tiny error and a vertical scale of 0.02 (it had flattened one image to a constant).
  * Plain NCC rewards a SHRINKING overlap — every direct vertical-offset search railed to its boundary.
Phase correlation is immune to both: it whitens the spectrum, so the peak does not depend on overlap size.

WHAT WORKED — PHASE CORRELATION ON PIXELS, circular in azimuth. The images share thousands of features; reducing them to one curve discarded nearly all of it. Results (reference = 14.14.37, span 358 deg):
  14.15.23  wide sweep, span 333 deg, az 347.2, peak 23.3x noise floor, refinement 20/20 windows, -0.67% scale, 2.3 deg relative tilt
  14.16.10  tilted at the tree, span 149 deg, az 334.6, peak 10.5x, 8 windows, -4.5% scale, 5.7 deg tilt
  14.16.32  portrait still, span 62 deg, az 20.8, peak 6.0x, refinement REJECTED -> constant offset
Cross-validation: skyline matching independently placed 14.16.10 at 335.1 vs phase correlation's 334.6 — two methods that disagree wildly elsewhere agree to 0.5 deg here. Composite verified visually via red/green overlay: roofline, porch posts, windows, garage door, fence lattice all coincide.

EXIF REMOVES TWO FREE PARAMETERS. All four are Pixel 9 Pro Fold at 24mm equiv. Panoramas share the stitcher's px/deg (so q=d=1 pano-to-pano); the still is rectilinear so a pinhole model gives its scale outright (still_pxdeg()). Fitting scale as an unknown was fitting information already in the file. Note the pano stitcher compresses horizontally: 55.8 px/deg horizontal vs 79.5 vertical, aspect 1.43.

WINDOWED REFINEMENT + SANITY BOUNDS. Measuring offset in windows across the overlap recovers scale drift (linear in az) and relative tilt (sinusoid in az). Works on wide sweeps. On the narrow still, 8 windows over mostly-moving foliage returned a 109 deg tilt and +17% scale — physically impossible. Now rejected on bounds (|scale|<5%, |tilt|<15 deg, az spread>25 deg), falling back to the visually-verified constant offset. A bad refinement is worse than none.

TREE SWAY IS REAL (Devon, 2026-08-03): photos span 14:14-14:16, so crowns move between frames. Rigid cues (rooflines, fence lattice) are trustworthy; foliage is not. This is why the still's windowed refinement failed — its overlap is nearly all foliage. Argues for robust/rejecting fits and for weighting rigid structure.

SKYLINE DETECTOR BUG FOUND AND FIXED: the rule must stop at the FIRST SUSTAINED run of non-sky. Any rule that keeps descending (last-sky-row, deepest-sky-pixel) traces the fence bottom instead of the treeline, because the lattice fence and the tree canopy BOTH show sky through their gaps. Run-length (~6px at 1/8 scale) tolerates a single branch crossing an open column. Also now returns a per-column 'clipped' flag (obstruction runs past top of frame) — those columns record the crop, not the sky, and must be excluded from matching.

*** BLOCKER FOR ABSOLUTE CALIBRATION — TWO FINDINGS ***
1. THE STORED CALIBRATION IS NOT REUSABLE ACROSS DETECTOR VERSIONS. Applying saved fit.npy to a re-detected skyline gave a systematic +20.1 deg bias (RMS 21 deg), not scatter. The fitted horizon-row parameter c0 had silently absorbed the OLD detector's bias. Calibration must be stored with the detector version that produced it, or refitted whenever the classifier changes. This would recur silently every time the sky test is touched.
2. REFITTING IS UNDERDETERMINED. Of 10 edge fiducials only 6 have enough valid columns, against 5 free params (az0, span, c0, tiltA, tiltB). That fit reports a flattering 0.57 deg RMS while returning a 23 deg tilt — vs 12 deg previously established and physically deliberate. Meaningless residual.
This is exactly the fiducial-count limit predicted in the DECIDED WORKFLOW note, arriving on schedule. NOT fixed by more photo processing — fixed by the denser baseline sweep (60 deg ceiling, 10 deg steps), which both raises fiducial count and lifts the ceiling that capped four columns.

TO ENCODE INTO terminus/panorama.py:
  * register on pixels via circular phase correlation; keep detect_skyline for reporting and steep-band planning, NOT as the matcher
  * read scale from EXIF (still_pxdeg for rectilinear frames)
  * windowed refinement with sanity bounds and explicit fallback
  * version calibration against detector; refuse to apply a calibration produced by a different detector version
  * never blend seams away — visible seams are how a person checks the fit
  * composite is a spherical mosaic with per-region provenance, as designed

Artifact updated in place: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0e9cf5f6-40c1-4f8f-b1a6-5173d4a8fe93
PANORAMA TOOLING INVESTIGATION (Devon, 2026-08-03: 'look into panorama tools, cause we are doing basic panorama stuff here'). Correct — the hand-rolled registration is reimplementing standard photogrammetry badly. Findings:

HUGIN CLI TOOLCHAIN IS THE RIGHT TOOL. Maps 1:1 onto what was hand-rolled:
  cpfind          -> real feature matching (replaces phase correlation / skyline correlation)
  cpclean         -> control-point outlier rejection (replaces the ad-hoc sanity bounds)
  autooptimiser   -> solves YAW/PITCH/ROLL per image + lens distortion. Yaw/pitch/roll ARE azimuth/altitude/tilt; the hand-rolled 'scale drift + tilt sinusoid' model was re-deriving this with a cylindrical approximation instead of a spherical one.
  pano_modify --projection=2 -> equirectangular output, where x IS azimuth and y IS altitude. This is exactly terminus's canvas, for free.
  nona            -> rendering (replaces warp_into)
  pano_trafo      -> converts image<->panorama coordinates. Reads 'imgnum x y' triplets on stdin; -r reverses. This is how scope fiducials map into the mosaic and how a mosaic point maps back to a source photo.

DECISIVE FACT — MIXED INPUT PROJECTIONS. The .pto image (i) line carries a per-image projection type: f0 rectilinear, f1 panoramic/cylindrical, f2 circular fisheye, f3 full-frame fisheye, f4 PSphere/equirectangular. Mixed types in one project are supported. Devon's dataset is exactly that: three already-stitched phone panoramas (149-358 deg) plus one rectilinear still, jointly solved.

OPENCV IS RULED OUT — and NOT on dependency weight. cv2.detail (BestOf2NearestMatcher, BundleAdjusterRay, SphericalWarper) does the same math and pip-installs with aarch64 wheels, so it would have suited the Pi target. But its camera model assumes PINHOLE inputs with a focal length, which is meaningless for a 358 deg panorama. It cannot represent three of the four inputs. Verified cv2 5.0.0 installs fine in a scratch venv; rejected on capability, not cost.

WHY THIS LIKELY UNBLOCKS THE ABSOLUTE CALIBRATION. Current blocker is 6 usable fiducials against 5 free params. Hugin solves ALL internal geometry (relative orientation, lens, distortion), so terminus's remaining job collapses to a single 3-parameter rotation (yaw/pitch/roll) of the whole solution onto the sky frame. 6 fiducials against 3 params is workable — possibly with data already in hand, before tonight's denser sweep.

DIVISION OF LABOUR: Hugin does photogrammetry; terminus does astronomy. terminus keeps the sky/terrain classifier, detect_skyline, the absolute north reference from scope fiducials, the horizon mask, .hrz/Stellarium export, and measurement planning — none of which Hugin has any concept of.

INSTALL PROBLEM (real, affects the dependency decision): hugin and enblend are NOT in Ubuntu 22.04 (jammy). PIPELINE THAT WORKS END TO END (this is Devon's per-image architecture, realised):
  1. segment each source photo -> binary sky mask PNG
  2. rewrite the .pto to point at the masks instead of the photos
  3. nona warps the masks through the SAME solved geometry
  4. combine warped masks (mean > 127) into the equirect sky map
  5. per-column first sustained non-sky run -> horizon
  6. fit 3-param rotation to scope fiducials
Result: RMS 2.76 deg, yaw 136.50, pitch +3.94, tilt 4.75.

WHY 2.76 IS NOT WORSE THAN THE HEURISTIC'S 2.23: the fit absorbs a UNIFORM ALTITUDE BIAS into its pitch term, so RMS is structurally blind to exactly the error class being fixed. This is why round after round of tuning 'improved' a number while the picture did not improve. Decisive evidence is instead (a) all three visible failures gone, (b) segmentation independently recovers THE SAME YAW 136.50 as the colour method. LESSON: for this problem, judge by looking at the image; keep RMS only as a guard against gross error.

Best heuristic found = hue (r<b+12 & g<b+10) + local adaptive brightness (0.30 x local p92 over +-15 deg azimuth) + upper envelope +-1 deg across azimuth. The envelope is what fixed rooflines: a gap narrower than mask resolution is not usable sky.

WHY IT CONVERGED NOW AND NOT BEFORE: the earlier attempt added columns in the order they happened to be measured and ran out at 8 while still moving (1.62 deg spread). Ordering by information gain front-loads the columns that constrain rotation — the planner asked for 170, 320, 90, 240 first, the steep parts of the horizon spread around the compass — so the later additions are precisely the ones that SHOULD NOT move it. That is what makes the stability test meaningful rather than merely a question of running out of data.

PRACTICAL RESULT: seven well-chosen columns, roughly twenty minutes of telescope time, reach the same orientation as a thirty-six column blind circle that took most of a night. This validates the adaptive design end to end on real hardware.

EXCLUSIONS (stated, not fitted): az 60 and az 190 were measured during the dawn brightening — the sky reference climbed 25 -> 82 counts mid-run — so they straddle the night/day model boundary and the two detectors disagree on them by 15-22 deg. They remain on disk with their profiles; only the fit excludes them.

FINAL: yaw 135.81 (converged) / 135.00 (twelve-fiducial fit, used for the rendered views; 0.81 deg apart, well inside the mask's 2.5 deg quantisation). Previously published: 130.25. NET MOVEMENT +4.75 to +5.56 deg, residual 3.10 -> 0.55.

Report republished at https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0e9cf5f6-40c1-4f8f-b1a6-5173d4a8fe93

title: The planner can recommend columns the Sun guard will refuse
description:
FOUND 2026-08-04 while checking whether a three-column 120 deg configuration (terminus-39) could
be measured. plan.py ranks candidates purely by information gain — next_column and rank_columns
call information() and nothing else. It has no notion of whether a column can actually be
reached. Pointer.point_to will then refuse it, and the planner has no way to know that happened
or to re-plan around it.

MEASURED, Sun at az 123.0 alt 55.8, anchoring a 120 deg trio on az 281.7:
    az 281.7   endpoint sep 116.7   path min 116.7   reachable
    az  41.7   endpoint sep  81.0   path min  81.0   reachable
    az 161.7   endpoint sep  59.4   path min   7.5   REFUSED

Note the third row carefully: the ENDPOINT is 59.4 deg from the Sun, comfortably outside the 30
deg cone, and the SLEW PATH passes within 7.5 deg. This is the EQ-goto-swings-past-the-Sun case
the guard was written for, caught in a live geometry check rather than in a postmortem. Worth
recording against terminus-3.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE UNDER THE THREE-COLUMN SCHEME. Today a refused column is an inconvenience —
drop it, pick the next best, the stability rule absorbs the loss. Under terminus-39 the value is
in a specific geometric CONFIGURATION (equally spaced points being D-optimal for the pitch/tilt
sinusoid). The Sun does not merely remove one column, it can destroy the configuration, and the
remaining two may be far worse conditioned than a different reachable trio would have been.

FIX: give the ranking a feasibility filter. Candidates whose path_min_sep falls inside the cone
are excluded BEFORE the information criterion is applied, not after. That is a small change —
next_column and rank_columns take an optional predicate — but it has to be the right way round:
filtering after ranking gives you the best infeasible column and a fallback, while filtering
before gives you the best FEASIBLE configuration, which is a different and better answer.

Feasibility is also TIME-DEPENDENT, which the planner currently has no concept of. A column
refused now may be fine in two hours, and under a deadline (terminus-17) the right move is
sometimes to wait rather than to substitute. At minimum, report WHY a candidate was excluded and
when it becomes available, so the operator can decide.

Do not solve this by widening the cone or by checking only endpoints. Both have been tried
elsewhere and both are how a tube ends up pointed at the Sun.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #8. plan.partition/next_column/rank_columns take an injected reachability predicate, applied BEFORE the criterion and before truncation. sweep.reachable_now builds it from the whole slew path (not the endpoint) — the ticket's case reproduced as a test: columns whose endpoint clears the cone while the path passes through it. sweep.hours_until_endpoint_clear reports the wait, named for what it measures since it cannot promise a slew. Nothing reachable returns (None, -inf) rather than raising.

title: Solar sighting: absolute pointing calibration in daylight, behind a filter
description:
IDEA 2026-08-04 (Devon): 'if we start this with a sun filter and you search for the sun, can we
use that information?'

YES, AND IT FILLS THE EXACT GAP. The mount's absolute pointing error is currently only knowable
by plate solving, which needs stars, which means night. But the photo workflow wants DAYLIGHT:
segmentation needs colour and scene context, and matching the phone panorama's appearance argues
for the same illumination (terminus-32). So the one calibration that matters is unavailable
precisely when the work happens.

The Sun's az/alt is known exactly from ephemeris at any instant. Sight it, compare commanded
against actual, and you have the mount's absolute error in one pointing, at noon. The 3.7 deg
polar drift that invalidated a published orientation would have been visible BEFORE the session
instead of days after it.

THE DEVICE ALREADY HAS A NATIVE SUN MODE — this does not need inventing. From seestar_alp:
    iscope_start_view, params: { mode: sun }
    Event: View, state: working, mode: sun, tracking: false, planet_correction: false
  (device/actions.py:13-15; front/app.py handles 'sun' alongside moon/planet/scenery/star, and a
  recorded view state shows mode 'solar_sys' with target_type 'sun')
Use ZWO's mode. Do not build a solar path out of raw gotos.

IT COMPOUNDS WITH terminus-39. That scheme needs FEW, VERY GOOD columns — three at 120 deg
instead of seven. Solar calibration removes the mount-error term from every fiducial, so each
column is worth more. Three excellent columns is a far easier claim than three noisy ones.

PRIOR ART, cite and use — no novelty available here and that is fine:
  * classical astro-geodetic azimuth: theodolite plus sun fixes. Patat 2011 names it directly.
  * Urquhart, Kurtz & Kleissl (2016), 'Sky camera geometric calibration using solar
    observations', AMT 9(9):4279-4294, doi:10.5194/amt-9-4279-2016 — solves fisheye orientation
    purely from the Sun's ephemeris position, open access.
  * Lalonde, Narasimhan & Efros (2010) for the CV framing.
A proven method makes the pipeline more credible, not less.

=== SAFETY. READ BEFORE WRITING ANY CODE. ===

SOFTWARE CANNOT VERIFY THAT A FILTER IS INSTALLED. There is no readback for 'is there glass on
the front'. Every solar capability is gated on a human promise, and a wrong promise destroys the
sensor instantly and irreversibly. This is the only feature discussed in this project where the
failure mode is unrecoverable hardware loss.

Therefore:
  * SunGuard is NOT to be weakened, parameterised, or made conditional. Its job is protecting the
    default path and it must keep doing that unchanged. CLAUDE.md: 'never suppress SunGuard'.
  * A solar sighting is a SEPARATE, EXPLICITLY INVOKED path — not a mode flag that relaxes the
    existing guard.
  * NO CONFIG FLAG. A 'solar_filter_installed = true' left in config.toml from a previous session
    is exactly how this destroys hardware. Confirmation must happen at the moment of use, in the
    invocation, and must not persist.
  * Prefer the device's own sun mode, which at least means ZWO's firmware knows what is being
    attempted.
  * The run must refuse to proceed into any other operation while in solar mode, and must exit it
    explicitly.

If any of that feels burdensome, the correct response is not to implement this. The horizon can
be measured without it; a destroyed camera cannot be undone.

OPEN QUESTIONS: does the S50 ship a filter and does the app gate sun mode on it? Does sun mode
report anything about filter state (almost certainly not, but check)? How accurately can the
solar centroid be measured through the filter, since that sets the calibration's precision? And
the Sun moves 15 deg/hour, so how fast does the calibration age — that is measurable and worth
knowing.
notes:
THE FILTER BECOMES DETECTABLE 2026-08-04 (Devon): 'you can take a photo then I can add the filter and then the filter is known because now the photo is dark.'

This answers the objection recorded above. A solar filter attenuates by roughly 10^5 — not a
subtle signal, but the largest brightness change the instrument can experience short of a lens
cap. Photograph a safe patch of sky, have the user fit the filter, photograph the SAME pointing
again, and the ratio is unmistakable. The precondition stops being a human promise and becomes a
measurement.

THREE REQUIREMENTS THAT MAKE THE CHECK AS STRONG AS THE IDEA:

1. EXPOSURE MUST BE LOCKED ACROSS THE PAIR, and today proved why. With auto-exposure the scope
   compensates: measured at az 281.7, a real sky-to-roof transition collapsed to a 2% luminance
   step (99.0 -> 101.5) purely because exposure was unlocked. Unlocked, the scope would raise
   gain until the filtered frame looked normal and THE TEST WOULD PASS WITH NO FILTER FITTED.
   lock_exposure already exists with readback verification; this must sit on top of it and must
   fail closed if the lock cannot be verified.

2. MEASURE THE ATTENUATION, DO NOT JUST CHECK FOR DARK. Darkness alone cannot separate a solar
   filter (10^5) from a photographic ND that someone assumed was adequate (10^1-10^2) — at a
   short daytime exposure both render black, and the second one destroys the sensor. The rigorous
   form: with the filter fitted, RAISE EXPOSURE until the same scene reads usably again; the
   exposure ratio IS the attenuation factor. Require a threshold (>= 10^3.5) rather than a
   boolean. This converts the dangerous near-miss from undetectable into rejected.

3. IT IS ALSO A CONTINUOUS INVARIANT, not only a precondition. Through a proper filter the solar
   frame is near-black with a small bright disc. If the filter loosens or falls — a real physical
   failure mode, which is why solar filters are meant to be secured — the frame saturates
   completely within one frame. Monitor it for the whole pointing and abort on saturation. A
   precondition checked once cannot see this; the invariant can.

RESIDUAL RISK, stated honestly: a user who deliberately defeats both the measured precondition
and the continuous invariant. That is not something the software can reach.

=== CONSIDER THE DAYTIME MOON FIRST ===
The Moon is above the horizon in daylight roughly half the month, its ephemeris position is
exactly as well known as the Sun's, and it requires NO FILTER AND NO SAFETY ARCHITECTURE AT ALL.
If the goal is absolute azimuth in daylight, the Moon supplies it for free whenever it is up.
That makes the solar path the fallback for the half of the month the Moon is unavailable, rather
than the primary route — and it means the first implementation can be built and validated with
zero risk to anyone's hardware, then extended to the Sun once the geometry is proven.
Bright planets (Venus) are a third option in principle but are hard to acquire in daylight.

Sequence this: Moon first, Sun second. The measurement chain is identical; only the safety
apparatus differs.
REFRAMED 2026-08-04. Devon: 'right now we are solving for daytime in case the person has not plate solved' — and 'moon is great too'. That changes what this bead IS.

ALT-AZ POINTING IS NOT AVAILABLE, so the frame problem cannot be sidestepped. seestar_alp's
Alpaca layer hardcodes canslewaltaz -> False (device/telescope.py:745-757); slewtoaltaz exists
only as a stub. The Seestar points by RA/Dec, full stop. terminus's use of RA/Dec goto was forced,
not chosen. (Worth noting because horizon mapping needs no tracking — terrain does not move — so
alt-az would otherwise be the natural frame, and would also remove the field rotation that
couples slope and roll in terminus-39. It is simply not on offer.)

THEREFORE A CELESTIAL SIGHTING IS NOT A CALIBRATION CHECK, IT IS THE ALIGNMENT. If RA/Dec is the
only way to point, and the RA/Dec frame is meaningless until the mount is aligned, then a user who
has not plate solved cannot point at anything meaningfully. Sighting the Moon and syncing anchors
the mount's frame to the sky IN DAYLIGHT, after which terminus's existing RA/Dec machinery runs
unchanged. That is the whole daytime story: one object, one sync, no night session.

THE DIVISION OF LABOUR MATCHES THE OBSERVED ERROR AXES EXACTLY:
    accelerometer -> ALTITUDE.  Recorded polar error in altitude: 0.2 deg. Already fine.
    Moon or Sun   -> AZIMUTH.   Recorded polar error in azimuth: 3.7 deg. The one that mattered.
Gravity is structurally blind to azimuth; a celestial object is the only thing that supplies it.
Each sensor covers precisely what the other cannot, and this is geometry rather than a
coincidence of this site.

SEQUENCING CONFIRMED: MOON FIRST, and not as the timid option — as the PRIMARY path that happens
also to be the safe one. No filter, no attenuation check, no continuous saturation invariant, no
residual risk to anyone's hardware. Build and validate the entire measurement chain against the
Moon, prove the geometry, and only then extend to the Sun for the half of the month the Moon is
unavailable. Everything in the safety section above applies to the Sun extension and to nothing
else.

DEPENDS ON terminus-42 for the coarse acquisition (compass to find it, accelerometer for tilt) and
feeds terminus-39, which wants few excellent columns rather than many mediocre ones. Check whether
the protocol exposes a sync method, and whether the device's own alignment routine can be driven
with a daylight target.
ECOSYSTEM GAP CONFIRMED 2026-08-04 (Devon, who owns the device): 'the Seestar app gives you nighttime alignment, but there's no daytime equivalent that you can use.' So this is not a terminus convenience — it is a capability the VENDOR'S OWN APP LACKS.

Two consequences.

1. MOST OF THE CHAIN IS ALREADY SHIPPED. seestar_alp shows the device supports mode: moon and
   mode: sun alongside scenery and star (front/app.py:3309, device/actions.py:13). ZWO already
   solved ACQUISITION for both targets. What is missing is the SYNC that turns a successful
   acquisition into an anchored RA/Dec frame. terminus adds the last step, not the whole chain —
   which materially reduces the work and removes the riskiest part (finding a target with a
   compass of unknown quality).

2. IT ANSWERS THE OPEN COMPASS QUESTION FOR FREE. If the app's moon or sun mode reliably puts the
   target in frame at this site, that IS the empirical evidence that the compass is adequate for
   acquisition. No code needed — just open the app and try it. Do this before building anything.

ADOPTION ANGLE, and it feeds terminus-22: daytime alignment is useful to people who do not care
about horizons at all — solar observers, terrestrial viewers, anyone wanting to be aligned before
dark rather than spending the first clear hour on it. That is a reason to install terminus that
has nothing to do with its actual purpose, and every install is a potential contributor site.

Record in terminus-30.7 tier 3 (engineering contributions): a working daylight alignment for a
device whose vendor application cannot do it. That is concrete, checkable, and exactly the kind
of claim JOSS reviews — the software IS the contribution.
ACHIEVED 2026-08-04, by an easier route than this bead proposed, and the result changes the design.

WE FOUND THE MOON AND MEASURED ABSOLUTE POINTING — in daylight, through heavy smoke, on a target
invisible to both the naked eye and a single frame, WITH NO FILTER AND NO SAFETY APPARATUS.

Method, accidental but reproducible: three frames at az 278.9, altitudes 5.7 / 9.7 / 13.7. The
on-target frame minus the mean of the two off-target frames, each normalised by its own median.
The instrumental gradient is FIXED IN THE FRAME while the Moon is not, so the subtraction cancels
the gradient and leaves the disc.

    disc excess           +0.449% of sky brightness
    radial profile        falls monotonically from centre, crosses zero at r ~ 450-500 px
                          against a geometric limb at 391 px — slightly wide, consistent with a
                          scattering halo through smoke
    centroid offset       95 px = 0.063 deg (~4 arcmin) from field centre
    per-pixel contrast    0.45%, against ~1% per-pixel noise — invisible in any single frame

An earlier attempt FAILED because it compared the disc against an annulus WITHIN one frame, where
the instrumental gradient (0.3-1.0%, and negative at centre) swamped a 0.45% signal. The gradient
is the confound; differencing is what removes it. Record that: the naive test is worse than
useless because it returns a confident negative.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE PLAN:
  * THE TARGET DOES NOT NEED TO BE VISIBLE. It needs a differential pair. That is a much weaker
    requirement than 'acquire and centre a visible object', and it survives haze, thin cloud and
    daylight sky brightness.
  * THE SUN BECOMES LARGELY UNNECESSARY. The Moon works at 0.45% contrast in conditions where
    nobody can see it. The filter, the attenuation threshold, the continuous saturation invariant
    and the residual hardware risk were all in service of the Sun as primary. Demote all of it:
    the Moon is the primary path in essentially every condition, and the Sun is a rare fallback
    for the part of the month the Moon is below the horizon or too close to the Sun.
  * ACQUISITION IS NOT THE HARD PART. The mount landed within ~4 arcmin of the ephemeris position
    unaided, so the compass-to-acquire step in terminus-42 may not be needed at all when the mount
    is already roughly aligned. It matters for a COLD start, not a warm one.

DELIBERATE VERSION TO BUILD: point at the ephemeris position, capture, offset by 3-5 deg,
capture, subtract, fit a disc, report the centroid offset as the pointing error. Two pointings and
two frames. Note the off-target frame must be far enough that the disc is fully outside it (>1.5
deg) but close enough that the sky gradient is similar (a few degrees).

CAVEAT ON THE NUMBER: the 0.063 deg centroid came from clipped positive weights on a noisy field
and should be treated as order-of-magnitude, not calibrated. A proper fit of a limb-darkened disc
with the halo modelled would do better. The claim is 'a few arcminutes', not '3.8'.
DEMONSTRATED END TO END 2026-08-04 evening. The mechanism is scope_sync, and it works.

    scope_sync [ra_hours, dec_deg]      (seestar_device.py:1142, via sync_target)

SEQUENCE, measured on a scope that had just been power-cycled and had NEVER been aligned:
    BEFORE   mount RA 9.12472 Dec  +9.25194  -> 8.149 deg from the Sun's true position
    scope_sync to the Sun's ephemeris RA/Dec
    AFTER    mount RA 8.97861 Dec +17.12833  -> 0.003 deg
The mount's model went from 8.15 deg adrift to agreeing with the sky to THREE THOUSANDTHS of a
degree, in daylight, with no stars. That is the capability the vendor app does not have.

AND IT HOLDS. Deliberately slewed 7 deg away until the disc vanished (sd 0.28), then issued a
plain goto to the Sun's ephemeris position: disc reacquired 0.258 deg from frame centre. No
search, no joystick, no human. Note the sync itself was taken with the disc 0.114 deg off centre,
so it carried that error from the start; the 7 deg round trip added only ~0.14 deg.

=== THE DISTINCTION THAT CONFUSED THIS ALL DAY ===
POLAR ALIGNMENT is mechanical — the wedge. It survives power cycles. It is what the afternoon's
thumb-screw session corrected.
MOUNT MODEL is the scope's belief about its own orientation. A power cycle WIPES IT, and an
unaligned mount's RA/Dec frame is arbitrary.
The morning's 3.045 deg was both mixed together. The evening's 8.149 deg was pure model error
with the corrected polar alignment sitting underneath, untouched. Measuring one while assuming
the other is why an entire afternoon of gotos searched coordinate space that did not correspond
to the sky. STATE WHICH ONE IS BEING MEASURED, ALWAYS.
