title: Read the scope's own compass and accelerometer to bootstrap orientation
description:
IDEA 2026-08-04 (Devon): 'the scope has a compass and it has an accelerometer, so you should be
able to get rough az and tilt.'

CONFIRMED IN THE PROTOCOL, from seestar_alp:
    get_device_state, params: { keys: [ balance_sensor, compass_sensor ] }   (device/actions.py:10)
    get_sensor_calibration -> result.compassSensor {x, y, z, x11, y11, x12, y12}
    set_sensor_calibration
    get_device_state keys also include location_lon_lat
seestar_alp applies magnetic declination to the compass bearing itself (seestar_device.py:1284).
So the scope can report where it is, which way is down, and roughly which way is north — enough
to bootstrap with NO user input and no phone. That matters for the one-device story
(terminus-38).

THE TWO SENSORS ARE NOT EQUAL AND THE ASYMMETRY IS THE DESIGN.
  * GRAVITY IS TRUSTWORTHY. An accelerometer gives tilt to well under a degree, and gravity has
    no local anomalies at this scale. Use it.
  * MAGNETISM IS NOT. It needs declination correction and is distorted by nearby iron — which
    describes a telescope, a parked car, and a house. Use it ONLY TO ACQUIRE, never as an answer.
This is the same conclusion clear-horizons reached from the other direction: its capture.js
corrects a magnetic heading by the World Magnetic Model and still leaves a manual offset for
local iron, because the model cannot fix what the local field does.

THE CHAIN THIS ENABLES, coarse to fine, each stage only needing to hand off to the next:
    accelerometer  -> tilt, sub-degree, trustworthy
    compass        -> azimuth to a few degrees, enough to POINT AT something
    Sun (filtered) -> azimuth to arcminutes (terminus-41)
The Sun is half a degree across and the brightest object in the sky, so a compass that is five
degrees off still lands it inside a modest search. Rough is sufficient for acquisition; it is not
sufficient for an answer.

WHY THE ACCELEROMETER ALONE WOULD NOT HAVE SAVED US, and this is the argument for the whole
chain rather than just the cheap half: the polar error that invalidated the published orientation
was 3.7 deg IN AZIMUTH and 0.2 deg in altitude. Gravity would have confirmed the altitude was
fine and been COMPLETELY BLIND to the azimuth error, because azimuth is not a gravity-referenced
quantity. The accelerometer is necessary and not sufficient. The Sun is the part that catches
what actually went wrong.

KEEP THE DISTINCTION STRAIGHT: this calibrates the MOUNT, not the PANORAMA. The panorama's tilt
comes from how the phone was held and remains a fitted quantity in orient.py. What is gained is
fiducials with the mount-error term removed — which is precisely what makes three columns viable
instead of seven (terminus-39).

WORTH CHECKING WHILE HERE: do the phone frames carry pitch and roll in EXIF as well as
GPSImgDirection? If so the panorama's tilt could also be measured rather than fitted, and the
fit would be left solving yaw alone. The earlier EXIF read only looked for direction.

FIRST STEP, read-only and safe at any time of day: call get_device_state for balance_sensor and
compass_sensor, log what comes back, and compare the compass bearing against the known azimuth of
a landmark. That single comparison tells us how bad the local magnetic environment is at this
site, which decides whether the compass is usable even for acquisition.

title: Aimed at the Moon and missed it: the RA/Dec frame is not trustworthy right now
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-04 17:2x UTC, daylight, Sun 108 deg away. Devon: 'the moon is not presently
visible... bet you could validate that' and then 'give it a shot, just don't get anywhere near
the sun'.

Pointed at the Moon's ephemeris position (az 278.92, alt +9.68) and at +/-4 deg in altitude:
    alt  +9.7   lum 104.9   gradient p99 1.50   max 146
    alt +13.7   lum 105.7   gradient p99 1.12   max 150
    alt  +5.7   lum 102.3   gradient p99 1.58   max 139
All three frames are FLAT BLUE SKY — uniform, unsaturated, no structure. Not defocused terrain:
terrain at any distance shows some brightness structure, and it is not blue.

TWO FINDINGS.

1. az 278.9 IS OPEN from at least alt 5.7 to 13.7 as seen FROM THE SCOPE. The mask's interpolated
   3.6 deg is consistent with that, so the mask was not wrong here — see the viewpoint note below
   before concluding anything about the eye/mask disagreement.

2. THE MOON WAS NOT IN THE FIELD, AND THAT IS THE REAL RESULT. The field is 0.72 x 1.28 deg and
   the Moon is 0.5 deg across; pointed correctly it would dominate the frame. Its absence means
   the mount's pointing error exceeds half a degree and plausibly runs to several. We aimed at a
   known celestial object through the current RA/Dec frame and missed.

   That is a LIVE demonstration of the gap terminus-41 exists to close, and it is worth far more
   than the argument it replaces: not 'a plate solve months ago found 3.7 deg of drift' but 'the
   frame is untrustworthy right now, measured this afternoon, in daylight, with no stars
   involved'. It also means every RA/Dec goto terminus has issued today carried an unknown
   pointing error, including the column walk at az 281.7 — the ALTITUDES are still valid because
   the scan is differential, but the AZIMUTH labels on those measurements are only as good as the
   mount's alignment, which is exactly what is in question.

NEXT STEP, safe at any time the Moon is up and far from the Sun: SEARCH for it. A bounded spiral
around the predicted position, capturing until the disc appears, measures the pointing error
directly — and that measurement IS the acquisition step of terminus-41. The scope also has a
native moon mode (iscope_start_view mode: moon), which is ZWO's own solution to the same problem
and should be tried first; note that switching view modes runs into terminus-15 (stop_view is
unreliable), so do it deliberately rather than mid-sweep.
notes:
WEAKENED 2026-08-04, same session. This bead concluded 'the Moon was not in the field, therefore the pointing error exceeds half a degree'. That inference is NOT established.

Devon: 'it's super hazy from smoke in that direction, so that may be why I can't see it.'

Heavy smoke at 10 deg altitude does two things at once: it extincts the Moon and it brightens the
sky around it. A daytime Moon is far lower contrast than intuition suggests even in clear air, and
under those conditions it can approach zero. So the Moon may well have been IN the field at
contrast below detection.

The large-scale check supports absence but does not prove it: a 0.52 deg Moon is 782 px across in
a 1080x1920 frame and the measured large-scale variation was only 2-3% with no coherent blob. That
rules out a NORMAL-contrast Moon. It does not rule out one flattened by smoke.

HONEST STATEMENT: the Moon was not DETECTABLE at the predicted position. Pointing error and
atmospheric extinction are both live explanations and this observation cannot separate them.

TO SEPARATE THEM, either: repeat on a clear day, when a non-detection really would indicate
pointing error; or use the scope's native moon mode, which if it acquires successfully proves the
pointing is adequate and the smoke was the issue. The second is cheaper and available now.

The broader point this bead was filed for still stands and does not depend on the Moon: the RA/Dec
frame's accuracy is UNVERIFIED, and terminus has no way to check it in daylight. That is what
terminus-41 is for. This observation simply failed to measure the error rather than demonstrating
it.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
AMBIGUITY LARGELY RESOLVED, later the same session, by the solar sighting rather than by any
further Moon work. The notes above left two live explanations for the non-detection — pointing
error or smoke extinction — and said this observation could not separate them.

The solar sighting separated them from the other side. Sighting the Sun through the filter
measured the pointing error DIRECTLY: 8.149 deg before correction, driven to 0.003 deg by
scope_sync. Eight degrees is sixteen times the half-degree the Moon argument needed. At that
error the Moon was nowhere near the field, and smoke is not required to explain its absence.

So this bead's ORIGINAL conclusion was right, and the retraction above over-corrected: the
pointing error did exceed half a degree, by a wide margin.

ONE HONEST CAVEAT, which is why this says 'largely'. The mount was physically disturbed between
the two observations — Devon re-seated the plate and turned the adjustment screws several times
— so the 8.149 deg figure is not proof of the mount's state during the Moon frames. What it does
establish is that errors of this size were real on this mount that day, which makes pointing
error the sufficient explanation and smoke an unnecessary one. The methodological point from the
notes stands and is worth keeping: a daytime Moon under smoke is a poor instrument for measuring
pointing error, and the Sun behind a filter is a far better one. That is terminus-41, now
demonstrated rather than argued.

title: The mask is specific to the scope's position, and nothing says so
description:
NOTICED 2026-08-04 while resolving a disagreement about whether the Moon was behind terrain.
Devon judged it blocked; the scope, pointed at the same azimuth, saw open sky at every altitude
sampled. Both can be true, because THEY ARE NOT IN THE SAME PLACE.

The mask records the horizon as seen from wherever the tripod stood. A person at a window, on a
deck, or ten metres across the yard has a different horizon — and how different depends entirely
on how close the nearest obstruction is. Parallax for a ridge two kilometres away is nil. For a
fence five metres away, moving two metres sideways swings its apparent altitude by degrees, and
moving toward or away from it changes it more.

That is a real limitation of the product and nothing in the mask, the exports, or the README
mentions it. A user who measures from the patio and then observes from the lawn is using a mask
that does not describe their sky. Worse, the error is largest exactly where the horizon is
highest and most consequential — near obstructions are the tall ones.

WHAT TO DO, in increasing order of effort:
  * STATE IT. The mask meta already carries lat/lon; it should also carry a plain-language note
    that the horizon is position-specific and that near obstructions make it sharply so. One
    sentence in the README and a comment in the exported files.
  * QUANTIFY IT WHERE POSSIBLE. terminus-32 proposes recording focuser position per column, which
    is a DISTANCE estimate. Distance is exactly what sets the parallax sensitivity, so a mask
    carrying per-column distance can also carry per-column 'how far can you move before this
    column is wrong'. That turns a caveat into a number.
  * For contributor bundles (terminus-22), record the tripod position more precisely than the
    site coordinates, since a returned mask is only re-judgeable against the spot it was taken
    from.

Also relevant to the DEM/lidar validation (terminus-24): a synthetic skyline ray-traced from a
coordinate is exquisitely sensitive to that coordinate for near obstructions. Comparing against
lidar requires knowing where the scope stood to a metre or so, not to GPS-typical accuracy.
notes:
PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-04. This bead was filed on the theory that Devon's 'the Moon is below my horizon' and the scope's 'open sky' could both be true because they were observing from different positions. THAT WAS NOT THE EXPLANATION. The scope found flat blue sky at az 278.9 across alt 5.7 to 13.7 — no terrain at all — and Devon subsequently identified heavy smoke haze as why the Moon was not visible to him. There was no parallax discrepancy to explain.

THE LIMITATION IS STILL REAL AND STILL UNDOCUMENTED, which is why this bead stays open: the mask
records the horizon from wherever the tripod stood, and for a near obstruction a few metres of
observer displacement moves its apparent altitude by degrees. Nothing in the mask, the exports or
the README says so. That is worth fixing on its own merits.

But the motivating incident was misattributed, and the correction matters because the original
text implied field evidence for a parallax problem that was never observed. Treat the limitation
as reasoned from geometry, not as measured here.
close_reason: PR #13. Position-specificity stated in the mask header, the .hrz header and the README, with numbers: a 2 m fence at 5 m shifts +11.9 deg for 2 m nearer, -5.9 for 2 m further, 0 along an extended fence, -1.4 past a narrow post; a 100 m ridge at 2 km moves 0.003. Closer and further are not mirror images and the text says so. Stellarium cannot carry the note (its format forbids comments) and the README says that too. Phrased as geometry per the ticket's own correction that the motivating incident was smoke haze, not parallax.

title: EPIC: guided EQ alignment, day or night
description:
GOAL (Devon, 2026-08-04): 'show an interface to a person and then re-solve as they make
adjustments. We can estimate adjustments by looking at the change in the magnetometer and
accelerometer to give live feedback, but only finally resolve off of solving off the sun (or
plate solving). This replicates the behavior of the seestar app, but for the sun as well, so a
person can set up EQ night or day.'

The Seestar app aligns at night only. There is no daytime equivalent (terminus-41). This epic
supplies one, and the same interface serves both: stars after dark, the Sun in daylight.

=== THE ARCHITECTURE: TWO RATES ===

FAST CHANNEL — onboard sensors, continuous, RELATIVE. Updates many times a second while the
user is physically adjusting the mount. Tells them 'you are turning the right way, keep going,
slow down, stop.' Never trusted as absolute.

SLOW CHANNEL — a celestial fix, roughly 45 seconds, ABSOLUTE. The Sun by day (validated today,
terminus-41), stars or a plate solve by night. Resets the fast channel's zero.

This is the standard pattern for disciplining a fast noisy sensor with a slow accurate
reference, and today's measurements say it will work here — see the children for which sensor
carries which axis, because they are NOT interchangeable.

=== THE INTERFACE MUST BE MECHANISM-AGNOSTIC ===

Devon: 'don't assume thumb screws, that's specific to my wedge.' Correct, and the live channel
is what makes this possible. If the display shows REMAINING ERROR IN DEGREES and updates while
the user moves the mount, the software never needs to know what is being moved. Thumb screws,
knobs, a worm drive, a sliding plate, or shoving the tripod are all identical to it. The user
stops when the number reaches zero.

So: do NOT model wedges, do NOT calibrate degrees-per-turn, do NOT ask what hardware they have.
Report degrees, update live, let the human close the loop. Any per-hardware calibration is an
optional refinement and must never be a prerequisite.

=== WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE ===

Today's manual version took the mount from 3.045 deg of pointing error to under a tenth, in
about twenty minutes of turn-measure-repeat, in daylight. The error it removed is the same class
that silently invalidated a published horizon orientation by 4.75 deg (terminus-30.7). Every
fiducial terminus takes inherits its session's alignment error, so this is upstream of the
project's core measurement, not a side feature.

It is also the strongest tier-3 claim in the register: a working daylight alignment for a device
whose vendor application cannot do it.

Children: fast channel, solar solve, and the interface surface.

title: Fast channel: live adjustment feedback from the onboard sensors
description:
The continuous half of the guided alignment loop (terminus-45). Reads balance_sensor and
compass_sensor and reports how far the mount has moved WHILE the user is moving it. Relative
only; the celestial fix supplies truth.

=== THE TWO AXES ARE NOT SYMMETRIC. THIS IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. ===

ELEVATION comes from GRAVITY and is ABSOLUTE, not merely relative. Measured 2026-08-04: gz held
0.6459-0.6509 across pointings spanning 90 deg of azimuth and 15 deg of altitude — a spread of
0.005, about 0.4 deg of axis direction. The sensor board sits in the base with its z-axis along
the polar axis (expected gz for a polar-axis vector at latitude 39.79 is 0.6400; measured 0.646).
So the polar ELEVATION can be read directly and continuously, to a few tenths of a degree,
without any celestial reference at all.

AZIMUTH IS INVISIBLE TO GRAVITY, BY GEOMETRY. Rotating the base about the vertical sweeps the
polar axis around a cone and leaves the angle between that axis and gravity unchanged. So gz does
not move and the accelerometer reports nothing. This is not a sensor limitation to engineer
around — it is why the azimuth error is the one that keeps going undetected (July: 3.7 deg
azimuth, 0.2 deg altitude; today: 3.2 deg RA-like, 0.29 deg Dec-like — same story twice).

AZIMUTH THEREFORE COMES FROM THE MAGNETOMETER, AND ONLY AS A DELTA. Measured today, the
magnetometer disagrees with the gravity-derived body rotation by up to 21.8 deg across six
headings — so its absolute bearing is unusable. Its CHANGE over a small adjustment should be far
better, and that is all the fast channel needs.

MANDATORY: APPLY THE STORED CALIBRATION. Raw horizontal magnitude ranged 43-133 across headings
(a factor of three, pure hard-iron). Applying the device's own coefficients from
get_sensor_calibration — offsets (78.478, 19.929), matrix [[2.42114,-0.022043],[-0.022043,
2.71981]] — collapses that to 114-125. Anyone reading compass_sensor raw and skipping this gets
nonsense. The 'direction' field the device reports appears not to apply it, or applies it
differently; do not use that field.

=== WHAT IT MUST DO ===
  * poll get_device_state {keys:[balance_sensor, compass_sensor]} at a few Hz;
  * report ELEVATION as an absolute angle against the site latitude;
  * report AZIMUTH as a signed change since the last celestial fix, never as a bearing;
  * degrade honestly: if the magnetometer is behaving badly (magnitude drifting after
    calibration, which indicates a nearby ferrous object), say so and fall back to
    'adjust, then re-solve' rather than showing a confident wrong number.

=== WHAT IT MUST NOT DO ===
  * never present the magnetometer's absolute heading as an answer;
  * never assume the sensors see the OTA — they do not, they are in the base and blind to the
    declination axis entirely (gz unchanged across a 15 deg altitude change);
  * never require a per-hardware calibration. The user watches a number and stops when it is
    zero; that works for any wedge (terminus-45).

title: Slow channel: absolute fix from the Sun, and the gotchas that cost us today
description:
The authoritative half of the guided alignment loop (terminus-45). Point at a celestial object of
known ephemeris position, compare where the mount says it is, and that difference is the pointing
error. Validated end-to-end on 2026-08-04 — the manual version took the mount from 3.045 deg to
under a tenth in about twenty minutes.

=== IT WORKS, AND HERE IS THE MEASURED SEQUENCE ===
    iscope_start_view {mode: sun}       enters solar mode (reports mode 'solar_sys')
    start_scan_planet                   the device's OWN acquisition. ~45 s to lock.
    capture, find the disc, compare mount RA/Dec against ephemeris
Use the vendor's acquisition. Do NOT hand-roll a slew toward the Sun and do NOT bypass SunGuard.

Measured error series across one alignment session, each point a full re-acquisition:
    dRA   -3.034 -> -4.403 -> -2.594 -> -1.350 -> -0.705
    dDec  -0.268 -> -0.435 -> -0.419 -> -0.291 -> -0.501
The error is almost entirely in RA. That matches July's independent plate solve (3.7 deg azimuth,
0.2 deg altitude) and is the signature this whole epic exists to remove.

=== FOUR GOTCHAS, ALL PAID FOR TODAY ===

1. THE SCAN DOES NOT CENTRE THE DISC. Measured offsets from frame centre across five
   acquisitions: 0.316, 0.030, 0.124, 0.350, 0.030 deg. So the raw mount-vs-ephemeris difference
   carries up to a third of a degree of slop. MEASURE THE DISC CENTROID IN THE FRAME and correct
   for it, or the loop stalls around 0.3 deg with no way to tell error from framing. Below about
   0.3 deg this correction is the difference between converging and thrashing.

2. THE FILTER CHECK MUST BE SATURATION AND ABSOLUTE MEAN, NOT STRUCTURE. Three false aborts today
   from structure-based tests: a flat pedestal read as transmitted light, a changed exposure
   regime raised the noise floor, and the Sun's halo just outside the frame produced a gradient.
   The invariant that cannot be fooled is that an unfiltered aperture pointed near the Sun
   saturates catastrophically. Check mean against the known unfiltered value and check saturation
   fraction. Reference numbers at one fixed exposure: unfiltered sky 93.8, filtered 3.97, shutter
   closed 0.94; with the Sun in frame and filter on, mean stays ~26 with 1-4% saturation.

3. CLOUD STOPS IT DEAD. Twice today the scan ran its full search without locking because the disc
   was behind thin cloud (preflight sky brightness rose from 27 to 37 as it thickened). Detect
   this and say 'cloud, waiting' rather than reporting a failure. Note the Moon differential
   technique worked through heavy smoke at 0.45% contrast, so a differential fallback would be
   more robust than the vendor scan — see terminus-41.

4. scope_move_to_horizon RETURNS code 0 AND MOVES NOTHING. Verified today while the scope was
   pointed at the Sun, which is the worst place for a park command to lie. Verify by readback and
   move away with an explicit goto whose Sun separation grows monotonically. This is the fifth
   command in this project to report success while doing nothing.

=== NIGHT USES THE SAME LOOP ===
Stars or a plate solve replace the Sun; everything downstream is identical. Building it solar-first
is correct because daylight is the case nothing currently covers.

title: The alignment interface: what the person actually sees
description:
The surface of the guided alignment loop (terminus-45). This is the part that makes it usable by
someone who is standing outside with one hand on the mount.

=== DESIGN CONSTRAINT: THE SOFTWARE KNOWS NOTHING ABOUT THE HARDWARE ===

Devon: 'don't assume thumb screws, that's specific to my wedge.' So the interface reports
REMAINING ERROR IN DEGREES and updates it live while the mount moves. The user stops when it
reaches zero. Thumb screws, knobs, a worm drive, a sliding plate or shoving the tripod are all
identical to the software, and no wedge model, screw pitch or degrees-per-turn table is needed.

That is not a compromise, it is the better design: today's manual session measured this wedge at
about 0.45 deg per half turn and the figure drifted (0.456, 0.452, 0.415) because the human was
not being precise. The closed loop absorbed it completely — every iteration moved the right way
and converged. A calibrated open-loop instruction would have been worse.

=== WHAT IT SHOWS ===
  * CURRENT ERROR, split by axis, in the terms the user is adjusting: azimuth and elevation, not
    dRA and dDec. Convert before display.
  * WHICH WAY TO TURN, in plain words, with the caveat that the sign is only known after the
    first solve — do not guess it up front (Claude guessed it today and was wrong).
  * A LIVE NUMBER while they move, from the fast channel (terminus-45.1), clearly marked as an
    estimate.
  * WHEN THE ESTIMATE IS STALE and a re-solve is needed, and how long that takes (~45 s).
  * HOW GOOD IS GOOD ENOUGH. Below about 0.3 deg the disc-centring scatter dominates unless the
    centroid correction is in (terminus-45.2). Say so rather than letting someone chase noise
    with a wedge bolt for an hour.

=== WHAT IT MUST REFUSE TO DO ===
  * never show a confident number derived from the magnetometer's absolute bearing;
  * never proceed toward the Sun without the filter check passing, and the check is saturation
    and absolute mean, not structure (terminus-45.2 gotcha 2);
  * never claim convergence from a single reading — today two consecutive acquisitions agreed to
    0.17 deg, which is what makes a reading believable.

=== SHAPE ===
terminus is a CLI, so the first version is a CLI: a loop that prints the error, waits, re-solves
on a keypress, and exits when the user is satisfied. That is enough to be useful and is what
today's manual session was, minus the human transcribing numbers between tool calls. A richer
surface can come later; nothing here depends on it.

Sequence note for the run itself: elevation first (the accelerometer reads it absolutely and
continuously, so it can be closed out without any celestial fix at all), then azimuth (which
needs the slow channel for truth). That ordering means the user does the easy axis while waiting
for the sky.
notes:
DESIGN CORRECTED 2026-08-04, and the correction matters more than the feature.

I proposed 'the human does coarse acquisition, software does the rest' on the grounds that a
person can see the Sun and no sensor on the mount can. Devon tried it: 'human doing coarse
correction sucked and I still see trails, I don't want to do that again.'

AFTERIMAGES. The design put a person's eyesight in the acquisition loop. That is not an
inconvenience to be weighed against convergence time — it is disqualifying. THE HUMAN MUST NEVER
BE ASKED TO LOOK AT OR TOWARD THE SUN. Remove it from the design entirely.

=== SOFTWARE DOES COARSE ACQUISITION. THE METHOD IS SKY BRIGHTNESS. ===
Through the solar filter, scattered sky brightness rises monotonically toward the Sun over tens
of degrees. Measured today: mean ~22-24 far away, 27-28 within a few degrees, 32-40 closer. That
is a usable direction signal THAT DOES NOT REQUIRE THE DISC TO BE IN FRAME.

    1. bound the search with the sensors — accelerometer gives elevation absolutely
       (terminus-45.1), compass gives azimuth to about +/-11 deg
    2. hill-climb on sky brightness at 5-10 DEGREE steps until it stops improving
    3. fine grid at ~0.6 deg to catch the disc
    4. scope_sync (terminus-41). Done — goto works from then on.
Roughly six minutes of unattended slewing, and nobody looks at anything.

WHY MY FIRST HILL CLIMB FAILED, so it is not repeated: I used 0.018 deg steps, which sampled
noise rather than a gradient, and I ran it while cloud was moving, which changes brightness
independently of pointing. Coarse steps in stable conditions have neither problem. Check for
cloud by re-measuring a reference direction periodically; if it has changed, the gradient is
untrustworthy.

=== THE JOYSTICK IS NOT IN THE LOOP ===
scope_speed_move rates measured today: ~7.5 deg/s at speed 200, ~0.009 deg/s at speed 10. A
factor of 800 in rate for 20 in speed, with nothing usable between — fast overshoots by degrees,
slow takes minutes to cross a field. Devon, after driving it manually: 'the joystick sucks', 'I
shot past it a dozen times'. Use scope_goto, which is exact once the mount is synced. Intermediate
speeds (50, 100) are untested and might be fine, but goto makes the question moot.

title: Manual slew control: scope_speed_move, and what the numbers actually mean
description:
Measured 2026-08-04 during the solar alignment session. These are protocol facts that cost real
time to learn and are not documented anywhere terminus can reach.

=== scope_speed_move ===
    {"method":"scope_speed_move","params":{"speed":N,"angle":DEG,"dur_sec":S}}
angle is a direction; speed and dur_sec set how far. The Alpaca collection ships two presets that
are really the two joystick modes in the app:
    fast:  speed 1000, dur_sec 4
    slow:  speed 10,   dur_sec 1

MEASURED RATE: speed 200 for dur_sec 2 moved the mount roughly 15 DEGREES. That is about
7.5 deg/s at speed 200. Two of those, intended as 'small probes', walked the scope 31 deg off
target and cost the rest of the session's acquisitions. If the relationship is linear, speed 10
for dur_sec 1 should give roughly 0.4 deg — which is the granularity fine centring wants, but
VERIFY IT rather than trusting the extrapolation.

Devon: 'joystick has two modes, fast and slow, and I left it on fast' — so the app's mode
selection is just which speed value it sends. There is no separate mode flag to read, which means
a caller has no way to know what regime it is in except by measuring. Always measure the step
before relying on it.

=== start_scan_planet SEARCHES AROUND WHERE THE SCOPE ALREADY IS ===
It does not slew to the target first. Five acquisitions succeeded today when the scope started
within a few degrees of the Sun; three failed outright after the scope had been left 31 deg away,
and a plain scope_goto to the Sun's ephemeris position did not put the disc in frame either. So
the sequence is: get close by whatever means, THEN scan. Treat the scan as a fine acquisition,
not a search.

=== WHY THIS MATTERS FOR terminus-45.2 ===
The alignment loop's measurement floor is set by how well the disc is centred — measured offsets
across five acquisitions were 0.316, 0.030, 0.124, 0.350 and 0.030 deg, and that scatter is what
stops convergence below about 0.3 deg. Slow nudges at ~0.4 deg per step would let the loop CENTRE
the disc deliberately rather than accepting where the scan drops it, removing the centring term
from the error budget entirely. That is a better method than the one written up earlier and
should be folded into terminus-45.2.

=== ALSO WORTH KNOWING ===
Sky brightness is a usable coarse proximity signal to the Sun through a solar filter: measured
means ran ~13-22 when far away and ~27-28 when within a few degrees. Weak, but it is enough to
hill-climb on when no disc is visible. Do not expect it to work through thick cloud — three
acquisition attempts failed today with the disc behind cloud, and the brightness gradient
vanished with it.

title: Calibrate the focuser: infinity focus, the near limit, and step-to-distance
description:
terminus-32 claims the focuser step count is a distance measurement, and calls it possibly
novel — no horizon mask found in the prior-art sweeps carries distance. The claim is currently
resting on a single anecdote (step 1838 read as 'roof at about 40 m') and on an assumed
infinity-focus position. Both need measuring before the claim goes in a paper.

Measuring it on 2026-08-04 evening also turned out to matter operationally, not just for the
paper: an entire evening of columns would not focus because they pointed at Devon's own house
at a steep angle, which is inside the scope's minimum focus distance. Contrast rose
monotonically to max_step_range and never turned over. Without a calibrated near limit there is
no principled way to tell that case from a focus failure, and the loop will hunt.

WHAT TO MEASURE, cheapest first:

  1. INFINITY FOCUS. Autofocus on a star field and record get_focuser_position. This is the
     anchor the whole curve hangs off, and it is one autofocus run. Everything below is
     uncalibrated guesswork until this number exists.

  2. STEP SIZE IN MICRONS. Either from ZWO's EAF spec or by focusing on two targets at known
     distances and solving. The working assumption of ~4.6 um/step is inferred, not looked up.

  3. THE NEAR LIMIT. Predicted from o - f = f^2 / extension with f = 250 mm, then confirmed by
     walking a target inward until contrast stops turning over inside the travel. The estimate
     of ~12 m is only as good as assumption 1.

  4. WHERE THE CURVE GOES FLAT. Beyond some distance the step count stops discriminating,
     because f^2/(o-f) shrinks below the ~7-step depth of focus. That distance is the upper
     bound of the useful band and is computable once 1 and 2 exist — likely a few hundred
     metres, which would mean a treeline reports 'far', not a distance.

THEN RECORD IT AS A BAND, NOT A NUMBER. Outside [near limit, flat point] the step count
saturates and carries a bound rather than a distance. The mask already has the right shape for
this in blocked_above (terminus-7) — a censored observation, honestly labelled. Reusing it
keeps one concept instead of inventing a second.

Feeds the distance half of terminus-32, the near-field caveat in terminus-24 (lidar DSM
comparison is least trustworthy exactly where objects are close), and the seasonality question
in terminus-13.

title: find_horizon fits the skyglow model to terrain, then cannot see the terrain
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-04 on az 60, a column with a 103-count cliff at alt 36.46 that is obvious by
eye in the profile. find_horizon returns None, 'open to the search floor'. It misses an edge
that could hardly be more visible.

MECHANISM, and there are three defects stacked, not one.

fit_skyglow is handed the WHOLE column, terrain included, so the terrain sets the slope. On az 60
it returns slope 4.244 counts/deg, intercept -55.115 — a model that predicts NEGATIVE sky
brightness below alt 13. From there:

  1. pred falls as fast as the real terrain does, so lums/pred never departs. The whole premise
     of the test is that the model describes sky; fitted this way it describes the column.

  2. At the true edge the ratio DOES trip: frac = 0.496 against MIN_DROP_FRAC = 0.5. It clears by
     0.004. The persistence check then computes median(frac below) = 0.536, decides it did not
     stay down, and discards the correct answer. The right answer was found and thrown away.

  3. Where pred crosses zero, frac = 421.836 (pred = 0.06). Below that the `pred > 1e-6` guard
     clamps frac to exactly 1.0 — so the DEEPEST TERRAIN SCORES AS PERFECT SKY. This is the worst
     of the three: the further into the ground the column goes, the more sky-like it looks, and
     the 421 poisons any median taken across it.

    alt   lum     pred    frac
     39  160.83  110.41  1.457
     37  148.58  101.92  1.458
     35   46.36   93.43  0.496  <- true edge, trips by 0.004, then discarded
     33   45.49   84.94  0.536
     13   24.58    0.06  421.836  <- divide-by-almost-zero
     11   24.33   -8.43  1.000  <- negative pred, clamped: terrain reads as sky
      3   23.13  -42.38  1.000

THE FIX IS SMALL: fit the model to the TOP of the column only, which is the part known to be sky,
rather than to everything. Verified on both az 60 profiles:

    coarse (2 deg steps)     slope -0.936  intercept 197.27  -> edge 35.00, persists
    fine   (0.25 deg steps)  slope  4.390  intercept -35.53  -> edge 36.25, persists

against 36.46 measured by hand. Coarse lands within one 2 deg step, fine within one 0.25 deg step.
A negative intercept, or any pred <= 0 inside the search range, should also be treated as a failed
fit rather than silently clamped — an unphysical model must not return a confident answer.

WHY THIS IS P0. Earlier this session find_horizon with sky_ref = 40 was shown to reproduce the
published column table EXACTLY, which means this is the function behind the current mask, and it
reproduces the table's errors along with its numbers. Six of the sixteen columns in
horizon_mask.yaml sit at exactly 35.0 — the search ceiling — and none of them are measurements.
Whether this defect manufactured them needs checking directly; the failure mode above (terrain
absorbed into the model, then unreadable) is exactly the shape that would.

Related but distinct: terminus-14 is the same class of error in sweep.find_edge, whose noise
estimate counts the sky gradient as noise. Both come from fitting a statistic over a region that
includes the thing being detected. Worth fixing together and testing together.

REGRESSION TEST IS ALREADY ON DISK, no observing needed: captures/2026-08-04-focus/focus_cols/
az60_coarse.json and az60_fine.json, both with the answer known independently.

comments.author: Devon Jones
comments.text:
SECOND REQUIREMENT FOR THE FIX, from az 190 measured the same night. The sky-only model fit
described above is necessary but not sufficient; this column shows why.

az 190 has THREE persistent drops against a 65.63 count sky reference, at alt 38 (62.88 -> 32.66),
alt 26 (38.78 -> 27.66) and alt 21 (36.26 -> 21.75). Every one of them 'stays down' — none recovers
— so the persistence test alone accepts all three. Only alt 38 is a SKY boundary; the other two are
different faces of the house, and the level immediately above each is already ~38 counts, i.e.
already far below sky.

So persistence is not enough on a multi-level column. The missing test: A BOUNDARY IS A SKY
BOUNDARY ONLY IF THE LEVEL ABOVE IT IS STILL SKY. Checking 'is the level above >= some fraction of
the absolute sky_ref' at EACH candidate cleanly keeps alt 38 and rejects 26 and 21.

find_horizon already takes sky_ref and already uses it correctly — but only ONCE, at the top of the
column, to decide whether the column is blocked above the ceiling. The same reference needs
applying per candidate. That is a few lines on top of the fit change, and without it the fix will
still return 21 or 26 on this column depending on threshold.

Consequence if left unfixed: a horizon 12-17 deg too low at azimuths with layered structure, which
is every azimuth pointing at a building. Reported as a confident number, not a bound.

Regression fixture on disk with the answer known independently:
captures/2026-08-04-focus/focus_cols/az190_recheck.json (1 deg, full column, all three drops
present) and az190_fine.json (0.25 deg through the real boundary). Correct answer 38.59.

title: orient.from_mask matches type strings no writer has ever produced
description:
FOUND 2026-08-05 by a reviewer during PR #15, out of that PR's diff. Predates it — introduced in PR #1 and orient.py has not been touched since.

orient.from_mask selects fiducials by checking type == 'edge' and type.startswith('blocked'). No writer in the codebase produces either string. Every real mask carries tree, structure, open, '' or unknown: obstruction_type emits tree/structure/open/'' and cli._type_name emits tree/structure/''. Fed a real mask, from_mask returns ZERO fiducials, always. It cannot fail loudly because returning nothing is a legal outcome.

WHY IT HAS NOT BITTEN. The live calibration path builds fiducials through plan.as_fiducial, not through from_mask. from_mask's only other reference is the worked example in __init__.py's module docstring — which is therefore documentation for a function that cannot work, and is the more damaging half: someone following it gets an empty fit and no error.

FIX: either map from_mask onto the vocabulary that exists, or delete it and correct the docstring example to show as_fiducial. Deleting is defensible; a second path into the fit that nothing uses is a liability, and the reviewer's point stands that a function returning zero results for every real input is not a function anyone is relying on.

Reproduce: build any mask with export.write_mask, call orient.from_mask on it, count the fiducials.

title: An unnamed column loses the vegetation buffer it probably deserves
description:
RAISED 2026-08-05 by a reviewer during PR #15, as a reasoned view rather than a regression. Not introduced by that PR and deliberately not fixed in it.

export.apply_tree_buffer raises columns whose type is tree/vegetation/plant. A column with an EMPTY type gets no margin.

Before PR #15 a night column was mislabelled 'structure', which also got no buffer, so the exported result is unchanged and this is not a regression. But the argument PR #15 makes for the empty type cuts the other way here: an unnamed column is most often a TREE measured at night, because that is exactly when colour typing fails. So the export is optimistic precisely where the ticket's own reasoning says it should be pessimistic, and apply_tree_buffer is live code that runs on every export — unlike boundary_model, which is still dead.

The buffer exists because planning tools take the horizon literally: N.I.N.A. will start a run at an altitude the mask calls clear. Around foliage that confidence is not warranted.

THIS NEEDS A DECISION, NOT A PATCH. Three options, and they are not equivalent:
  (a) Buffer unnamed columns as if vegetation. Safe for planning, but it silently invents a type for export purposes, which is the habit terminus-13 exists to break.
  (b) Leave them unbuffered and make the mask say so — the header already explains that empty means unnamed. Honest, but it ships the optimistic horizon.
  (c) Buffer them and record that the margin was applied on an ASSUMPTION rather than on a measured type, so the file admits what it did.

(c) is the only one that is both safe and honest, and it costs a field. Devon's call — it is a judgement about what a horizon file is FOR, not a code question.

title: sweep --azimuths: scan an explicit list of columns
description: Add 'terminus sweep --azimuths 55,57,82,172' to measure a specific list instead of a uniform az-start/az-end range, merging results into an existing mask rather than replacing it. Required by the panorama-planning workflow (terminus-4 step 5): the plan is a list of interesting azimuths, and today sweep can only walk a uniform grid. Also useful for re-measuring the columns that came back as floors or unresolved.
acceptance_criteria: sweep --azimuths accepts a comma list, scans only those, and merges into --out if it already exists, preserving columns not re-measured.
close_reason:
Merged as PR #14 (9003f85). terminus sweep --azimuths 55,57,82 measures an explicit column list and merges into an existing --out rather than replacing it.

Four review rounds. What they found, because the merge turned out to be the hard part rather than the column list:

- Merging true-north scope columns into an unoriented photo mask, or across a tripod move, was unguarded. _check_mergeable now refuses both.
- meta.update() let a two-column patch describe the whole file: a patch that skipped nothing overwrote skipped_az [190,195] with [] while those columns stayed absent. The record of WHY was destroyed.
- The position check compared one degree threshold against both lat and lon, which is not one distance — a degree of longitude shrinks by cos(lat), making the east-west test 23 per cent tighter. Now compares metres.
- A mask with no recorded position merged silently, and the merged file was positionless too, so the hole propagated to every later patch.
- skipped_az: "190" iterated to the characters 1, 9, 0 — three wrong columns recorded as skipped, silently.
- A column measured in one patch and Sun-blocked in the next went back onto skipped_az while horizon: still held its altitude.
- Antimeridian: two points 2 m apart read as 39,466 km.

Every fix mutation-checked. 146 tests.

title: Sun guard: goto could fail silently (fixed, needs commit)
description:
FOUND AND FIXED LIVE 2026-08-03 while validating terminus-3 with the Sun above the horizon.

BUG: Pointer._goto_wait polled until GOTO_TIMEOUT and then FELL THROUGH SILENTLY. point_to then returned whatever the scope's current position happened to be, and the CLI printed it as a successful landing. Observed for real: with the arm closed, 'terminus point 90 30' reported 'landed az 179.9 alt -39.9' while the mount had not moved at all.

WHY THIS IS SAFETY-CRITICAL, not cosmetic: every Sun-safety guarantee is planned from the believed current position. If a slew silently fails to arrive, the next path is computed from a position the mount never reached — so the guard can authorise a path that actually sweeps somewhere else entirely. This is the same class of failure as the incident that swept the scope past the Sun.

FIX APPLIED to src/terminus/sweep.py:
  * new PointingError exception
  * _goto_wait now returns only on confirmed arrival, and otherwise raises PointingError naming the wanted and actual RA/Dec plus the likely cause (closed / parked / not tracking)
  * added Pointer._moving() (reads mount.move_type) and the deadline EXTENDS while the mount is demonstrably still slewing — a long RA swing can outlast any fixed timeout, and giving up mid-slew is the dangerous case because the scope keeps moving after we stop watching
  * GOTO_TIMEOUT raised 35 -> 90 s (a real ~118 deg RA slew took longer than 35 s and was being reported as a failure)
  * cli.py catches PointingError, prints 'POINTING FAILED: ...' and exits 2

VALIDATED LIVE: with the arm closed it now refuses loudly instead of lying; with the arm open, 'point 90 30' completed and preflight confirmed az 90.3 alt 30.4. 16 tests pass, ruff clean.

STATUS: code is edited in the working tree but NOT COMMITTED. Needs a commit (and ideally a regression test that a non-arriving goto raises rather than returns).
close_reason: PR #1: _goto_wait raises PointingError on non-arrival and tests arrival by angular separation, not raw RA. PR #1 follow-ups added the miss counter and partial-sweep recovery.

title: Mask: record per-column search ceiling, treat blocked_above as a bound
description:
DESIGN (Devon, 2026-08-03): 'report the top of the column being used, and clamp to that, that way we CAN use 60 degree columns from today'.

PROBLEM. The mask records the search ceiling once, in meta.alt_search, and stores a capped column as {alt: 35.0, type: 'blocked>35'} — a value that LOOKS like a measurement but is really a lower bound. Two consequences:
  1. Merging masks from sessions with different ceilings loses which columns were bounded at what. Last night ran a 35 deg ceiling; tonight runs 60. A merged file cannot express that.
  2. Capped columns were being DISCARDED from the photo-vs-scope fit entirely, throwing away real agreement: if the scope says '>=60' and the photo says 61, those agree exactly.

FIX. Every column carries its own ceiling, and a capped column is stored as a bound:
    {az: 0, bound: 60.0, type: 'blocked_above', ceiling: 60.0}   # horizon >= 60
    {az: 80, alt: 22.5, type: 'edge', ceiling: 60.0}             # exact
Downstream code clamps each fiducial to ITS OWN ceiling rather than a global one.

RESIDUAL RULE IS ONE-SIDED, NOT PLAIN CLAMPING. For a censored column the residual is 0 when the photo also exceeds the ceiling, and (photo - ceiling) only when the photo falls BELOW it. Naive two-sided clamping is wrong and actively harmful: it also clamps EXACT columns, which hides genuine disagreement — at az 40 the scope measured 32.5 exactly while the photo said 61.4, and clamping turned that 29 deg error into 2.5 deg and produced a flattering RMS 1.48.

MEASURED EFFECT (2026-08-03, SegFormer mosaic vs scope fiducials):
  exact edges only (10)                RMS 2.76  yaw 136.50
  + tonight censored at 60 (14)        RMS 2.60  yaw 136.50   <- yaw UNCHANGED
  (for contrast, earlier bad variants: two-sided clamp -> yaw 138.50; one-sided with a single global ceiling of 35 -> yaw 143.25)
The point is not the RMS but the STABILITY: adding four strong '>=60' bounds pinned yaw where 10 fiducials alone left it drifting across 135-143 deg. Bounds constrain the fit even though they contain no exact value.

Per-column agreement with tonight's data: az 0 (photo 61.2), az 10 (65.6), az 20 (64.6) all satisfy '>=60' exactly; az 30 falls 4.3 deg short (55.7) and is a specific, testable disagreement worth a targeted re-measure.

ALSO: scan frames are named by the REQUESTED azimuth, not the one actually used. With pole avoidance now nudging azimuth (az 0 alt 40 is measured at az 3.0 at this latitude), the filename az000_alt040 is misleading. Record the actual az/alt used, per frame and per column.
close_reason: PR #1: Fiducial carries a per-column ceiling and a bound flag; orient.residuals scores bounds one-sided. plan.as_fiducial turns a no-edge column into a bound rather than dropping it.

title: A too-low search ceiling can manufacture false edges
description:
FOUND 2026-08-03 by comparing two sweeps of the same site at different ceilings.

OBSERVATION. Azimuth 40:
  2026-08-02 sweep, ceiling 35 deg -> alt 32.5, type 'edge'   (looks like a clean measurement)
  2026-08-03 sweep, ceiling 60 deg -> alt 48.8, type 'edge', SNR 6.14
A 16 deg disagreement between the same scope at the same azimuth.

DIAGNOSIS. Tonight's value is the credible one and last night's is an ARTIFACT. If the true horizon is 48.8, then last night's entire search range (0-35) lay INSIDE the obstruction: every sample dark. The correct output was 'blocked_above', but find_edge fitted a step to brightness variation WITHIN the terrain and reported it as an edge with apparently adequate SNR. Supporting evidence from the gradient: az 30 is >60 and az 80 is 22.5, so 48.8 at az 40 fits that descent and 32.5 does not.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE COLUMN. The 2026-08-02 mask has been used all day as the ground-truth fiducial set for every photo-to-sky fit. If a too-low ceiling can manufacture false edges, some of those 10 fiducials are wrong — which plausibly explains the fit instability seen repeatedly (yaw wandering 135-143 deg across reasonable treatments) and why az 40 was a persistent outlier at +4.8 to +10.7 deg under every variant.

DATA POLICY (Devon): 'once we have good columns for today, we can toss the ones from yesterday, which were missing data we have for these columns now.' The general rule is NOT 'prefer newer'. It is:
  * a column is TRUSTWORTHY when its result is comfortably below the ceiling it was scanned with
  * a column that reached its ceiling is a BOUND, not a value
  * when two sweeps disagree, prefer the one whose ceiling exceeded its own result
  * a column whose result equals its ceiling should never be stored as type 'edge'

FIX DIRECTIONS:
  1. find_edge should refuse to report an edge when the profile shows no sky at ANY sampled altitude — a column with no bright end has no sky/terrain transition to find, whatever steps exist inside it. Probably a test on the profile maximum against the sky reference, not just on step SNR.
  2. Store the ceiling per column (see the per-column-ceiling ticket) so this is detectable after the fact rather than only by re-measuring.
  3. Consider re-scanning any column from an older mask whose alt is within ~5 deg of that sweep's ceiling; those are the ones most likely to be artifacts.
close_reason: PR #1: orient.fit takes min_headroom and drops exact fiducials sitting too close to their own ceiling, which is the signature of a manufactured edge.

title: Orientation fit: use exact rotation, not the small-angle sinusoid
description:
RAISED BY DEVON 2026-08-03: 'RMS may morph the photo's shape'. Correct, and quantified.

CURRENT MODEL. The photo horizon is corrected by alt - (c0 + A*cos az + B*sin az). That is a FIRST-ORDER approximation to a rigid rotation of the sphere. To first order it can only re-orient the horizon, not reshape it — but the higher-order term is not always negligible.

MEASURED APPROXIMATION ERROR (approx minus exact rotation, max over azimuth):
  tilt  4.8 deg (Mode A as fitted): 0.04 deg at alt 10, 0.11 at alt 30, 0.34 at alt 60
  tilt 12.0 deg (Devon's deliberate pano tilt): 0.23 / 0.73 / 2.19
  tilt 20.0 deg: 0.68 / 2.05 / 6.10

WHY THIS MATTERS DESPITE MODE A BEING FINE. The error grows with BOTH tilt and altitude, and Mode B's documented instruction is to tilt up so the horizon sits inside the frame — the 14.15.23 panorama carried ~12 deg of intentional tilt. At alt 60 that is a 2.2 deg distortion, comparable to the whole RMS budget (2.2-2.8 deg), and it falls exactly on the tall tree, the feature that actually costs targets. The approximation degrades precisely in the configuration the tool tells users to produce.

FIX. Replace the sinusoid with a true rotation: build the unit vector from (az, alt), apply a rotation matrix about the horizontal axis perpendicular to the tilt direction, read altitude back from the z component. Same three parameters (pitch, tiltA, tiltB -> magnitude + direction), no approximation, error zero at any tilt. Prototype verified in scratchpad.

SECOND, INDEPENDENT ISSUE — OUTLIERS TIP THE WHOLE SPHERE. A rigid rotation cannot invent a bend in the horizon, but it can tip everything, so a single bad fiducial drags the global solution. This is not hypothetical: az 40 from the 2026-08-02 mask is very likely a false edge (see the too-low-ceiling ticket), and plain least squares will happily rotate the sphere to reduce its residual, corrupting every other azimuth. Use a robust loss (Huber or trimmed least squares) or explicit outlier rejection, and report per-fiducial leverage so a dominant point is visible rather than silent.
close_reason: PR #1: orient.rotate is an exact rotation. Review then found it was still not exact — residuals sampled the photo at az-yaw and scored it against az, which is wrong for tilt — fixed by native_column solving for the column that actually lands at the fiducial.
